channel.title: BBC News — Most read
channel.description: Stories discovered in BBC News' Most read list, retained after they leave. Unofficial feed.

item.title: New Zealand's ruling coalition falls short of parliamentary majority by one seat
item.description: The right-leaning ruling bloc led by the National Party has fallen short of the majority needed to govern.
item.content:encoded:
New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters.

It now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.

The incumbent National Party led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon secured 40 out of 130 seats, while its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First took 13 and 12 respectively.

A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not possible, official results on Friday show, as the bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity threw its weight behind it.

Luxon on Friday acknowledged that negotiations "may be challenging" and will take some time.

"Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls," he told reporters.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said his party "ran an incredible campaign" but acknowledged that it doesn't have negotiating power despite winning the popular vote. "More New Zealanders voted for change at this election than for the status quo," he said.

New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each person casts two votes – one for their preferred political party and another for their choice of local representative.

Labour secured 36 seats, The Greens took 17, while Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, picked up five.

Opportunity, which has been described as this election's kingmaker, secured seven seats. Opportunity's leader Qiulae Wong told reporters her party will negotiate with National, but that all options remain on the table.

"There are seven parties in parliment and everyone is responsible for making sure we do everything we can to deliver a stable government for New Zealand. It's not just up to us," she said on Friday.

Preliminary results on 7 November, election day, had projected that National combined with its coalition partners would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc.

But today's official tally shows it had lost two seats on special votes - cast by citizens who were overseas or outside of their registered electorate on election day - which typically skew left.

Some of National's key election pledges include lower taxes, cheaper energy, more renewable generation, and a greater focus on defence.

Labour, meanwhile, had campaigned to cut healthcare, public transport and fuel costs, more government support for social housing, among other things.

In earlier interviews with the BBC, many voters had expressed frustration over spiralling costs of living and high unemployment across the country, with declining faith in their political leadership.

"There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread," said 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger.

A 40-year-old man said he didn't vote as he could not bring himself to tick any of the boxes on the ballot paper.

More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to a survey by the Helen Clark Foundation, a public policy think tank.

Kiwis have been leaving the country in record numbers, with many of them, including former prime minister Jacinda Arden, moving to Australia.

item.title: US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough, Zelensky tells BBC
item.description: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is "strange" Trump has described Vladimir Putin as a friend.
item.content:encoded:
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying that delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough during peace talks.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president also said it was "strange" that Donald Trump had posted a picture of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend".

"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, suggesting it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during WWII.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.

Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".

But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.

And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.

The Kremlin appears to be resisting.

Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.

Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.

So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".

"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.

The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.

In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.

Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.

Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.

But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Amercians were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.

"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.

"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."

He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.

So whose decision was that?

"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."

Tough winter

Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.

On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.

Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".

He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.

He declined to be more specific.

But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.

Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.

Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.

They have also plunged much of the city into darkness.

"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.

"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

item.title: Jason Arday research for Queen's University cleared in investigation
item.description: The 41-year-old was found dead in August following weeks of media coverage over plagiarism allegations and questions about his achievements, which he denied.
item.content:encoded:
Research by academic Jason Arday, who was accused of plagiarism before his death, has been cleared by one of the institutions that was investigating him.

Queen's University Belfast (QUB) began looking into Jason Arday's work after he resigned from his University of Cambridge roles.

The university had published a paper on its academic research site co-authored by Arday and other academics from Queen's.

In a statement, a spokesperson for QUB said: "Having reviewed the matter, we are satisfied that the paper meets the appropriate academic standards and have no concerns regarding its publication."

The paper, published in 2021, was corrected in 2024 to clarify that it used methodologies similar to a previous study Arday had written, which in turn had been based on another research paper published in 2016 by a team of academics at Brighton and Sussex Medical School.

Arday, who became Cambridge's youngest black professor in 2023, was found dead in Battersea on 14 August, having resigned as a professor of sociology of education the week prior.

The 41-year-old's death followed weeks of media coverage over plagiarism allegations and questions about his achievements. He denied the claims. An inquest into his death is under way.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham described the death of the former professor as "a tragedy on so many levels".

Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher and self-defined "race realist".

Cofnas has previously written that black people are less intelligent than other groups and would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment" under a meritocratic system.

He claimed on the online publishing platform Substack that he had put Arday's work through a plagiarism detection software, which found that "many passages are lifted with minimal editing, sometimes retaining copy-editing mistakes from the original source".

Following Arday's death, Cofnas was suspended from his post at Ghent University, after it launched an investigation into him "for discriminating against" the former Cambridge professor. He was later handed a three-month teaching ban.

Public figures and friends of Arday had called for a public inquiry into media coverage surrounding the former professor before his death.

Labour MP Diane Abbott and actress Jameela Jamil were among 30,000 signatories of a letter to the prime minister, which claims Arday's death followed "two weeks of relentless harassment".

The University of Cambridge launched a two-part independent review examining the support available to Arday before his death, as well as the wider context of his time at the university.

Liverpool John Moores University - which awarded Arday his PhD in 2015 - concluded that he had not plagiarised work.

Other institutions including Glasgow University, Durham University and Queen's University Belfast all began investigating Arday's work or his appointments to various positions.

Back in August, Queen's University said it was "looking into" a paper, published in 2021, on the impact of what was taught in universities on "Black, Asian and Minority Ethnic (BAME) learners" and "academics of colour".

The paper was called "Attempting to break the chain: Reimaging inclusive pedagogy and decolonising the curriculum within the academy".

item.title: Major Thanksgiving storm brings flooding, flight delays across US
item.description: Almost one million customers in the US had no power on Thursday evening as storms descended on both US coasts, bringing wind gusts, heavy rain and flooding.
item.content:encoded:
A massive Thanksgiving storm hammering the Midwest and north-east with heavy rain and winds, along with high tides out west, is causing widespread disruptions across the US.

More than 80 million Americans expected to be travelling this week. More than 400 flights in the US were cancelled on Thursday and another 2,200 flights into, out of, or within the US were delayed, tracking site FlightAware said.

The FAA has previously warned that delays would be possible "throughout the week" as a result of the rain and wind that are forecast.

Meanwhile, almost one million households were without power on Thursday night, with Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia the hardest hit states.

On Thursday, a powerful storm hit the eastern US, bringing damaging winds of up to 70mph, torrential rain, and major coastal flooding.

New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency as several communities along the Jersey Shore saw widespread flooding.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul also declared a state of emergency for New York City, Long Island and Westchester County.

In New York City, organisers of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have postponed the event to Saturday.

Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds and waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk.

In Maryland, almost two million customers have been asked by the water utility to use water for essential use only due to "intermittent power disruptions".

On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport, according to the National Water Prediction Service.

More than 980,000 households were reporting power outages by Thursday evening, with Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey hit particularly hard.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said that utility providers were working tirelessly to restore power. Meanwhile, energy companies in Virginia and New Jersey warned it may take some time, even days, for power to return, as crews had to wait until it was safe to access damaged areas.

On Thursday afternoon, President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds for the east coast as it faces down the holiday storm.

Across the US, severe weather is also descending on the West Coast. The NWS has warned of a series of Pacific storms that are expected to bring rain, mountain snow and strong winds.

Many are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak along the coast.

Water levels along California's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Thursday, according to the NWS, breaking records set just last month.

Both San Diego and Los Angeles reported a high tide of over 8ft earlier in the week, and beach-goers were advised to avoid coastal areas.

Train services along the Amtrak Pacific Surfliner, which runs along the California coastline, cancelled several trains due to "washout conditions from high tides", the company shared on social media.

Storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia.

In Miami, some travel delays persisted into Thursday after a FedEx plane overshot the runway the night before, which prompted the closure of all but one runway at the airport for a brief period.

A statement FedEx provided to US media confirmed that one of its flights had "experienced an issue upon landing".

It added: "We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA."

An airport employee who spoke anonymously to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, raised the possibility that rainy conditions had been a factor.

"They tried as hard as they could to stop, but I don't know if it was the weather because the rain and the wind were really bad, and they just couldn't stop in time and went right off the runway and veered off into the grass," they said.

Wednesday's incident in Miami came 11 weeks after a cargo plane crashed on landing at the same airport, killing five people and injuring five others in vehicles on the ground with which it collided.

The American Automobile Association (AAA) predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for the Thanksgiving holiday over a seven-day period.

Rebecka Pieder contributed reporting.

item.title: Asia made a big AI bet on Nvidia. What happens now?
item.description: Asian stocks have been on a rollercoaster ride after Jensen Huang's shock return as Nvidia CEO.
item.content:encoded:
Jensen Huang's extraordinary return as Nvidia's boss rocked not only its shares in New York but also sent shockwaves through the artificial intelligence (AI) industry around the world.

Those jolts were felt particularly in Asia as the saga highlighted the region's huge exposure to the technology.

Tech-heavy stock indexes in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan went on a rollercoaster ride this week. Markets soared after a near-trillion dollar surge in Nvidia's share price but then slumped as concerns about political and regulatory scrutiny hit investor confidence.

The chipmaker is a "symbolic bellwether" of the AI trade that is fast becoming key to places like South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia," says Dylan Loh, an international studies lecturer at Nanyang Technological University.

From chip manufacturing to data centres to foreign investments, AI has become a strategic priority for these economies - and they are now increasingly dependent on Nvidia's fortunes.

Nvidia is everywhere

In Nvidia, the AI industry has the unrivalled power of cutting-edge chips and the financial clout that turned it into "the bank of AI". And in Huang, it has a high-profile evangelist.

That combination has put it at the heart of the AI ecosystem in more ways than one.

For one, Nvidia was able to grow rapidly by outsourcing chip production instead of having to spend heavily to build its own manufacturing plants.

It contracts out most of its production to Taiwanese chipmaking giant TSMC.

That means Taiwan is vulnerable to changes in AI tech demand, says Paul Cavey, founder of Taipei-based research firm East Asia Econ.

"The surge in [Taiwan's] real economic growth since 2024 has been because of the big increase in AI related exports".

Huang said earlier this year that Nvidia plans to invest around $150bn (£114.4bn) a year in Taiwan at a launch to celebrate the firm's planned headquarters on the island.

To a lesser extent, South Korea and Japan are also exposed to the industry, Cavey adds. They are among its suppliers of key components such as memory chips and testing equipment, with firms like Samsung and SK Hynix making the firm's processors.

On top of that, Nvidia is a financial backstop and major lender to companies in the AI supply chain.

It is difficult to overstate the role Nvidia, with Huang at its helm, has played in the region's AI industry. Nvidia's chips fill its data centres, power its AI models and feed the companies making cars and electronics.

"Asia isn't just a customer base for Nvidia. It is an indispensable engine of the company's AI dominance because of East Asia's semiconductor manufacturing and memory ecosystems," Loh says.

In the Asia-Pacific region, the data centre market, which is largely powered by Nvidia chips, is in the midst of an "unprecedented boom", according to property services firm CBRE. The volume of investment has been rising steadily in recent years to reach a record of $11.6bn (£8.85bn) in 2025.

In South East Asia, Singapore-based AI company Megaspeed had become the region's biggest buyer of Nvidia chips before it was accused of smuggling them to China. Megaspeed has said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".

The US has said it intends to ban Megaspeed Ltd from doing business in the United States.

But in a timely example of the importance of AI to this region, Singapore this week further raised its growth forecast for this year as the technology boosts its economy.

The world's biggest tech firms - Google, Microsoft, Oracle - also plan to boost their spending on infrastructure in the region by roughly 60% this year, CBRE added.

The demand for neoclouds, which are specialised data centres which power AI, has also risen rapidly, it said.

For economies betting heavily on AI, Nvidia has become "hugely important", with vast sums being spent on its chips and factory activity increasingly dependent on its technology, Loh told the BBC.

Huang's return carries risks

In many economies, news of Huang's return to Nvidia was met with jubilation.

In Taiwan, where he was born and the home of "Jensanity", investors jokingly described his return as a "one man saves the village" story.

Social media and groups on messaging platform Line saw posts like "Old Huang is back," while some investors said "Daddy is back to save my life" and "the humanitarian corridor is open."

However, some said the episode should also prompt a closer look at how effective Taiwan has been in building a "non-China" semiconductor supply chain, and how risks from the industry's heavy reliance on Nvidia should be managed better.

Asia's technology industry has been under increasing pressure from the US in recent years. The administrations of both Joe Biden and Donald Trump have tightened rules on the export of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China.

Those efforts seem to have been renewed. Just last week, Washington announced new rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

The latest move not only restricts the export of high-end chips to China, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train AI models.

This will hit South East Asian countries, which have invested billions in data centre infrastructure to cater to Chinese firms. Nvidia has already paused shipments to the region, according to the Financial Times, although it is unclear if this is only a temporary move while it figures out how to comply with the new export rules.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a BBC request for comment.

Then there is the growing bipartisan backlash against President Trump and Nvidia after he said he "made the deal" to "convince" the company‘s board to reinstate Huang.

Huang is also due to testify before Congress next week. And as Democrats prepare to take control of the US House and Senate in the New Year, Huang is likely to face further risks.

"Jensen's return may resolve the immediate leadership crisis, but it does not resolve the legal and political overhangs," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist from Saxo Bank.

Investor concerns about the trillions of dollars being poured into AI and the pivotal role Nvidia plays in the industry were already sending tremors through global stock markets.

Some fear that while the company and its charismatic leader have been crucial in driving AI's growth that concentration of influence also poses a threat.

Especially now when it appears that Huang's future - which is still uncertain - could impact economies that are heavily exposed to the AI industry.

"I would say the President and White House would love to brush this over and say its fine but I believe Democrats in Congress will definitely be probing", Ray Wang, founder of San Francisco-based Constellation Research said.

"The story is not over yet... Jensen coming back is probably the biggest, baddest return ever. The question is what will happen next?"

Additional reporting by Benny Lu, BBC Chinese

item.title: The big fat wedding of politician's daughter making headlines in India
item.description: Half a million people are estimated to have attended the wedding of Shivangi Singh, daughter of Anant Singh.
item.content:encoded:
The big fat wedding of a politician's daughter in the northern Indian state of Bihar has been making headlines for its over-the-top celebrations in the country's poorest state.

The wedding of Shivangi Singh, daughter of Anant Singh - a legislator in the state assembly - culminated on Wednesday after days of high-voltage celebrations that included plans for a horse race.

Hundreds of thousands of people, including the speaker of the state assembly and several prominent local and national politicians, attended Wednesday's ceremony at the family's ancestral home in Nadawa village, about 65km (40.4 miles) from the state capital, Patna.

At a press conference earlier this month, Singh - a five-time legislator from the Mokama constituency - had said "everyone has been invited... Not only from Bihar, but from across India and Pakistan too".

And reports from the ground yesterday said it seemed "everyone did turn up".

Media reports estimated that half a million people attended the wedding, turning the village into a large fairground and stalling traffic for several hours on the road leading to and from Patna.

Six helipads were set up in the village to receive important guests, and more than 150 dishes, including eight million pieces of sweets, were prepared by hundreds of cooks in temporary kitchens.

The biggest attraction at Wednesday's wedding was meant to be the horse race, for which 52 horses had been brought in. But it was postponed at the last minute because of the huge crowds that turned up to watch the event, with many spilling on to the racing ground.

A viral video from a pre-wedding practice session for the race showed tens of thousands of spectators gathered to watch, with several hundreds perched high above the ground over an electricity tower to get a better view.

Last week, the legislator shared a video on his X account of a white SUV costing between 1m-2m rupees (£8,300-£16,500; $10,800-$21,600), announcing that it would be the prize for the winner. A motorcycle and a scooter were promised as the second and third prizes.

The finale is now planned for Thursday.

The bride, Shivangi, a Delhi university graduate, arrived in a Land Cruiser while the groom Rishikesh Kumar, an MBA from Georgia State University in Atlanta, came in a convoy of 151 cars.

Anant Singh also made a grand entry, rising through the sunroof of an SUV as a sea of supporters pressed in around it, news channel NDTV reported. He "was arriving for his daughter's wedding, and he did it in a style that would upstage any groom".

Media reports said the groom received a car worth 23m rupees, as well as gold and silver, from the bride's family, although Singh has not revealed how much the wedding cost.

The scale of the wedding is not comparable to the 2024 festivities India saw during the marriage of Anant Ambani, the youngest son of Asia's richest man Mukesh Ambani.

But the extravagant wedding in Bihar, a state where one in every three citizen is counted as multidimensionally poor, has been dubbed "a royal wedding" and become a huge talking point.

One political rival - Neeraj Kumar, a Bihar legislative council member - has also called on the investigative agencies to look into where the money for the wedding came from.

The interest in the wedding, though, has less to do with the couple than with the father of the bride, a controversial politician.

Popularly known as "Chhote Sarkar" (Hindi for younger lord or mini government), Singh is often described as a "bahubali" - a word that translates as strongman and is used to describe powerful local leaders in many parts of India.

In videos on his social media accounts, Singh is often seen twirling and turning up the ends of his moustache - a gesture of pride and masculinity.

Local people say he travels in a convoy of 20-25 cars and a local journalist said that, on one occasion, Singh chased away tax officials who visited him by turning up with live snakes wrapped around his neck.

Singh first won Mokama in 2005 and has retained it in subsequent elections in 2010, 2015, 2020 and 2025.

According to the affidavit he submitted to the Election Commission before last year's polls, he described himself as a social worker who has businesses and agricultural land.

He declared that his combined wealth with his wife added up to 1bn rupees and that there were more than two dozen criminal cases pending against him. In some of these cases, he's accused of serious crimes such as murder, attempt to murder, extortion and rioting.

According to reports, he's done several stints in prison, but the only time he was not a legislator in the past two decades was in 2022 when he was convicted and sentenced for 10 years in jail. It was in a case from 2019 when arms and ammunition, including an AK-47 assault rifle, were seized from his home.

The state assembly disqualified him, but he remained on bail and appealed against the court order. He contested and won last year's election and returned to the assembly.

He's also been named as the main suspect in a murder case during last year's election and the Supreme Court has ordered him to surrender by 1st December. Singh, who spent three months in jail in connection with the case, has said in interviews that he would abide by the court order.

item.title: I spend £200 a month on fancy meals by myself - would you dine solo?
item.description: Solo-dining is being embraced as a self-care trend and it's reshaping the restaurant industry.
item.content:encoded:
Catherine Smith is perusing the menu at a high-end Mediterranean restaurant she has been excited to try. She has a new outfit on, and as she sips her rosé, she looks across at the empty seat - bliss.

"I think what is so special about solo dining is that you don't have to wait for people to make those plans. You can go out and do them yourself," says the 23-year-old.

The self-confessed foodie is part of a growing trend of people booking tables for one - not because they're away with work but as a treat.

As food trends analyst Charles Banks puts it: "[Eating alone] is becoming an intentional act, a little pocket of independence, indulgence and self-care."

We spoke to solo dining fans and hospitality industry experts about how the trend is shaping the restaurant experience and asked if you would book a table for one.

Catherine, from Yorkshire, began dining solo at university and now does it at least once a month, choosing high-end restaurants she would not usually go to with friends and family.

She has been to a range of places both in the UK and abroad, doing "lots of research" to find new spots, typically spending £100 to £200 per meal.

"I think because a lot of my friends are vegan or vegetarian, I find that difficult sometimes because I'm quite a big meat eater," she says.

"I find it nice to be able to go out and pick a restaurant where I haven't had to scour through the menu to make sure that it's suitable for them."

Catherine says the sense of freedom she gets from picking where and when she eats "feels empowering".

"It definitely feels like not only a form of self-care but also a form of female liberation."

Online booking platform OpenTable says it covers more than 5,000 restaurants in the UK. It says solo dining makes up the smallest proportion of its bookings in the UK but it is the fastest-growing category.

Figures from 1 January to 31 August this year saw a rise of 23% in solo bookings compared to the same time period a year ago. It did not provide the data to the BBC to verify.

Nishi Singh was an avid solo diner when she lived in London, but found it wasn't widely accepted after moving to Delhi.

"Someone approached me and said that they assumed I'd been stood up," she tells BBC World Service's The Food Chain podcast.

"It sparked a conversation about the culture around solo dining in Delhi and I was really shocked to hear that it's not really something people do."

A couple of days later, she started documenting her solo dining experience on social media.

"Quite a lot of people have reached out and said that this is something they'd like to do and they're too scared to do it themselves," she says.

Banks, joint managing director of The Food People, a food trends and ideas agency, says that while solo dining isn't a "new consumer behaviour", changes in society mean it has become "almost aspirational".

But he notes that not every restaurant has welcomed the trend.

"A single diner could therefore feel like an inefficient use of a table rather than a customer the restaurant actively wanted."

SoloTable, a website that helps identify restaurants suitable for solo diners, found that one in eight of 178 restaurants it surveyed in London did not accept online reservations from solo diners.

Catherine says she has previously been turned away. "There are a lot of restaurants that I've wanted to go to before where they don't actually allow solo diners. And I've always found that to be really disappointing."

However, some restaurants like Jungli, an Indian restaurant in Newcastle upon Tyne, is working to attract solo diners.

Co-founder and director Yousaf Khalid has included high tables and bar seats in his recently opened restaurant. They also have charging points for laptops and phones.

"We want people to feel comfortable in these sorts of environments, being able to walk in on their own," he says.

He has hired staff with "bigger personalities" to engage customers in conversation but they also know when to leave diners alone if they want a more solitary experience.

Catherine urges anyone who fancies solo dining to give it a go.

"Food is a great way to bring people together, but it's also a great way to have good experiences on your own.

"I think with time, people will see and will start to accept it as something that's more normal."

Additional reporting by Jemma Crew and Emma Jackson.

item.title: 'Think twice': Banff officials issue warning over thin ice after skater's death
item.description: After three separate incidents, one fatal, at Lake Louise, Parks Canada is warning visitors to be cautious after a warmer than average November.
item.content:encoded:
A 70-year-old local resident of Banff, Alberta, has died after falling through ice on Lake Louise, prompting warnings about outdoor safety as Canada experiences warmer than normal November temperatures.

Police said the man, who has not been identified, was ice skating alone on Tuesday evening when he fell through thin ice. He was found two hours later by a rescue team and pronounced dead at a nearby hospital.

It comes after two other ice skaters fell in the lake's frigid waters on Monday, though both survived.

Canadian park authorities have issued a warning to visitors of the world-famous Banff National Park urging them to "think twice" before stepping on the ice.

"Visitors must be able to self-rescue should they fall in the water," Parks Canada said in a notice posted on Monday.

"If you choose to skate on natural ice, you do so at your own risk."

In a statement, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police offered condolences to the 70-year-old's family. It also warned the public of the dangers of being on the ice.

Parks Canada said that early season ice can be unpredictable, and that it does not actively monitor natural ice surfaces for safety or mark potential hasards.

The incident comes as temperatures in Alberta and other parts of Canada have been warmer than average for this time of year.

Canada's largest city, Toronto, experienced unseasonable highs of 15C (59F) this month.

In Alberta, temperatures have been about three degrees Celsius warmer than what has been historically observed for November, Alysa Pederson, a meteorologist with Environment Canada, told the BBC.

On average, temperatures would dip below -10C for a number of days in November. But this year, Pederson noted that the coldest November day was -6C.

"It's going to become a challenge to form ice when your temperatures aren't really getting that cold," Pederson said.

Environment Canada's seasonal forecast suggests that much of Canada, from Vancouver to Halifax, will likely be seeing a warmer than average winter.

It is due partly to the weather phenomenon known as El Niño, where changing wind patterns over the Pacific Ocean result in heat being released into the atmosphere that can drive major shifts in global weather patterns.

"We're currently in a very strong El Niño event, potentially record-breaking by the time it peaks here in the next couple of months," Pederson explained.

She advised those who are eager to get outside in the winter to stay vigilant, as warmer weather can not only mean thin ice, but a higher risk of avalanches.

She added that while falling through ice in Banff is always a risk, the recent back-to-back incidents came as a surprise and called it "unfortunate".

item.title: Faisal Islam: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
item.description: Other countries have rerouted trade in response to his first tariff salvo, now they are looking beyond Trump's tenure.
item.content:encoded:
There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.

Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.

"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.

Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.

The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.

Still, the USA is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.

The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.

It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.

The tariffs will have to be finalised under a Democrat Congress, which has influence, but not power. The Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said this week that the new House would in its first 100 days "move aggressively to… repeal the Trump tariffs".

The Chinese rate of 20% is the truce rate from last year's Trump-Xi deal. The truce is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, no retaliation, criticism of industrial overcapacity as a "false issue", and a call to implement the Xi-Trump deal. The leverage over China has weakened, with the US share of its exports dropping to around 10% this year, down from 15%, just two years ago, and 19% in 2018.

However, the most interesting spot to focus on is closer to home for Trump. Over half of Canada tariffs are authorised under "Section 338" of the 1930s Smoot-Hawley act. There is already a Senate Bill to repeal them, and it is possible that there would be enough rebel Republicans in the House and Senate to threaten to over-ride any Presidential veto. The incoming Senate Finance Committee chair Ron Wyden last week said Democrats were focussed on "figuring out a way to beat Trump and his veto".

Before that an interim deal is being sought, and Democrat senators such as Chris Coons are appearing on Canadian TV, telling CBC: "Frankly, if you can get an interim deal, I'd take it, and then put it to us in the new majority to legislate an even better deal."

The rest of world is watching the machinations in Washington and also looking beyond Donald Trump's tenure.

It pays to look at how the initial Trump trade-quake has reshaped the pattern of world trade already.

The rest of the world has rerouted its trade flows around Donald Trump's tariff wall, proving far more resilient than expected. In cash terms, China's exports so far in 2026 are down about 8% on 2024, but that is more than 25 times made up for by its increased exports to everywhere else.

Canada has seen flat exports to the USA since tariffs, fewer cars and lumber, but pricier flows of energy. Its exports, especially commodities, to the rest of the world have rocketed.

This means that next month's G20 summit at the president's Miami resort is an important moment. In general US allies have not rocked the boat, accepting the lower level of tariffs as part of the new reality. Could the middle powers choose to upset their host in Florida next month?

The bigger question however, is how much the Democrats decide to keep of the America First trade agenda. It will not be all, but nor will it be nothing. Economists now expect some of these tariffs to stay in place for years.

item.title: Madi's last Christmas wish inspires hospice appeal
item.description: Katharine House Hospice describes helping Madi Foster celebrate Christmas in May as a privilege.
item.content:encoded:
A 22-year-old hospice patient who celebrated Christmas in May, weeks before her death, has inspired a festive appeal at the site that cared for her.

Madi Foster from Stafford fought adrenocortical carcinoma for three years, raising thousands of pounds for life-lengthening treatment abroad.

She spent her final weeks in Katharine House Hospice, where staff in May helped her decorate her room, cooked a Christmas dinner, and dressed up to join her family and friends in festive games.

As the hospice launched its Care this Christmas appeal to raise money for vital services, Foster's dad Craig said the "fantastic" team there had helped grant his daughter's "last wish".

He explained that her type of cancer had been "very aggressive" and that "survival rates are very very low", but she remained optimistic.

"She had seven operations, she had six different types of chemotherapy, she had radiotherapy as well on three occasions.

"She used to say 'I try the best, I'll try anything, I'll do anything to try and help myself'.

"She was still taking medication two, three days before she passed, with just a glimmer of hope that something might work."

She had initially not wanted to go into the hospice, he said, but immediately felt relaxed around the staff.

"The name hospice has certain connotations and understandably, for a 22-year-old, you don't want to be associated with that," he said.

"But actually within an hour of being [there], Madi just felt at home."

The festive celebration came after Foster had been too unwell to celebrate the previous December.

"We did a full Christmas dinner, turkey and stuffing and pigs in blankets - and everything you can imagine that we'd normally do in December we did in May," her dad said.

"It just happened to coincide with the heatwave that we had and it was about 30-odd degrees outside, even warmer in the room due to all the bodies and the food."

He said the staff were "fantastic" and had even bought cards and presents.

"It was just a lovely day and obviously one that we'll look back on forever, just thinking about and remembering with fondness."

The family said they would now celebrate "Madi's Christmas" every year on 24 May.

Inpatient Unit lead nurse Georgia Simmons said staff had got to know the patient well and felt privileged to have helped create a lasting memory.

"She's just such a positive, inspirational, special person," she said.

"And this story is just something that really means a lot to us all. And it's just a great representation of something that hospices and palliative care can provide.

"It was a difficult day, certainly very difficult day, but there was also a lot of laughter in that room. You could hear the laughter down the corridor, people telling jokes, Christmas crackers, Christmas music, in May and that is just something that is just incredibly special."

The hospice provides free care and support to those with incurable illnesses across Stafford and neighbouring areas.

Its Christmas appeal aims to contribute to the £5m needed annually to run its services.

"We are a charity and we are only able to do the things that we do because of the huge generosity and kindness from the public and from our local community," the nurse added.

"By supporting our Care this Christmas appeal, you could help a nurse manage someone's pain, reassure a worried family or give families valuable time together."

Follow BBC Stoke & Staffordshire on BBC Sounds , Facebook , X and Instagram .

item.title: Diesel tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes capsizes near Ibiza, killing one
item.description: The possible environmental damage is still being assessed by Spain's sea rescue service.
item.content:encoded:
An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.

The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.

The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.

The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service.

"There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X.

Regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk, as had been originally reported. The vessel remains, however, partially submerged.

That made conditions more favourable for carrying out recovery operations, he said, "as we have gone from the possibility of the vessel being at a depth of 1,000m to a situation that allows operations to be carried out on the surface".

The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia. It is unclear what caused the sinking.

The chemical tanker was en route from Algeciras, in southern Spain, to Barcelona in the north-east.

Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call around 22:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday, according to Spanish media. Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle.

The injured crew members have been taken to hospitals in Valencia and Can Misses Hospital in Ibiza, President Prohens said.

Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.

In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline. It spilled more than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil into the sea.

item.title: Pregnant US inmate escapes in prison vehicle after medical appointment
item.description: Rebecca Taylor had been imprisoned in New Mexico for multiple theft and burglary charges.
item.content:encoded:
A pregnant inmate has escaped from custody in the US state of New Mexico, after taking control of a police vehicle while returning to prison from a prenatal appointment, the state's corrections department has said.

Rebecca Taylor, 26, took control of the Dodge Journey and drove away when the team transporting her and another inmate stopped to pick up food in Albuquerque, local media reported.

The New Mexico Corrections Department said that the vehicle and her prison jumpsuit were later recovered, but Taylor remains on the run.

She had been imprisoned for multiple theft and burglary charges, the department said in a Facebook statement.

Local media reported that another inmate, also travelling back from a prenatal appointment, was able to get out of the car as Taylor took control on Wednesday morning.

The corrections department has said that a multi-agency search for Taylor is under way. The BBC has approached it for an update.

The Albuquerque Journal reported that Taylor is currently in her second trimester of pregnancy. For this reason, she was not restrained during transportation, department spokesperson Brittany Roembach said.

"It is the understanding right now that one officer was with the vehicle but not inside of the vehicle when this occurred," she was quoted as saying.

All prisons in New Mexico went into lockdown following Taylor's escape, but it was lifted at 06:00 on Thursday.

However the prison where she was being held, the Western New Mexico Corrections Facility, will remain on "modified movement", and no visitors are currently allowed.

The public has been told not to approach Rebecca Taylor if they see her, and call police straight away.

item.title: Jilted bride who went ahead with her wedding alone finally walks down the aisle
item.description: Guests burst into applause as Swansea bride Kayley Stead, jilted in 2022, finally says "I do".
item.content:encoded:
A bride who became a social media sensation after being jilted at the altar has described the "pure magic" of finally walking down the aisle.

Kayley Stead's fiance did not turn up for her big day in 2022, but she surprised everyone by letting the celebration continue with many agreeing to "just go with this madness".

Four years on and she has found love again, reconnecting with an old university friend who did turn up for their ceremony on Friday 13th November.

Stead walked down the aisle in a bespoke wedding dress to applause, later saying she felt everyone was relieved the wedding was actually happening this time.

Marrying Richard Perrott was everything she had imagined, Stead told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast.

"As soon as I started walking down the aisle, everyone just started clapping, because I think everyone was relieved that this is actually happening," she said.

She described exchanging vows with Perrott as a moment when "everyone else just kind of disappears and it's just you two in the room".

"It just felt magical," she added.

Her new chapter in life was also marked by a change in style.

Stead described her dress in 2022 as being "kind of like an armour, rather than a bridal dress".

Her new dress, from designer April Brambury, made her feel "a million bucks".

"I wanted a dress that celebrated my body, who I am as a woman, and I didn't want to shy away from that."

She said being able to hold his hands and share vows "was everything I pictured and more".

item.title: Desperate appeals from women on death row in Iran after protests
item.description: Female protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, a rights group says.
item.content:encoded:
Taraneh Rahimi is on death row in Iran.

In recent weeks, the 21-year-old has been unable to walk properly after her legs were beaten, and an ear-infection caused by an untreated head injury has affected her balance, her cousin says.

She is "keeping her spirits up" but "there are days she breaks down in tears," Masoud Nourmohammadi tells BBC News Persian.

He says Taraneh and her twin sister Romina were arrested after joining the anti-government protests that swept the country in January.

When the twins' mother first saw them in prison, their faces were so swollen and bruised, and their hair pulled out, that she could only recognise them by their voices, Nourmohammadi says, speaking from the US.

He says Taraneh signed a confession after interrogators threatened that her sister would be raped in front of her.

Taraneh is one of six women who have been sentenced to death this year in connection with the January protests, according to the UN's human rights rapporteur for Iran, Mai Sato.

The figure for men is much higher. However, women protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, as part of a "horrific rise" in politically motivated executions, Amnesty International's Iran researcher Raha Bahreini says.

The Iranian embassy in London told the BBC that claims of an increase in the use of the death penalty in protest-related cases were "misleading".

It categorically rejected allegations of the use of torture and any allegations that the death penalty has been imposed solely for peaceful protest, which it said is a "legitimate, and protected right".

It said death sentences in relation to the "riot in January 2026" were issued in cases involving "intentional murder" or "Moharebeh (the taking up of weapons with the intent to threaten or wreck the people's lives or property)".

The twins were seized in late January, Nourmohammadi says.

It was two weeks after the end of the protests, which began in late December over economic grievances and grew to become Iran's largest against the clerical establishment since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (Hrana) says it has identified more than 7,000 people killed in the crackdown that followed, most of them protesters, but believes the true figure is much higher.

The Iranian government accuses the US and Israel of fomenting the unrest, blaming "terrorists" and "rioters" for the deaths, which it says totalled 3,117 including some members of the security forces.

The twins' family did not find out where they were being held for more than three months, their cousin says. They were tried over protests in Isfahan, in an area of the city where a member of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) security force was killed.

Court documents have not been published, but the BBC has seen part of a sentencing document which says Taraneh was convicted of moharebeh, which is a capital offence under Iran's Islamic Penal Code. The offence included "drawing a bladed weapon with the intent to endanger people's lives", according to the document.

Romina was sentenced to 25 years in jail for the lesser charge of aiding and abetting moharebeh, according to Sato, the UN rapporteur.

Nourmohammadi, who has been in contact with relatives and others in Iran familiar with the case, says both women deny all the charges against them and that there is no evidence Taraneh had a "bladed weapon".

Sato says the sisters were part of a case in which 10 people were sentenced to death, but that there was "no clarification of the acts attributed to each individual".

According to sources familiar with the case, the twins' lawyers have submitted a complaint alleging they were tortured and sexually abused during interrogation, but the investigation into it is being overseen by an official they accuse of torture.

Voice messages from other women on death row contain a mixture of desperation and defiance.

Mahboubeh Shabani - widely reported to be 33 and a civil engineer - was sentenced to death in September under Iran's espionage law after transporting injured protesters, according to rights groups.

She called for help for herself and other prisoners from jail in the city of Mashhad in north-eastern Iran: "Everyone is in a terrible place mentally, especially those whose sentences have been finalised," she said.

Also jailed in Mashhad is Najmeh Amini, reported to be 23, who was initially arrested in the wake of the January protests, and later sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, according to rights groups.

"As long as I am alive, I have one hope, and that is to see a free and prosperous Iran before my life ends by the noose," a voice message attributed to her says.

In addition, Mojdeh Hashemi Bazargani - reported to be aged 27 - is also facing execution, according to rights groups. They say she was convicted of charges including "espionage", after being arrested in April, during the current war between Iran and Israel and the US.

The US-based Iranian rights group Tavaana has shared audio it says is of a phone call she made from prison, describing being beaten in the head, neck and body and made to sign a confession.

The woman in the recording says: "They accused me of espionage. They say you've been paid for it. If I had been paid for espionage, I would have a car or a house. I have nothing."

Amnesty International describes the charges in all three of these cases and also the twins as "politically motivated".

In response to the BBC's questions, the Iranian Embassy in London said "any allegations of the use of torture in connection with the mentioned cases are categorically rejected". It did not comment further on individual cases, but said "confessions obtained under duress have no legal validity".

At least 39 people have already been executed in connection with the January protests, according to Sato.

She notes a "sharp" increase in arrests and sentences across both men and women, and sees the rise in death sentences for women as an "escalation and expansion" of an "established pattern of repression".

Iranian human rights lawyer Musa Barzin, who is based in Turkey, says "it appears that factors such as gender or age now carry less weight in determining the severity of punishment".

Official detail on cases is often scant and some may go unreported.

However, Sato says as well as the six women she identified as being arrested in connection with protests, a further three have received death sentences this year - for "blasphemy" and "corruption on Earth charges, in relation to the war in March" and "espionage and moharebeh".

In comparison, these nine sentences are more than Hrana recorded for women for similar offences over the whole decade to 2025 - with no more than three in any one year.

The death sentences in three of the cases Sato identified as being linked to the protests have since been overturned – though two of those have been sent for retrial. She says she is concerned by an "increasingly frequent pattern" where overturned death sentences are later "reimposed by a parallel branch of the judiciary once public attention has subsided".

Sato says there was a "turning point" for women in Iran during the 2022 protests over the death of Mahsa Amini, who died in custody after being detained over an alleged breach of Iran's dress code.

Women "were at the forefront of challenging state policies and structures of control," says Sato. "Their political agency, visibility and leadership have made them targets of state repression."

The Iranian embassy said judicial proceedings in Iran are conducted in accordance with the Constitution and rule of law. It adds: "Cases involving the death penalty have included charges such as serious criminal offences, violence, terrorism, espionage, cooperation with hostile intelligence services and Moharebeh."

Iran executes more people per head of population than any other country, according to UN experts. Human rights groups say last year saw the highest number in decades.

Hrana recorded 2,003 executions in the year to October 2026. The vast majority - including 47 women - were for crimes such as murder and drug trafficking.

Nourmohammadi says the family are trying as best they can to support the twins.

Romina enjoys music and often asks relatives to play songs over the phone, he says.

Taraneh loves horses and has always wanted to set up a horse breeding centre, he says, and they tell her they plan to help her do so in the future: "That's how we try to give her hope."

item.title: Veruschka: Striking images of one of the world's first supermodels, who has died aged 87
item.description: Veruschka was a model and artist who became one of one of the first global fashion stars in the 1960s.
item.content:encoded:
Veruschka, the model and artist who became one of one of the first global fashion stars in the 1960s, has died at the age of 87.

She became known as the striking subject of fantastical photoshoots that helped expand the boundaries of fashion and beauty in the 60s and 70s, appearing on the cover of American Vogue 13 times.

Vogue's obituary described her as "the shape-shifting supermodel who defined an era", explaining: "One of the original supermodels, Veruschka was also among fashion's great performance artists."

She also made memorable appearances in classic swinging 60s film Blow Up and 2006 James Bond movie Casino Royale.

Veruschka was born Vera von Lehndorff into an aristocratic family in 1939 in Königsberg, then in Germany, now known as Kaliningrad in Russia.

Her father, Heinrich Count von Lehndorff, was executed in 1944 for his part in a failed plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler.

She studied art in Hamburg and Florence before beginning her career as a model "and soon became a legend", her sister Countess Catharina von Lehndorff wrote in a tribute.

"She worked with Yves Saint Laurent, Karl Lagerfeld, and Valentino, but also immersed herself in avant-garde photography projects in which she painted, staged, and deconstructed her body.

"Veruschka was never just a model – she was an artist, a boundary-pusher, a rebel. Her work is considered a feminist precursor to performance art."

item.title: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds
item.description: Nearly a third of crossings in early 2026 allegedly involved boats or engines from the German man's firm.
item.content:encoded:
A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.

Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.

The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.

His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.

We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.

Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.

Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.

Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.

At least 82 boats from Reuter's firm reached the English coast in just over two years to May, according to French investigations.

There are also press photos dating back five years showing the MaReBoote logo on dinghies crowded with migrants.

In 2021, Reuter told the Sun and Guardian he felt "frustrated" and "anxious" that his vessels had ended up in the hands of smugglers.

There was no suggestion, at that time, that authorities suspected him of wrongdoing as a German detective reportedly told the Sun: "This would be like if somebody buys a Mercedes and does something in another country which is wrong. The Mercedes seller can't help that."

It is not exactly clear when police suspicions were aroused.

French prosecutor Samuel Finielz would not comment on the details of the investigation but confirmed the head of a German company is currently the subject of a European Arrest Warrant.

The warrant was issued in May this year and relates to alleged offences dating back to December 2024.

While selling boats is "perfectly legal" it becomes illegal, said Finielz, "when one is fully aware that they will be used by networks involved in illegal immigration or human trafficking".

Case files we have seen say that German police had learned from UK authorities that 29% of detected crossings this year, up to the end of April, involved boats and/or engines linked to MaReBoote.

In France, five other men have already been charged as part of the investigation - an Iranian, three Iraqis and a Syrian.

In one of the two fatal incidents where Reuter's equipment is suspected to be involved, one of those who died was also Syrian.

Suliman al Husein would have just turned 20 when he died, according to a birth date listed in the files.

News reports at the time say he suffered a cardiac arrest after likely being crushed on a packed dinghy during a failed launch, west of Calais, in January 2025.

He was the first migrant to die in the English Channel that year. His body was found on the floor of the boat which, investigators allege, bore the MaReBoote logo.

The case against Reuter also stems from a chance arrest when French police pulled over a vehicle with German plates, near the northern port city of Boulogne-sur-Mer.

The BMW, which was towing a trailer, was spotted overtaking another vehicle at speed in the early hours of a morning in May this year - police records say.

Inside the car were two German nationals who - according to a subsequent search - were transporting jerry cans of fuel, a boat engine, pumps and a rolled up inflatable dinghy.

The men claimed they had been paid up to €1,000-a-time (£830) to make several, similar drops to "foreigners" on the coast, interrogation records show.

"Of course I knew that it wasn't legal," one is said to have admitted under questioning. "The money made me turn a blind eye."

  • Take a look at BBC Verify's UK migration tracker - the latest numbers on net migration, visas, asylum and small boats

Both men, who have since been convicted for smuggling offences, allegedly implicated Marvin Reuter as the man who had hired and paid them for this work.

Police files say both the BMW and the boat it was carrying had MaReBoote logos on them.

Marvin Reuter was arrested in Germany in May and later released, pending extradition.

On the day of his arrest, German police also seized more than 30 dinghies and 9,000 life jackets. Equipment which, we can now reveal, was allegedly linked to Reuter.

The BBC was previously granted access to see this haul, held in a police warehouse at a secret location in western Germany.

Meanwhile, further evidence has been gleaned from the bugging of a jail cell of a suspected gang chief, who is being held in pre-trial detention in France.

Recordings captured the inmate talking about buying nautical equipment from a German firm run by a man with Reuter's first name: Marvin - according to files we have seen.

The MaReBoote company address was also discovered on the alleged smuggler's phone, the case files say.

When we confronted Reuter last month at his business in the town of Werne, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, he told us to leave and drove off.

He then returned a short time later and said he was reporting us to the police. He did not answer our questions.

We approached him in writing before and after this encounter including a detailed request for comment. In response to that request, he did not address the specific allegations but accused us of harassment.

It is understood Reuter's lawyers have challenged his extradition, citing overcrowding in French prisons as one reason. Their client should face any allegations in Germany, they argue.

In Germany, it became explicitly illegal to aid smuggling to the UK at the end of last year after a prior BBC investigation exposed the country's role as a storage hub for gangs. Before then, some anti-smuggling laws in Germany had no longer applied to the UK because of Brexit.

The raid that saw the seizure of equipment that was allegedly linked to Reuter marked the first time the new law had been used.

Small boat crossings have dropped significantly in 2026, with British authorities citing law enforcement as a "key factor". However, illegal migration into Europe has also been falling.

The UK National Crime Agency's (NCA) deputy director for organized immigration crime, Dan Cannatella-Barcroft, praised Germany's "commitment" to tackling people-smuggling but acknowledged the country would remain "an important piece of the puzzle".

While a gap in the law has been closed, Germany's proximity to France, wider transport links and the fact that some of the Kurdish-dominated gangs are based there, means it is expected to stay as a transit point in the illegal small-boats trade.

The "vast majority" of small boats equipment in the past few years has come through Germany, Cannatella-Barcroft told the BBC - much of it made in China and having been routed through Turkey.

item.title: Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approved
item.description: The Starmind constellation aims to be the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for AI computing power.
item.content:encoded:
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.

The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, would "support America's booming super intelligence economy".

However, rival firm Amazon has criticised it as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan", while astronomers in the US said the move would "significantly undermine" the public's ability to study and observe the night sky.

There is increasing opposition to data centres on earth, including in the US where experts say they were a factor in the Republicans big losses in the midterm elections.

SpaceX believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".

"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.

Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites must begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.

The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.

It is unclear whether a million satellites will indeed be launched or whether SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.

Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).

Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.

Speaking to the Today programme, on BBC Radio 4, Prof Sir Martin Sweeting, founder and executive chairman of Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd, said while the idea of data centres in space seemed "technically feasible", whether it "makes sense at scale yet" still needed to be analysed.

Being able to get the data from the network of satellites, he added, would depend on being able to use laser links from the ground to them.

"That has not yet been perfected to the level at which it would be able to support the huge amounts of data that are likely to be transferred backwards and forwards," he said.

Meanwhile, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the decision.

It said the proposed constellation would "significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities" as well as "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky".

It noted that the constellation "involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects", meaning the satellites would "be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky".

Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney at the non-profit group Earthjustice, said in a statement: "Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people's everyday lives as well as the future of our planet."

The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.

The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.

New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.

An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.

Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.

Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

Sign up for our Tech Decoded newsletter to follow the world's top tech stories and trends. Outside the UK? Sign up here.

item.title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies aged 65
item.description: The musician, who co-wrote some of the band's biggest hits, had been treated for prostate cancer.
item.content:encoded:
Andy Taylor, the guitarist for the pop group Duran Duran, has died at the age of 65.

Born in Tynemouth, he co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits, including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film; and also worked with artists like Robert Palmer, Rod Stewart and Belinda Carlisle.

In a statement, his bandmates said Taylor had fought "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer" and "passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23 November".

His wife, Tracey, said the musician "was the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day".

The son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.

He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran in Birmingham in April 1980.

The group went on to achieve global fame through the New Romantic movement, which combined slick, melodic synth-pop with aspirational music videos and chiselled good looks.

Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.

"Andy was there at the very beginning of our story," said his bandmates Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes, John Taylor and Roger Taylor (his bandmates were unrelated, despite sharing the same last name).

"From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.

"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.

"Our thoughts are with his wife Tracey, his children Georgina, Isabella, Bethany and Andrew, and grandson Albie. They all loved him deeply and we ask that their privacy be respected at this very difficult time."

Duran Duran were one of the biggest pop acts of the 1980s, and its five members became global hearththrobs.

Their indelible hooks and airbrushed music videos found a natural home on the newly launched MTV, giving their career a huge boost in the US.

They became so popular in the States that the press labeled them the leaders of a "Second British Invasion" of the charts - alongside groups like Spandau Ballet, Human League and Eurythmics.

During a hiatus in 1984, Andy and John Taylor enlisted Robert Palmer for their successful but short-lived side project the Power Station.

The following year, the guitarist decided to quit Duran Duran, after a miserable experience performing at Live Aid.

"We'd reached rock bottom and we had absolutely nothing to say to each other," he wrote in his autobiography, Wild Boy.

"We drove to the venue through streets packed with excited rock fans, but inside the bus the atmosphere was as if we were on a way to a funeral."

He went on to play on Robert Palmer's Addicted To Love, and released a solo album, Thunder, in 1987.

After a period writing and producing albums for other artists, he rejoined Duran Duran in 2000, lasting for just one album (2004's Astronaut) before parting ways again.

In 2022, when the band were inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Taylor was notably absent from the ceremony, despite public plans for a reunion.

When the group took the stage, singer Simon Le Bon read a letter from the guitarist, in which he revealed his diagnosis with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.

Nonetheless, he contributed to the following year's Halloween-themed album Danse Macabre, marking his final collaboration with the band.

"Andy never took the easy musical route," said Le Bon in a personal statement marking his friend's death.
