Animal lovers were rooting for a recovery for Fiona, who became a social media star after her premature birth in 2017.

Cincinnati Zoo's director of animal health, Dr Mike Wenninger, said in a statement that an upper and lower GI endoscopy were unable to reach the object.

"The location and anatomy made laparoscopic removal impossible," Wenninger added. "No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked."

Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, had said that the woolen hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.

"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.

While Fiona showed no symptoms at first, her appetite started to decrease a few days later, and the zoo staff tried to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system to no avail.

Christina Gorsuch, The zoo's director of animal care, Christina Gorsuch, said on Friday that the other hippos - Bibi, Tucker and Fritz - were so far eating and behaving normally after Fiona's passing.

"It's difficult to know how they're feeling, but they appear to be their normal selves, Gorsuch said.

"We have received so much love from our community and beyond," said Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike. "We were touched when we saw stadiums, bridges, and buildings lit in purple last night" in Fiona's [honour], he added.

The US Senate even adopted a resolution on Friday to honour the beloved hippo.

Fiona first rose to fame when she was born premature at Cincinnati Zoo in 2017 and at first struggled to survive. At birth, she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species.

"The support that we're feeling from all over the world reminds me of the time when everyone pulled together to root for her to survive," Jenike said. "She did, and she gave us almost a decade of smiles."

item.title: Anthropic shares fall after blockbuster opening as wider tech sell-off continues
item.description: Other tech companies have also taken a hit as share markets broadly slump.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off deepens.

The fall in tech stocks continued to weigh on markets, with the S&P 500 down more than 2% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 0.7% by lunchtime.

Both US indexes touched correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index also fell more than 3.4% by the middle of trading on Friday.

The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.

Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping more than 12% to about $85 by lunchtime, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.

The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.

The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.

Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.

Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.

But many, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.

Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.

While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.

"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.

"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."

Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday.

Nvidia and SpaceX were both down more than 6%, while Tesla shares fell more than 3% and Meta was down 3.4%.

Apple, Amazon and Microsoft experienced smaller falls, while Alphabet was up by 1.2%.

Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.

Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.

Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.

South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.

Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

item.title: Texas death-row inmate screams as execution takes more than one hour
item.description: This prolonged execution comes weeks after Christa Pike survived the lethal injection of the same drug.
item.content:encoded:
A US death row inmate has screamed in apparent pain during his Texas execution which lasted more than an hour.

This is "not working the way it should be," Reinaldo Dennes, 70, said as he was being injected with the drug pentobarbital, according to witnesses.

A spokeswoman for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice said there had been unsuccessful attempts to find veins for the injections, but added that Dennes had reported pain in parts of his body where there were no attempted injections.

Dennes's case comes weeks after the botched execution of Christa Pike, who survived two lethal doses and is believed to be the only individual to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.

Dennes was sentenced to death over the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer who was found shot multiple times.

His execution came on the same day another inmate was put to death in Florida.

Executions with a lethal drug usually last from a few minutes to over an hour.

Michael Graczyk, an Associated Press reporter who has witnessed many such executions, described how they had waited for an unusually long time before being taken into the chamber. According to him, such delays are usually due to an inmate resisting the procedure or difficulty in finding veins.

When the witnesses were finally allowed in, Dennes almost immediately exclaimed, "The pain! Go! Go!", Graczyk said. He then uttered an expletive and asked "the father" to "take this pain".

He then shouted: "My right leg is killing me!", describing it as a cramp. After another expletive, he grunted and said, "I don't think this is normal."

Another witness, the reverend Jeff Hood, told USA Today that Dennes's execution was "by far the worst one" he had seen.

"He [Dennes] screamed out, 'my leg, my leg, my leg'," Hood said. "He screamed out twice, 'it's not working like it's supposed to.'"

The use of pentobarbital has been under renewed scrutiny since Pike, a 50-year-old convicted murderer, survived two attempts at execution via the lethal injection in September. She was taken to hospital in a critical condition and has since returned to prison.

Her botched execution captivated and shocked the world.

Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.

Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".

The Biden government banned its use in federal executions, but that did not bind individual states, which can choose their own methods.

item.title: Catherine Zeta-Jones' daughter says parents warned her about 'nepo baby' label
item.description: Carys Douglas, 23, made her stage debut this year in Anton Chekhov's play, The Seagull, in the US.
item.content:encoded:
Catherine Zeta-Jones's daughter has said her parents warned her people might have "preconceived notions" about her embarking on an acting career, as she shared her views on the "nepo baby" label.

Carys Douglas, 23, made her stage debut this year, playing the lead role of Nina in Anton Chekhov's The Seagull in Brooklyn, New York.

Zeta-Jones, who is married to Michael Douglas, son of Hollywood star Kirk, previously said the "nepo baby" term was "horrific". It refers to children of famous parents perceived to have achieved riches and success off their parents' backs.

But the young actor said her parents taught her to build her "own identity" and she has learned how to deal with the "pressure".

During an interview with Elle Spain, Carys Douglas said her parents "do not hide" from her that people would have preconceived ideas about her.

"They taught me that building my own identity depended on me and no one else. It was my responsibility, and it still is.

"As time has gone on, I've come to understand that there are different ways to deal with that kind of pressure," she said.

Her father, star of hit 1980s films such as Wall Street and Fatal Attraction, recently stated that he is not a fan of the "nepo baby" label, calling it an "unfortunate title".

"I guess you could say that about any business. The same thing with Hollywood royalty. My father's father was a junkman," Douglas, 82, said, referring to Kirk, who was considered a Hollywood Golden Age icon.

Zeta-Jones, 57, from Mumbles, Swansea, also criticised the phrase, saying it was "horrible because these kids didn't ask to be born into this, they're finding their own way in life".

"You have to go with your dreams, your passion," Zeta-Jones said.

She added: "But they love it, and they're good. Otherwise, Michael and I would be the first to go, 'you know what? Maybe law school looks really good'."

Zeta-Jones' big break came when she landed a West End role in 42nd Street in 1987, before she became a household name in the UK in 1991 after starring in the ITV hit The Darling Buds Of May.

She has since become a global superstar, with roles in The Mask Of Zorro, Entrapment, Traffic and 2002's adaptation of Chicago, for which she won an Oscar for Best Supporting Actress.

The couple's children, Dylan and Carys, have both followed in their footsteps into acting.

Michael Douglas said his children have been performing "since they were in kindergarten".

"Every play, every show, summer theater camps, graduating... I mean, they've done so much work. It's unbelievable," he said.

Douglas and Zeta-Jones' children predominantly grew up in the US, but the family regularly travels to Wales, a place they are fond of.

Speaking to British Vogue last November, Carys Douglas said her summers were spent reading on her grandmother's sofa and travelling around the Gower Peninsula in Swansea.

"I feel so lucky that this is where I'm from," she told the magazine, reflecting on the "weird but magical places" scattered across the peninsula.

"Those beaches are some of the most beautiful in the world," she said.

"The Gower Peninsula is breathtaking."

She also spoke about her "theatrical" family's traditions, recalling how "there'd be lots of little competitions for singing and pantomime shows all summer".

"It's true, the Welsh love to sing," she added.

item.title: 'What happens in GTA 6 stays in GTA 6': Police across US warn fans about taking the game to their real lives
item.description: The game's fans waited over a decade for this moment, and now police are reminding them "real-life laws don't come with cheat codes, respawns, or mission restarts".
item.content:encoded:
Police departments are reminding Americans that street racing, auto theft and gun violence are still crimes in real life, as excitement over Grand Theft Auto 6, a game following the lives of career criminals, reaches a fever pitch in the US.

"Play the game. Don't play yourself," Atlanta police warned in a social media post, while Denver authorities said that "running from police is still illegal".

Over 20 million units of the game have been purchased worldwide since its release this week, making GTA 6 likely the biggest entertainment launch in history.

The game, known for its freedom of play, ranging from buying a cheeseburger to firing a grenade launcher, is set in a Florida-inspired state.

"Assaulting someone for extra points, it's not worth it," an officer from the San Antonio Police Department, in Texas, said in a video.

Since Rockstar Games' 1997 inaugural release in the Grand Theft Auto series, the game has been both celebrated and condemned for its depictions of violence and its invitation to players to virtually participate.

It allows players to do everything from selling drugs to soliciting prostitutes and shooting law enforcement officers.

GTA 6's release in the US on Thursday ended a 13-year break in the series, unleashing a surge of fan enthusiasm and also concern among police departments.

"We need to talk," the San Juan Police Department, also in Texas, said in a video published on Instagram the same day the game launched in the US.

"We know you're excited and we know you've been waiting a long time, but what happens in GTA 6 stays in GTA 6."

In Arizona, the Pima County Sheriff's Office told GTA 6 fans in a Facebook post: "Real-life laws don't come with cheat codes, respawns, or mission restarts."

Law enforcement officials weren't the only ones worried, with one pundit on Fox News wondering if the game might "destigmatise crime". Rosanna Scotto also raised the question of whether it made young people "more inclined to use guns at an earlier age now because of these kind of video games".

Research on the relationship between video game violence and its effects on players is mixed.

The American Psychological Association (APA) issued a resolution in 2020 that said "violence is a complex social problem that likely stems from many factors".

"Attributing violence to violent video gaming is not scientifically sound and draws attention away from other factors," the APA said.

But the APA also said research showed an association between violent video games and increased aggressive behaviour and decreased moral judgement.

Despite concerns, the release of GTA 6 has had a meteoric landing, topping $2.36bn (£1.8bn) in first-day sales, and generating news headlines over the surge in people skipping school and work in order to play.

item.title: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
item.description: Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
item.content:encoded:
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.

Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".

The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.

Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.

He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.

A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.

"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.

Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy".

In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".

European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.

The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.

At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.

This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.

Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.

Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.

The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

item.title: Mysterious Mercury is about to get a visitor - after spacecraft's eight-year epic voyage
item.description: The mission is set to give us our best ever view of Mercury - the closest planet to the Sun.
item.content:encoded:
After an eight-year journey travelling almost six billion miles (10bn km), a spacecraft called BepiColombo is about to reach its final destination and get into orbit around Mercury.

It will be entering an extremely hostile environment: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and temperatures can reach a fierce 430C and then plunge to -180C, and it is constantly blasted with intense solar radiation.

Until now, the planet has been little explored but the hope is this mission will solve some of Mercury's major mysteries.

These include uncovering why there is ice in its craters despite its proximity to the Sun, and understanding the mysterious hollows that are dotted all over its surface.

"I think it's a little bit of an under-loved planet in the inner Solar System, but I think that's one of the reasons why it is so compelling," said Prof Emma Bunce, from Leicester University, who is a principal investigator on the mission.

"There are lots of reasons, scientifically, why we really want to understand Mercury, how it formed, how it evolved, what it looks like today, but also how it interacts with the Sun and the extreme space weather that it experiences."

The BepiColombo mission, which is a collaboration between the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japanese Space Agency (JAXA), blasted off in 2018, launching from French Guiana.

With the spacecraft heading deep into the inner Solar System, it has had to battle the Sun's immense gravitational pull.

So it has had its brakes on for the entire journey, and has also taken a very convoluted path - looping once around the Earth, twice around Venus and six times around Mercury - to slow it down enough to get into orbit.

This journey should have taken seven years, but a problem with BepiColombo's propulsion system meant the already epic voyage was extended by a year.

The final manoeuvre to get into orbit is a perilous one: it needs to perform a 37-minute handbrake turn to be grabbed by the planet's gravity.

If anything goes wrong, the spacecraft could hurtle past Mercury.

Only two spacecraft have visited Mercury until now - both Nasa missions.

Mariner-10 flew past the planet three times in the 1970s, and then the Messenger spacecraft arrived at Mercury in 2011 and spent four years in orbit.

But there is still much to discover about this tiny world.

Mercury is only a bit bigger than our Moon, and is covered in ancient volcanoes, towering cliffs and colossal craters.

And time on Mercury passes in a mind-bending way.

The planet zips around the Sun so quickly, a year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days. But it turns incredibly slowly on its own axis, so a single day there lasts 59 Earth days.

As well as investigating why Mercury has ice in its craters in the polar regions, the mission will also spend time studying strange dents in the planet's surface.

There are thousands of hollows all over it. They are shallow but with steep sides and often clustered together, and in planetary terms, they are young: about 100,000 years old.

Scientists know they are not impact craters - larger pockmarks on the surface caused by colliding space rocks - but they are not really sure what the hollows are or how they formed.

BepiColombo will also help to study another aspect of Mercury that has been puzzling researchers. Despite the planet's tiny size, it has a huge metal core.

Prof Emma Bunce said that the planet could once have been much bigger, but was potentially the victim of a "hit and run" early in its history.

"One of the explanations is that the mantle was stripped away in a large collision," she explained.

"Or it's a combination of collisions over a longer period of time that then strips away its outer outer regions, its mantle and its crust, and leads to the planet that we see today."

Or she said, it could have just formed that way in a metal-rich part of the early Solar System.

Unusually, this is a sort of "buy one get one free" mission - there are two spacecraft onboard.

A few weeks after arriving at Mercury they will separate.

An ESA craft will study the surface close-up, the other, which belongs to JAXA, will view the planet from a distance.

A life-size model of BepiColombo is on display at the Science Museum in London. It was used to test the craft while it was being put together.

Jessica Marshall, a systems engineer at Airbus, who built the spacecraft, showed us Bepi's key features - and said the moment of separation would be "nerve-wracking" for the team.

The two spacecraft had to be very securely attached together for their launch and long journey, but now, eight years later, they have to delicately disconnect.

"We have designed a special mechanism that we have thought very carefully about," said Marshall.

"It's been exposed to the harsh radiation of space and highly different thermal temperatures, and after eight years this is a spring mechanism that has to then release very gently… As it releases, it actually also twists in order to start the spin of that spacecraft as well."

With two orbiters at Mercury, both packed with instruments, the BepiColombo team hopes to find answers to Mercury's mysteries.

Of course, they may uncover many more once they arrive.

item.title: China issues Mount Fuji warning as family of missing climber offers reward
item.description: The $75,000 reward offered by Chen Jie's family has sparked fears of more reckless climbing attempts.
item.content:encoded:
The Chinese embassy in Japan has warned its citizens against off-season ascents of Mount Fuji amid concerns that the hefty reward offered by a missing hiker's family could encourage more reckless climbing.

Chen Jie, 25, vanished on 8 November on the mountain. His family is offering 500,000 yuan ($75,000; £57,300) to anyone who finds him alive, and 100,000 yuan to anyone who recovers his body, say Chinese and Japanese media reports.

Strong winds and blizzards pose serious risks during the closed season, especially as shelter and first-aid centres are not operational, the embassy said on Tuesday.

Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from around early July to early September.

Earlier this year, authorities of Yamanashi province, where the northern part of Mount Fuji sits, had said that people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service from next year on.

Authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season to submit detailed climbing plans.

"We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Kotaro Nagasaki, the prefecture governor, said at the time.

On Wednesday, Nagasaki told reporters that attempts to find the missing climber could lead to "secondary disasters"

According to Japanese news outlet the Mainichi Shimbun, Nagasaki appeared to appeal to Chen's family, saying: "I understand that your family is important, but please refrain from doing anything that could endanger others."

Some social media users in Japan have similarly expressed fears would entice people to venture into the mountains ill-prepared and lead to more accidents,

Yamanashi police said Chen had set out on his hike on 8 November with two friends, who turned back after they realised the mountain was closed and that they weren't suitably equipped for the conditions of the trails.

Chen pressed on alone from the fifth station of the Yoshida Trail, which sits at around 2,300m (7545ft) above sea level.

A friend last heard from Chen at 10:30 that day, when he sent a video message saying: "I'm going up the mountain... There's no one in sight."

The highest point of Mount Fuji, which is Japan's tallest peak, stands at 3,776m.

Local authorities launched a search for Chen on 10 November, but it had to be halted several times because of poor weather.

Chen's father reportedly arrived in Japan on 13 November. It is not clear when he posted the reward offer.

item.title: Tens of thousands of UK fridges secured from hackers in secret nationwide operation
item.description: Supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants and stadiums have been scrambling to make their devices safe.
item.content:encoded:
A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned.

Recent waves of cyber-attacks in Europe have seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage.

France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets, a claim Tehran denies.

It was thought the UK had largely escaped such hacks as the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix.

In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK.

Since then, researchers, IT teams and the National Cyber Security Centre have been working around the clock to warn dozens of companies.

The BBC has not reported on the large-scale, secretive operation until now to reduce the chances of hackers causing harm if they found the vulnerability.

Thousands of fridges taken off-line

The security threat was discovered by staff at refrigeration consultants Omega Solutions - it was then verified and expanded upon by experts at Pen Test Partners who helped raise the alarm.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) were then involved in the campaign to plug the security holes.

They held industry conference calls and tasked teams to contact firms at risk.

Thousands of devices controlling tens of thousands of refrigeration devices were taken off the open internet either remotely or, in some cases, physically - with staff ordered to remove internet cables and monitor temperatures manually.

BBC news has learnt most major supermarkets have been forced to divert IT teams to address the risks, with a worker at one large chain saying they took hundreds of devices offline every day over the course of a week.

"It did feel like a race against time as we were expecting another wave of these fridge hacks to come," said the person, who did not want to be publicly named.

"From a business perspective it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems. Our warehouses have millions of pounds worth of food that could have been spoiled if any hackers found out about this method of attack," they added.

There have been three waves of hacks on refrigeration temperature controllers so far this year:

  • In August, fridges at a small number of US military bases were impacted
  • On 11 and 12 October hundreds of supermarkets and food processing sites in France were hit when Danfoss temperature control systems were targeted
  • On 1 and 2 November dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries were hit, with Belgium and Luxembourg the worst affected. A small number of blood bank sites in France were also impacted

The waves of attacks prompted an expert at Omega Solutions to examine the security of the most popular refrigeration controllers in the UK, made by British firm Resource Data Management (RDM).

RDM disputes the critical nature of the vulnerabilities exposed but has been praised for its professional response to address the concerns, the BBC understands.

As well as supermarkets, multiple other areas of UK food and beverage industry were also warned to take action about the risks.

These include convenience stores, petrol stations, restaurants and fast food chains, sports arenas, hotels, food processing plants and cold storage sites.

"These popular controllers had a similar weak password problem to the Danfoss and other controllers that were attacked so successfully in previous hacks so we had to get the message out as soon as possible and keep it secret," said Ken Munro of Pen Test Partners.

"There is so much extra attention on these ubiquitous bits of kit now that it was likely a matter of days until criminals or nation state hackers figured it out," he added.

RDM, though, says comparisons with the units attacked in mainland Europe are not fair because hacking their fridges and freezers would have involved getting hold of a piece of hardware.

The ethical hackers say this would have been achievable as the hardware in question can be purchased cheaply online on sites like eBay.

"This was a vulnerability identified in a test environment," said Ged Evans, CEO of RDM.

He said the test "went beyond" what such exercises usually involved, as it "included dismantling our hardware".

"In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps," he added.

RDM confirmed that there was no sign of any malicious activity on the controllers and that it continued to work with the NCSC and other authorities to monitor the situation.

item.title: Three Kyiv bridges hit during major Russian missile attack
item.description: Five people were killed in a wave of strikes which follow Ukraine's successful targeting of the Crimean Bridge.
item.content:encoded:
Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.

Ballistic missiles hit three bridges in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least eight dead.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied peninsula.

The latest Russian strikes coincided with a flurry of talks around the war, and as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to ongoing Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.

The three Kyiv bridges targeted in Kyiv overnight - the Podilsko-Voskresensky Bridge, the Darnytskyi Bridge and the Southern Bridge - have been closed to traffic, adding to disruption created by retaliatory strikes on bridges earlier this week.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to "avoid travelling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary".

He added that an unspecified critical infrastructure facility was also damaged and seven medical personnel were injured during the night's assault.

Ukraine's major operation to take out the road section of the Crimean Bridge earlier this week was a tactical and symbolic blow for Moscow.

Since illegally annexing Crimea in 2014, Moscow has housed troops and military equipment there, with occupying forces travelling through the peninsula towards the front line.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said an operation to weaken the bridge's defences and ultimately cause part of it to collapse had been weeks in the making.

Russian President Vladimir Putin - who personally opened the bridge in 2019 to international condemnation - said the Kremlin's retaliation for the strike would be "far more painful".

Air raid sirens lasted non-stop throughout the night and were ongoing into the morning.

Ukraine's air force says almost 100 missiles were launched by Russia in its overnight attack - one of the largest attacks since the invasion began in 2022. It also involved around 400 drones.

The attack was "one of the most powerful" yet, according to Yuriy Ignat, head of communications for the Ukrainian air force.

Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky said 28 people were injured, with an ambulance hospital in Kharkiv among the targets of an attack which hit nine regions.

Two people were killed in a hit on the Sknyliv railway station in the south-west of Lviv, the city's Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said.

He shared a picture of the ruined remains of what he said was the station's ticket terminal.

Ten people were injured and a rescue operation at the site is ongoing.

A Russian cruise missile landed in Poland around 50km (31 miles) from its border with Ukraine, the Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Friday.

Two more unidentified projectiles, suspected to be a drone and a second missile, landed in villages nearby and no one was harmed, he added.

Polish and Swedish jets were scrambled on Nato's eastern flank as Russia's attack on western Ukraine continued. They have since been stood down.

The attack began hours after European leaders including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said they were ready for negotiations involving Moscow to end the war in Ukraine.

The Berlin meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing, an international alliance of Ukraine's allies committed to providing security support in the event of a peace deal, was attended by Zelensky and US President Donald Trump's envoys.

Jared Kushner said the US "wants to make a deal with Europe by his side" after fears of an agreement negotiated between the US and Russia were reignited by Trump's one-to-one talks with Putin earlier this week.

He claimed Russia was "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on Nato's Article Five, which requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.

On Monday, Russia's deputy foreign minister Sergei Ryabkov pushed back against that, saying "quasi-Nato" membership for Ukraine would be "unacceptable" to Russia. The Kremlin has long cited the prospect of Ukraine joining Nato as a key justification for its war effort.

The US president dialled into the Berlin talks from Air Force One on his way back from China, where he met his Russian counterpart and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

He reportedly questioned the decision of European leaders to commit €70bn (£58.6bn; $76.bn) in military funding for Ukraine.

item.title: I've only sold five copies of GTA 6, says shop owner
item.description: Games shop owner Richard Tewksbury says the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 has been a "write-off".
item.content:encoded:
The owner of an independent game shop says he has only sold five copies of the highly anticipated open-world action-adventure Grand Theft Auto 6.

GTA 6, as it is known, is estimated to become the biggest entertainment launch in history following the blockbuster video game's debut on Thursday, after a 13-year wait.

But Richard Tewksbury, who runs Super Game Shack in the Silver Arcade in Leicester, said he had seen "embarrassing" sales of the game because it was only released as a digital download and not on disc.

"People are super, super, super hungry for this game - so it's already doing crazy numbers already - but that's not translated for us."

"I've only sold four copies on PS5 and one copy on Xbox," added Tewksbury.

"It's because it's all digital - no-one sadly wants to buy a code in a box. We gave it a little go, but they just knocked it dead with making it digital. For game shops, it's a write-off.

"I'm really behind the game - I think it's amazing - but for shops, it's just not great."

In June, developer Rockstar Games said physical copies would contain a code for a digital download rather than the more traditional format. The company has been contacted for comment.

Tewksbury said, while he thinks the game is "amazing", the choice to not sell physical copies with discs was "not great" for smaller stores.

The release of the blockbuster came after two delays to its initial launch date in autumn 2025.

In advance of the launch, GTA 6 generated an estimated £1.25bn ($1.65bn) in revenue based on an estimated 17.07m units sold, sales tracker SensorTower said.

However, Tewksbury said sales at local stores had been poor because physical editions contain download codes rather than discs.

"It is possibly the biggest game hype there's ever been - 13 years people have been waiting for this," he said.

GTA 6 is one of the first major games to only be released without a traditional disc version.

However, Tewksbury said the reality for game shops was that this style of release would be the future of the industry.

Many consoles are now without physical disc drives and PlayStation announced in July that its games would no longer be released on discs from January 2028.

Sony, which owns PlayStation, said the move came "as consumer preferences and the broader entertainment industry continue to shift away from physical discs to digital".

"This is the way it's going to be," Tewksbury said.

"It's a big effect for us because it was such a massive game - everyone wants it.

"A lot of people aren't even aware that you could actually get it as a code in a box in a shop.

"Suddenly everyone's already pre-ordered it months in advance because the download is so large and [they] aren't thinking about us."

item.title: Cancer patient waited two days in chair, son says
item.description: NHS apologises after patients and families describe "awful" conditions at Lincoln County Hospital.
item.content:encoded:
The son of an 83-year-old cancer patient says she spent almost two days in a chair at A&E while waiting for a bed in hospital.

Nigel Wass says he had to bring his mother fluids, turn off alarms and find a wheelchair to take her to the toilet during "close to 48 hours" at Lincoln County Hospital, because staff were "run ragged".

One in 20 patients using Lincolnshire's emergency departments waited longer than 12 hours for a hospital bed, according to NHS figures for the year to October.

United Lincolnshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust (ULTH) apologised and said it "continued to implement improvements", including more rapid patient assessment and "timely patient discharges" to "free up beds".

Wass's mother had multiple infections during 18 months of cancer treatment, all needing emergency treatment.

He says he accompanied her to Lincoln County Hospital seven times between May and August and the emergency department was overwhelmed on each occasion.

On a visit in the summer, he says his mother was put in a chair in a side room, because she is immunosuppressed, but then forgotten about.

"The staff on the ground were amazing but there's simply not enough of them, so I'm caring for mum best I can, taking her to the toilet," Wass recalls.

"Fresh water wasn't available because the drinks machine has been broken for months. There are people in there that are dehydrated and that was the same with my mum.

"She had a drip, often the alarm would be going off it and it would take ages to get somebody to just come and press the reset button. In the end I did ask how to do it myself."

He describes his experience of the department as "crazy", with people "crying and afraid", lying on the floor, or "screaming in agony".

Paul Grantham-Rae says he was "absolutely disgusted" by his 85-year-old mother's experience at Lincoln's emergency department last month, after she spent 25 hours in a chair, then another seven sitting on a ward before a bed was found.

He says his mother had a leg wound, but because she takes blood thinners, the bandage was soon soaked and blood dripped on to the floor.

"We were asking the nurses if they could come and change it, and they said 'yes we'll be there shortly, we'll be there shortly," he recalls.

He says when he asked if staff knew how much blood she had lost, a nurse replied it was "a question we need to ask".

"I thought that's something that should have been detected straight away.

"There was one stage where her lips were quite blue."

Other patients and family members have told the BBC about similar experiences at Lincoln County Hospital. They include:

  • A man brought in by ambulance having a heart attack, who spent almost two days in a chair in the emergency department and waited five days for a bed on the cardiac ward.
  • A woman with a spinal fluid leak who spent 32 hours in a chair before being transferred to a specialist unit.
  • The daughter of an elderly woman with suspected sepsis, who says a nurse told everyone in the waiting area to go home, as the department was full.

NHS figures show the scale of pressure on emergency departments at Lincoln County and Boston Pilgrim hospitals.

The two departments saw 264,017 people in the year to October, with 5.2% waiting more than 12 hours to be admitted.

Fuelling the backlogs are delays in discharging patients who no longer need a bed. The figures show an average of 191 patients a day no longer required care in Lincoln, Boston and Grantham hospitals, but could not leave because of delays in social and community care, family arrangements, or organising medication.

Caroline Landon, the group chief operating officer at ULTH, says the trust's teams work "tirelessly" to monitor and care for those waiting to be admitted.

"Our hospitals, like many others in the country, are continuing to experience significant demand.

"During September alone, our A&E teams saw approximately 1,000 more patients compared to the previous September."

She says ULTH has "continued to implement improvements", including "quicker access to same-day emergency care" and "more rapid assessment" for those needing admission.

According to Landon, the trust is also "working closely with our Lincolnshire system partners to support timely patient discharges and improved access to community or home-based care, so that we free up beds in our hospitals".

Another patient frustrated by long waits is Martin Gibbs, who went to Lincoln's A&E with chest pains in October, two days after a heart procedure.

He says he spent 20 hours in a chair, waiting for an echocardiogram (ECG) and was not given his regular medication, as A&E staff were unable to access his records.

According to Gibbs, he was only given pain relief once, because a doctor in A&E signed him off to the cardiology unit, despite there being "no chance of getting me a bed".

He left after his partner, Nikki Applewhite, booked an ECG at a private hospital.

Applewhite says the department was "just awful".

"There was a man sitting there, it looked like his jaw was broken and he was bleeding. He just had a basket to catch the blood. There were two people either side of him on drips, both were bleeping, which obviously needed attending to.

"The water machine had broken, the vending machine had broken, the phone charging machine had broken.

"We talked to so many people and they said 'oh it's always like this' and you think, and you accept that that's normal?"

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: "October was the busiest month ever for A&E, but thanks to the hard work of NHS staff, almost three quarters of people were seen within four hours."

Listen to highlights from Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds, watch the latest episode of Look North.

item.title: White House removes cyber-security chief after series of tech outages
item.description: CBS is reporting he has been fired after losing the confidence of White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.
item.content:encoded:
The top cyber-security official in the US government is leaving his post after a string of tech outages which hit the National Security Agency (NSA), the US air traffic control system and some banks.

Sean Cairncross had been national cyber director since August 2025.

CBS, the BBC's US news partner, reported he had been fired after losing the confidence of White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio posted on X to say Department of Defense chief information officer Kirsten Davies was the new national cyber director.

The AFP news agency and CBS both said sources had told them Cairncross was fired, in a move supported by President Donald Trump.

The news, first reported by Axios, follows security concerns, including the ability of advanced AI models - mostly from US companies - to discover vulnerabilities which humans would not be able to find on their own.

Earlier this week, Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the outages were connected, adding "we are not under systemic attack".

But the fact that so many have happened in quick succession has left some people worried about the safety of the tech which is heavily relied on in all aspects of daily life.

Cairncross was previously a lawyer in the Republican Party, before becoming the chief operating officer of the Republican National Committee.

In the first Trump administration, he was part of the team of the White House chief of staff.

He later worked in the private sector, before returning to government in August 2025.

The White House has not publicly confirmed the departure or given a reason to why Cairncross left his role.

item.title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in stock market debut
item.description: Anthropic is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, creating a test for the entire industry.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion).

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.

Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each, showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.

Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?

In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.

Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.

The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.

The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.

"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."

While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.

The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet more quickly.

It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.

As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.

The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.

That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.

Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.

Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.

But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.

With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.

"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.

So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.

"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."

A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.

One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.

Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."

The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.

A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.

Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.

Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".

"AI carries real risks," she added.

Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

item.title: William and Catherine's India tour was 'particularly special', aide says
item.description: Prince William's most senior advisor described the royal couple as "very much a team".
item.content:encoded:
The most senior advisor to the Prince of Wales has said this week's visit with the Princess of Wales to India was "particularly special" and described the royal couple "as very much a team".

Prince William and Catherine are now back in the UK after spending three days in Mumbai and Delhi - the first time they have travelled together on overseas royal duties since the princess's cancer treatment.

The visit focused on the prince's Earthshot Prize which were hosted in Mumbai. His wife last attended the Earthshot awards when they were held in Boston in 2022.

"The prince has really enjoyed having the princess alongside him for Earthshot, and for her to see first-hand how much it has grown in scale since she last attended in Boston," Ian Patrick, the prince's private secretary told reporters.

"She's enormously proud of what he's achieved, and it has been particularly special for them to experience this moment together. They are very much a team."

The prince and princess also met the Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi at his residence in Delhi where they discussed UK-India partnerships.

In a social media post after the meeting, the prime minister said it had been "a pleasure to meet their Royal Highnesses" and praised the Earthshot Prize for "showcasing Indian ingenuity in addressing global environmental challenges".

The meeting was a late addition to the prince and princess's plans. Prime Minister Modi altered his schedule to return to India from a summit in the Philippines to ensure he could meet the royal couple.

"The prince and princess have had a thoroughly enjoyable time in India. They've been incredibly touched by the warmth of the welcome they've received," said Patrick.

The couple were last in India for an official tour in 2016.

"It's been wonderful for them to return together after ten years," the private secretary said. "They were incredibly inspired by the people they met. They leave with very happy memories and a real enthusiasm for building on the connections they've made with the next generation."

There was a focus on young people and their potential during the three day visit. This year, for the first time, there was a Children's Earthshot Awards where 15,000 schools across India took part creating solutions for environmental problems in their own communities.

"We cannot look into the eyes of the next generation and tell them that we knew what was happening, we knew what was at stake, and yet we did not do everything in our power to change it," Prince William said in his speech at the Earthshot Prize Awards Ceremony. "They will not judge us by the promises we made, but by the world we leave behind."

"The prince and princess don't want young people to feel unheard or that the challenges facing the planet and society are beyond their control," said Patrick. "They want them to feel optimistic, empowered and part of the solutions."

The Earthshot Prize was designed as a ten-year project - it is now in its sixth year and Prince William remains ambitious for it.

"Companies including Amazon, IKEA, Nvidia, Standard Chartered and Uber are now stepping forward to help their impact spread even further," said Jason Knauf, the chief executive officer of the Earthshot Prize.

"This is enormously encouraging but the prince wants to see more of the world's biggest businesses and investors get involved... every business and investor who joins us helps these solutions grow faster, building a healthier, happier and more prosperous future for us all."

Now that the prince and princess are travelling together on international duty, the visit was an insight into way their royal trips will operate in future.

The days of royal tours lasting two weeks will not be the approach of the royal couple who think they make a big impact over shorter trips with the additional help of social media to amplify their engagements. They also want to limit the amount of time they spend away from their three children.

"The prince and princess want their overseas travel to have purpose, meaning and impact. It's about building stronger relationships, creating opportunities for collaboration and supporting projects that deliver real results," explained Patrick.

Despite plans to keep future royal tours short, it's believed a visit to Australia could be in the plans for the couple in 2027.

At the Earthshot Prize Awards ceremony on Tuesday, Prince William was heard by reporters saying "Big year next year, Australia!"

Kensington Palace has not yet confirmed any further travel plans for the Waleses.

They last visited Australia in 2014 with nine-month-old Prince George. It is possible that their three children could join them on a future Australia trip.

Additional reporting by Charlotte Scarr in Delhi

item.title: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
item.description: European allies of Ukraine say they have a "united" negotiating position at a summit in Berlin.
item.content:encoded:
European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.

Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.

In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.

Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."

But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".

Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".

Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.

Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.

Zelensky and the three European leaders – Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron – were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."

The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".

"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.

He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.

"A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945.

He also sought to downplay the Shenzhen summit as above all "a photo opportunity."

"The US understands that there can be no peace without us. We, in turn, know that with the United States by our side, the prospects for peace increase," Merz added.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also took exception to Trump's description of Putin as a "friend" at the Shenzhen summit, saying: "Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be."

Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.

The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.

There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.

But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.

It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials have not budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory.

As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.

And Putin also vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.

He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.

Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready to make compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not.

"I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said, despite the fact that Russia has in recent months intensified its attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure as cold winter approaches.

Kyiv and its European allies say that – in the absence of any major success on the vast front line – the Kremlin leader is seeking to break Ukrainian resistance by leaving millions of civilians without electricity and water supply.

item.title: Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back
item.description: Shark Tank's Kevin O'Leary is among the big investors looking to Canada as a data centre development destination, while his US project faces local opposition.
item.content:encoded:
As Americans have grown increasingly sour on artificial intelligence (AI) data centre development, Canada's industry leaders are sensing an opportunity.

"Data centres in Canada looking pretty appealing right now," Lucy Hargreaves, CEO of non-profit policy group Build Canada, wrote on X the day after American voters passed 40 of 41 local ballot initiatives aimed at limiting or preventing data centre development in this month's midterm elections.

While the number of proposed AI data centres in the US dwarfs that of its northern neighbour, in recent months Canada is being increasingly pitched as a hub for these so-called "hyperscale" projects.

Those in favour argue that Canada's abundant land, natural gas and cold climate make it uniquely positioned to address some of the problems facing US AI infrastructure, from data centres' proximity to populated areas to noise pollution and strain on electricity grids.

"Some of the capital that would have been deployed to build data centres in the US is now more available for Canada," Hargreaves told the BBC in an interview.

"The question really is whether or not we want to go for that."

Unlike in the US, pushback to these projects in Canada has been muted - at least so far. Many are going ahead without significant disruptions, and legislators have openly embraced them without major political consequences.

At the heart of Canada's AI data centre boom is Alberta, where 90% of all currently proposed sites are set to be built.

The western Canadian province, rich with natural gas deposits, has pitched itself as "North America's destination of choice" for AI data centres, including by offering a "concierge" service for investors to help build these projects at "unparalleled speed".

One of those investors is Kevin O'Leary, the Canadian businessman, TV personality and an ally of Donald Trump, who announced plans this year to build two large AI data centres - one in Alberta and one in the US state of Utah.

His planned sites, both named Wonder Valley, are being received in very different ways on either side of the border.

Residents in Utah have organised a fierce opposition campaign. The pushback led outgoing state senator Stuart Adams to demand in June that O'Leary scale down the project by 75%, from 40,000 to 13,000 acres.

Financing for the Utah Wonder Valley data centre is still underway, and it is unclear when - and if - shovels will hit the ground on the project.

The proposed 7,000-acre, 7.5-gigawatt Alberta Wonder Valley project, meanwhile, has received strong backing from both the provincial government and the local municipality.

The project is billed as "off-grid", relying on its own power system fuelled by natural gas sourced from the region. In April, the Alberta government exempted the project from an environmental impact assessment, arguing it was unnecessary, though it will still need to obtain permits prior to construction.

The project was met with only limited opposition at a local town hall earlier this year. One resident, Dan Harms, told Bloomberg in June that he saw the economic benefits of the Wonder Valley data centre and that it was being built "out in the middle of nowhere".

In an interview with BBC News, Reeve Ryan Ratzlaf, of Greenview Municipality in north-western Alberta, said the project was the "perfect fit" for his rural community, which had been looking for an industrial tenant to fill a resource-rich parcel of land for 13 years.

Some community members have expressed concern about the amount of water needed to cool the proposed site annually, which is projected to be six million cubic metres, or about the size of 2,400 Olympic-size swimming pools.

Ratzlaf argued the amount was a drop compared to the annual flow of the nearby Smoky River, from which the centre would pull water. More broadly, he said he believed that economic benefits to the region outweighed potential risks.

"It's a giant warehouse with computer equipment inside," he said, arguing that it was less risky than petrochemical plants that could have been built in its place.

Speaking to BBC News, the CEO overseeing both O'Leary projects, Paul Palandjian, said the two were proceeding at an "equal" pace.

He acknowledged it had become more of a "hot topic" in the US than in Alberta. But there are signs public anger towards AI data centres in Alberta has grown in recent months.

Recent public information sessions on provincial AI data centre plans were attended by some furious residents.

"If no one wants this, why are you pushing forward with this?" one resident asked in an August town hall reported on by the Canadian Press, held shortly after Alberta announced that Meta would build a C$13bn ($9bn; £6.8bn) AI data centre in the province.

Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation has also recently sued the government over its decision to override the environmental assessment for O'Leary's Wonder Valley data centre, labelling it "irrational" in court filings.

This week, the Alberta government proposed legislation that would put restrictions on where data centres could be built in a bid to ease some concerns.

There are also signs that public cooperation may be fading elsewhere in the country.

On Saturday, hundreds of protesters gathered in Canada's Atlantic province of Nova Scotia against a proposed AI data centre that will be used by technology giant Anthropic.

But experts say the US backlash offers a cautionary tale for Canada as it tries to capitalise on the AI boom.

"AI is generally not very popular. This is both true in Canada and the United States," noted Sean Mullin, a senior fellow at the University of Toronto and former adviser to Canada's prime minister on the national sovereign AI compute strategy.

"I think we could experience some of the same backlashes if we're not thoughtful about it," he said.

So far, lawmakers in Canada have stood firm.

The Carney government, which has made reducing Canada's reliance on the US a priority, has framed the development of AI data centres as a matter of national security and sovereignty. It has projected that Canada needs to expand its computing capacity 16-fold over the next four years to meet domestic demand.

Alberta is defending its data centre plans by saying they will create jobs and generate revenue, and that sites will be developed "responsibly".

In Ontario, Premier Doug Ford has said that his province needs to move "full steam ahead" with building data centres.

Mullin said one reason the backlash had been less severe in Canada was simply due to scope and timing.

"There has been less of these projects happening, and as a result, they've attracted less attention," he said.

Canada has released some high-level guidance on data centre development, which has been co-signed by Anthropic, Meta and other big AI players. It calls on data centres to pay for electricity costs, minimise water use and create long-term benefits for the regions they are in.

If politicians don't tread carefully, Bek MacIntosh, an Alberta resident who has fought a proposed hyperscale data centre in her community, said she believed public discontent could translate into angry votes, like those seen in the US.

MacIntosh successfully halted a data centre in Olds, Alberta, over concerns with its scale, scope and proximity to her home. Even after her eight-month battle, she said she was not opposed to all AI infrastructure and believed Canada had the resources and landscape to build them responsibly.

But she fears Alberta has opened the door to "the most reckless of reckless developers", and warned that voters might have a "knee-jerk reaction" if provinces don't take care to develop AI data centres responsibly.

"And I don't think any political party in Canada is prepared for it."

item.title: Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish
item.description: Daily pill daraxonrasib appears to shrink and possibly even eliminate tumours in some patients with one of the deadliest cancers.
item.content:encoded:
Experts are calling it the biggest breakthrough in pancreatic cancer treatment for decades - a daily pill that appears to shrink and possibly even eliminate tumours in some patients with one of the deadliest and hardest-to-treat cancers.

Cancer became undetectable on scans in one in 12 of the patients given daraxonrasib along with chemotherapy in early medical trials.

Tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 participants who had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.

But doctors stress it is a long way from knowing how long it might keep the disease at bay and should not be seen as a cure.

Incredibly exciting

Cancer Research UK called it "the biggest leap forward in decades" for pancreatic cancer patients.

The charity's Dr Sam Godfrey told BBC News that the results were incredibly exciting. "What this new drug has done is it's found a way of drugging the undruggable.

"We are finally seeing progress in pancreatic cancer which is so long overdue."

Pancreatic cancer is notoriously hard to treat and has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK.

Although chemotherapy can shrink tumours a bit, the cancer often grows again.

Most patients with advanced disease survive months, not years.

Doctors hope the new treatment might offer patients more time, even if it cannot stop cancers for good.

The trial followed patients for a year and a half, on average, and some did not see their cancer return during this time.

Longer studies are needed to understand if any of these cancers can be put into remission and for how long.

In the trial:

  • tumours stopped growing in 90% of patients
  • just over 60% of patients saw their tumours shrink or disappear
  • for around 8% of patients, or one in 12, tumours became undetectable on CT scans

Longer survival

Dr Wungki Park, from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in the US and who is involved in the trial, said the results were extremely encouraging so far.

"We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival," he said.

Daraxonrasib is a KRAS inhibitor treatment that has already been approved in the US. It works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations, called RAS, found in most pancreatic cancers that drive tumour growth.

Dozens of other cancers, including lung and ovarian, can have similar mutations, meaning the drug might help lots of other patients too.

Dr Godfrey said: "I would hope that the early success that we are beginning to see in pancreatic cancer can also be rolled out to other cancers."

He said longer trials and results were vital. "Cancer can come back and even if scans show there is no sign of it, you don't necessarily know you are cancer-free until more time has passed."

Prof Elena Garralda, chair of a European cancer conference called EORTC where the work is being presented to other doctors, said: "These results are exciting because they show the combined treatment could potentially significantly improve patients' overall survival, as well as the time before tumours start to grow again."

There are 11,500 diagnoses of the disease in Britain each year and around 10,200 deaths, according to Cancer Research UK.

Actor Alan Rickman died of the disease in 2016, five months after diagnosis.

Symptoms can include jaundice, itchy skin, darker pee, paler poo, unexplained weight loss, tiredness and high temperature.

item.title: Fiona the hippo dies after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo
item.description: Fiona, who became an internet star after her premature birth in 2017, "fought until she couldn’t anymore", the zoo says.
item.content:encoded:
The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona has died just days after swallowing a knitted hat that slipped into her enclosure.

"It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency," the zoo said on Thursday afternoon.

Fiona, who became a social media star after her premature birth in 2017, swallowed the hat about 10 days ago and required emergency care.

The vet staff "tried everything they could to help her" but "it was ultimately too much to overcome", the zoo said.
