"We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore."

Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, had said that the hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.

"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.

While she seemed fine at first, her appetite started to decrease a few days later, and the zoo staff tried to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system.

An ultrasound before her death showed the hat passing through Fiona's small intestine. A zookeeper said surgery was not an option for full-grown hippos and "our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own".

The zoo also tried a different approach to attempt to get the hat to pass by encouraging Fiona to stand on a vibration plate platform borrowed from a local horse farm.

"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Jenike said.

Fiona was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo in 2017 and at first struggled to survive. At birth, she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species.

Her death is also very premature, with hippos normally living up to 50 years in human care, according to the zoo.

"Although this was not an intentional incident, of which, regrettably, there are many, Fiona's painful death is a tragic reminder that everyone should behave carefully and respectfully around animals," Debbie Metzler, the Managing Director of Captive Wildlife for the animal rights group Peta.

"Peta expects that the zoo will review its protocols to help prevent anything like this from happening again, and we urge every visitor to secure their belongings and never toss objects near an animal's enclosure."

As well as being famous online, Fiona's story inspired an ice cream flavour and a character in Cincinnati's ballet.

Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval said Fiona "was a symbol of perseverance and joy" in the city.

"She brought smiles to so many faces, from kids to parents to visitors from around the world," he wrote on X. "Our city is heartbroken, but we couldn't be more grateful that she was part of our lives and our community as a whole."

item.title: Trump posthumously pardons US baseball legend Pete Rose
item.description: Rose, who died in 2024, was given a lifetime ban from the sport for betting on games but was reinstated last year.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump has posthumously pardoned baseball legend Pete Rose.

"I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday.

Rose, who died in 2024 at the age of 83, pleaded guilty in 1990 to two counts of filing false tax returns. He was also given a lifetime ban from Major League Baseball (MLB) after an investigation revealed he bet on games.

The baseball star was posthumously reinstated to MLB, in which he played for 24 seasons, last year and made eligible for the Baseball Hall of Fame.

Trump also said on Thursday that Rose's "record of 4,256 Hits in a Season will never be broken".

In fact, Rose accumulated a record 4,256 hits - which MLB defines as a batter striking the baseball into fair territory and reaching base without doing so via an error or a fielder's choice - during his career, which is more than any other player. He played a total of 3,562 games.

According to Trump, Rose "was treated terribly by Major League Baseball in not allowing him to go into the Baseball Hall of Fame. Politics, I guess".

The US Constitution gives a sitting president the broad power to grant a pardon, which represents legal forgiveness and ends any further punishment.

Because Rose's pardon was issued after his death, it is largely symbolic and does not change Rose's Hall of Fame status. The Department of Justice (DoJ) typically does not process posthumous pardon applications, though presidents have still issued them.

The BBC has contacted the Hall of Fame and the DoJ for comment.

The US president had previously floated the idea of pardoning Rose in March last year before the MLB reinstated him.

"Major League Baseball didn't have the courage or decency to put the late, great, Pete Rose, also known as 'Charlie Hustle,' into the Baseball Hall of fame," he wrote on Truth Social at the time.

"Now he is dead, will never experience the thrill of being selected, even though he was a FAR BETTER PLAYER than most of those who made it, and can only be named posthumously. WHAT A SHAME," Trump added.

MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred issued a decision in May 2025 that created a pathway for Rose to be eligible to be inducted into the baseball Hall of Fame - a ruling that also applied to 16 other people - as early as 2028.

In August 1989, Rose agreed to the permanent ban from the sport after MLB investigators found that he bet on his team, the Cincinnati Reds, multiple times while he was playing on and managing the team from 1985 to 1987.

In July 1990, after Rose admitted to failing to report $354,968 (£271,107) in income over a four-year period, he was sentenced to five months in prison. He also was fined $50,000 and ordered to perform community service at the time.

item.title: Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting
item.description: While the presidents have previously met for one-on-one meetings, this is their first trilateral discussion.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following historic trilateral talks.

The three leaders met for 90 minutes in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

While the presidents have previously had one-on-one meetings, these are their first trilateral talks.

In the declaration, they said "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and that the countries planned to increase the production and supply of petroleum. They also said they were "committed to reform the UN" to respond more effectively to global challenges.

Thursday's statement also flagged the issue of immunity enjoyed by state officials and said "they agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction".

Trump praised the trilateral meeting calling it "a great and highly consequential trip", in a social media post while flying back to Washington on Air Force One.

In the same post, the president announced he would host a news conference to talk about the trip on Friday at the White House.

While in China, Trump met Putin ahead of the trilateral, in their first meeting since August 2025, where the US president greeted his Russian counterpart as his "friend".

He also spoke with Xi in a separate conversation, describing the pair's relationship as "very special".

Beyond the warmth and shared niceties, however, the three men had different goals and motivations for the sit-down.

The opening remarks of the trilateral gave some indication about what was to be discussed during the closed-door meeting.

Before giving the floor to his fellow leaders, Xi said that "positive interaction among major powers is not a matter of choice, but a mandatory requirement".

Putin followed this by highlighting a shared interest in ending the Ukraine war and said the conversation would also touch on food and energy security.

China has officially remained neutral since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, rejecting accusations from Kyiv and its allies that it has been tacitly supporting Moscow, including by exporting dual-use technology used by the Russian military.

Beijing has also repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's aggression.

Meanwhile, Trump closed by saying the presidents of three of the world's largest countries have a "special responsibility" to maintain productive dialogue.

"Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," he said, adding: "We feel the opposite."

Trump referenced the three countries' nuclear capabilities and said they are "uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth".

It is "vital" that they co-operate to "combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world", he said, adding: "That's what we're doing in Iran."

"We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon".

Trump then turned to Ukraine and said he and Putin have had a "long discussion" on the conflict there already.

He added that Putin "and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war".

Putin addressed the media following the trilateral meeting and described it as an "important chapter in the history of diplomacy".

He said Ukraine and Europe were not yet ready to make compromises to resolve the conflict in Ukraine - but he said Russia had invited EU representatives to Moscow to better understand Europe's position.

As the talks were under way in China, and even as Putin was holding his press conference claiming to be ready for peace, Ukraine's capital Kyiv was under attack from Russian drones.

Putin has repeatedly rejected all ceasefire offers from Ukraine, insisting on his maximalist demands which Kyiv and its European allies say are tantamount to de facto capitulation of Ukraine.

In Shenzhen, the Kremlin leader also vowed a "far more painful" retaliation in response to Ukrainian attacks on the bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea. A missile and drone attack on Tuesday destroyed its central road section.

There was no mention from Putin of almost five years of Russian attacks on power plants, bridges and residential buildings in Ukraine.

The Russian president also directly addressed comparisons between his meeting with Trump and Xi and the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the US met towards the end of World War Two.

"Nobody divided up the world at Yalta. It simply codified the realities that had emerged after WW2.

"And when it comes to today's conflicts, the realities on the ground will have to be accepted."

The Kremlin released a video showing Putin leaving the summit venue and saying goodbye to Xi.

"Thank you for organising this," Putin said. "I don't think anyone even expected everything to go so well."

Meanwhile, China's president described his meeting with Putin and Trump as "positive, constructive, and highly productive", according to the country's state broadcaster CCTV.

It added that Xi recalled "the history of fighting side-by-side during WW2", as the three leaders emphasised the importance of "cherishing the hard-won peace".

Thursday's trilateral meeting was reportedly the idea of Putin.

Some Russian newspapers called it a "diplomatic victory" as after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine many Western leaders were trying to isolate him.

The summit also marked the first time since Russia's war in Ukraine began that Putin took part in an international gathering attended by leaders from countries including Canada, Japan and Australia.

US lawmakers responded with frustration to Trump's warmth towards America's geopolitical adversaries.

"I was encouraged by some of the commitments that came out of the President's meetings in Asia, particularly the recognition that nuclear war must never be fought," Republican Senator John Curtis said in an emailed statement to the BBC.

But Curtis also said he was concerned about Trump's approach to the foreign leaders, adding that "Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are not our friends".

"We should not treat them as though they share our values or interests," Curtis, who sits on the Senate foreign relations committee, added.

"Doing so risks undermining our national security, weakening trust with our allies, and sending the wrong message about where America stands."

Jeanne Shaheen, a ranking Democratic member on the same committee, chose harsher words in her comment.

"President Trump's 'friend' is a murderous war criminal," she wrote on X.

With additional reporting from Brandon Drenon

item.title: Susan Smith denied parole again 32 years after drowning her two sons
item.description: At a hearing on the possibility of parole, Smith said she wished she could change the past, and her two children "did not deserve to die".
item.content:encoded:
A South Carolina woman who admitted to drowning her two sons 32 years ago has been denied parole for a second time.

Susan Smith, 55, was convicted of killing her boys by strapping them into their car seats and rolling her vehicle into a lake in 1994.

"I got to my lowest when I let that car go into that lake," Smith said during a hearing on Thursday with the state board that decides whether to release those in prison on parole.

The seven-member board later unanimously turned down her request to be freed. The father of the two boys has vowed to continue to oppose her release, and several people spoke against her in the hearing.

Smith, whose lawyers had argued she suffered a mental breakdown during the crime, can apply to the South Carolina Board of Probation, Parole and Pardon Services for parole every two years.

She told the board that she had changed and matured since killing three-year-old Michael and one-year-old Alex, and that "I am not the same person I was 32 years ago".

She also said she was "very, very sorry" and that she would go back and change the circumstances if she could.

"They were innocent children," Smith said. "They did not deserve to die."

Her children's father, David Smith, attended the hearing so he could advocate for their sons, he said.

The 32 years, he said, do not take away what Smith "deliberately" did.

"I know in my heart granting her parole would be a huge injustice to Michael and Alex," said David Smith, who had pinned a photo of both his sons to his lapel.

Prosecutors argued during the trial that Smith killed the boys after a man with whom she was having an affair told her that her sons were the reason that the pair did not have a future together.

At Thursday's hearing, Smith said: "This did not happen because of a man. That's just not true."

When the boys first disappeared, Smith said she was carjacked late at night and a man drove away with her car. While she pleaded publicly for their safe return, her sons were at the bottom of a nearby lake.

But ultimately she confessed to the crime.

Defence lawyers said she had wanted to die with her children but left the car at the last minute.

Smith was convicted of murder. Under South Carolina law at the time, she was allowed to request parole every two years after serving 30 years in prison.

In the US, some people convicted of crimes are eligible for parole, which means they can be released from incarceration.

She would have needed two-thirds of the board members present to vote in her favour to be freed.

item.title: Florence Pugh hits out at weight loss and cosmetic surgery speculation
item.description: The actress said how stressful" it was with people "talking about you... in ways you can't comprehend".
item.content:encoded:
Florence Pugh has said she was "disturbed" to see "thousands of people" discussing her recent appearance at the Governors Awards, and denied speculation about weight-loss drugs and facial surgery.

The actress wrote on Instagram how "stressful" it was waking up to people "talking about you and your body in ways that you can't even comprehend".

"I have never been on Ozempic. I have never done any face surgery," she wrote. "And don't ever say that I didn't make my own nose, I've always had that beautiful ski slope. Even as a baby!"

She added: "For the first time in my entire career, I have had the opportunity to be rested, to sleep, to wake up and work out and to eat regularly and healthily."

In her eight-page statement, the Oppenheimer, Dune and East of Eden star told followers: "I'm looking after myself, and that's literally it."

Pugh highlighted that losing weight had not been her goal, and she had lost "two pounds".

"The thing that's most important to me and my trainer is muscle," she said. "I think it's the most important thing a woman can do. Build muscle and be strong. I can now do six pull-ups and lift 110kg.

"Which I'm sure to many of you isn't a lot... but to me?! It's everything."

The actress said that from the moment she entered the acting industry she was "subjected to fat shaming".

"I have loved every time I get to tell someone they are being inappropriate about my weight, and I'm not changing that now just because you've all said so."

She also said she was "disturbed" that "women who now think that I'm someone I'm not, for having my body dissected and pointed at again".

"I have spent my whole career defending and protecting bodies that just grow the way they grow."

Professor Heather Widdows from Everyday Lookism, which campaigns to end body shaming, told BBC News: "Pugh is right that we are in a place where 'beauty standards are changing, getting harder and harder to keep up with'.

"A global beauty ideal makes impossible demands and normalises what were once extreme," added Widdows, who is Professor of Philosophy at the University of Warwick.

"We know that body-shaming individuals is harmful. Given this, we should not say negative things about other people's bodies... in a world where our bodies are increasingly ourselves, when you shame bodies you shame people."

Pugh, who was Oscar-nominated for Little Women in 2020 and played Black Widow assassin Yelena Belova in this year's Spider-Man: Brand New Day, has previously spoken out against judgement about women's looks.

In 2024, she told the Times she aimed to "challenge how women were perceived".

"Look, not everybody has legs that go on for days. I remember watching this industry and feeling that I wasn't represented," she said. "I've loved challenging ideas I don't like."

She also spoke about why she thinks she receives criticism about her appearance.

"I've always been aware that seeing a confident woman be happy in her skin is triggering to a lot of people and for a long time just accepted that I will receive commentary like that," she said.

"But now this...? I'm asking us all to just be mindful. We are real people, living real lives."

Pugh did not have comments turned on for her post, but it was liked by celebrities including Ashley James, who is known for speaking out about body positivity, plus Carol Vorderman, Zoe Ball, writer and actress Katy Brand and doctor and broadcaster Amir Khan.

'Please be gentle'

Pugh also said she had sued several publications earlier this year, claiming they published AI-generated images appearing to show her receiving cosmetic injections that were presented as real photographs.

"I was... horrified," she wrote, claiming the articles had damaged her reputation.

The actress concluded by urging followers to think about their attitudes towards physical appearance.

"I understand that we are in a warped part of image history right now, with beauty standards changing, getting harder and harder to keep up with," she said.

"But please be gentle to yourselves and others when you go in on people's physical appearance.

"I'm not angry at you, I'm angry at the situation that's being projected onto us.

"It feels inescapable, but part of changing the tide is on you as much as us in the public eye."

item.title: Venezuela signs military deal with US less than a year after Maduro's removal
item.description: The US Secretary of Defence says Venezuela has "gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner".
item.content:encoded:
The United States and Venezuela have re-established military ties less than a year after US forces seized the then-leader of the South American country, Nicolás Maduro, in a raid on the capital, Caracas.

The interim government led by Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro's former vice-president, signed a military co-operation agreement with US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth on Wednesday.

Few details about the deal have been released so far but Hegseth said that Venezuela had "gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner" in less than 12 months.

Interim President Rodríguez said the deal would help confront "common threats".

Military co-operation between the two countries was terminated in 2005 by Hugo Chávez, Venezuela's left-wing president at the time.

Chávez alleged that US military personnel sent to Venezuela to train their counterparts had made disparaging remarks about his government.

He also accused the US military office located in Fuerte Tiuna, Venezuela's largest military complex, of being "an organ of the CIA... conspiring against the government".

Under Nicolás Maduro, who succeeded Chávez after the latter's death from cancer, relations between the two countries deteriorated further.

They reached rock bottom late last year when the US doubled its reward for information leading to Maduro's capture to $50m (£38m) and eventually seized him on 3 January in a military raid.

Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are now in custody in New York on charges of drug-trafficking and conspiracy to commit torture, which they deny.

Hegseth addressed the change in the two countries' relationship since Maduro was seized in his speech at the US embassy in Caracas on Wednesday.

"It's a great honour to be here as the first United States Secretary of War this century to set foot in Venezuela. The weight of this moment does not escape me," he said.

"Just one year ago, my presence here, our presence here would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable," he added before recalling a public appearance by then-President Maduro which had angered the Trump administration.

"Exactly one year ago today, the indicted narco-terrorist fugitive Nicolás Maduro, the man who spent more than a decade handing Venezuela's borders and territory to terrorists from all over the world, stood on a stage, not too far from here, and yelled mockingly: 'Come and get me!'. Well, we answered that call."

Hegseth added that the result of the US military raid on 3 January had been as Maduro predicted, quoting the deposed leader's words: "No war, yes peace."

He described the deal signed by him and Venezuela's defence minister on Wednesday as a "new chapter for the United States, for Venezuela, for the Venezuelan military and for the Western Hemisphere through the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition".

Rodríguez described it as "extraordinarily relevant for our bilateral relations".

"In a matter of months, secretary, we have turned very difficult moments for our people into a space for co-operation and mutual benefit for both of our countries," she said addressing Hegseth during a meeting at the presidential palace.

While no details of the deal have been published, in her speech Rodríguez mentioned the training of Venezuela's armed forces and improving its "operational equipment" and access to new technology "to confront shared threats".

In his speech at the US embassy, Hegseth was more direct about who he considers to be those threats. Addressing "the narco-terrorists who abuse this [Venezuela] as a safe haven", he warned that "we will hunt you down, we will find you, and we will kill you".

From Venezuela, Hegseth travelled on to neighbouring Colombia, whose president, Abelardo de la Espriella, is a close ally of the Trump administration.

Colombia is already part of the US-led Americas Counter Cartel Coalition and in August, Hegseth had floated the possibility of joint US-Colombian military operations against armed groups.

On Wednesday, President de la Espriella took to X to deny a report by the New York Times which had stated that he had rejected carrying out joint operations.

In his post, he stressed that any decision would be taken while respecting Colombia's constitution, and the country's laws and sovereignty.

Hegseth reposted the tweet commenting that the US-Colombian partnership "is stronger than ever before".

item.title: Men guilty of abusing woman drugged and advertised for sex by husband
item.description: Philip Young, 50, drugged and raped his wife, Joanne Young, over a 13-year period.
item.content:encoded:
Four men have been found guilty of sexually abusing a woman whose husband drugged and secretly advertised her for sex on the internet, in the first trial of its kind in the UK.

Philip Young, 50, had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and raping his wife, Joanne Young, over a 13-year period at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire.

Norman Macksoni, 48, Richard Wilkins, 62, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were found guilty of multiple sexual offences by a jury at Winchester Crown Court. Wilkins and Macksoni were each found guilty of one count of rape.

Joanne Young, who divorced Philip Young last year, beamed at police as she left court wiping her eyes.

On the steps outside the court, Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity, said the abuse had "cost me my life as I knew it".

"The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way.

"This has resulted in a devastating impact on the lives of myself and my children."

She continued: "What happened to me was not the act of one man alone, others were invited to take part and they chose to.

"That choice makes them complicit in what was done to me and today's verdicts recognise that."

She said the verdicts were significant "more broadly for women and girls who have been abused by men," sending the message "that you can be believed and understood".

She urged the government to look at the law of consent "as a priority" so that women were "properly protected in the future", adding her abuse case raised "serious questions".

Judge Mr Justice Saini had asked for calm as the verdicts were read out, with Joanne Young sitting in the public gallery surrounded by her family, her hands clasped over her mouth.

She gasped as the first guilty verdicts were read out against Connor Sanderson-Doyle, who dropped his head as he was convicted of one count of sexual assault by touching and one count of sexual assault by penetration.

The jury of eight men and four women also convicted Wilkins of one count of assault by penetration.

Hassan was found guilty of one count of sexual assault by touching.

A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, of Street, in Somerset, admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape at an earlier court hearing in February.

The judge commended Joanne Young and said she had shown "amazing bravery through these proceedings".

One police officer could also be seen sobbing as they left the court.

As all defendants were led from the courtroom after being told by the judge to expect lengthy jail terms when they are sentenced on 21 and 22 December, Joanne Young's family could be seen hugging.

Philip Young - who served as a Conservative Swindon borough councillor between 2007 and 2010 - drugged and raped his wife over 13 years and invited the men via websites and apps such as Craigslist, Grindr and Fab Swingers to have sex with her without her knowledge.

He pleaded guilty at an earlier court hearing to 56 charges made up of 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing obscene articles in relation to his wife.

James Foster, specialist Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) prosecutor, said: "This is the first time in the UK that a jury have convicted or been asked to consider a case of organised drug-facilitated sexual abuse, which has been organised by the husband."

The crimes of the former Tory councillor emerged after the highly publicised case in France of Gisèle Pelicot, whose husband, Dominique Pelicot, drugged and raped her and invited 50 other men to abuse her. Gisèle Pelicot also waived her right to anonymity in that trial.

Her husband was jailed for 20 years in France in 2024 and all the defendants were found guilty of at least one charge.

  • If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

Police and prosecutors building the case against Philip Young sought the expertise of the French investigators to assist them in bringing him to justice.

Detectives discovered that Philip Young, whose most recent address was in Enfield, north London, had taken 480 intimate images and videos of his wife on 200 occasions and posted images online on at least 500 occasions – with the vast majority of these taken at the family home in Swindon.

The trial of the four defendants heard the investigation into Philip Young had begun after police were alerted to the fact he had uploaded extreme pornographic images to the internet in 2023.

Wiltshire Police said it was still looking for another man wanted in connection with alleged sex offences against Joanne Young.

They described him as being of "a large build, hairy, with scarring on the back of his head, prominent lips, short or shaved hair, and a distinctive tattoo on the left side of his chest".

Wiltshire Police added the extent of drug-rape offences was unknown because victims might not know they had been targeted.

A police spokesperson said: "While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly under-reported crime type.

"Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption.

"These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging."

item.title: Ella Langley sweeps Country Music Awards as Taylor Swift performs
item.description: Langley won six awards, weeks after her hit Choosin' Texas broke a Billboard chart record in the US.
item.content:encoded:
US singer Ella Langley has swept the Country Music Association Awards (CMAs), following the huge success of her breakthrough hit Choosin' Texas.

The Alabama-born singer was named entertainer of the year at Wednesday's ceremony, weeks after the song became the longest-running number one in Billboard chart history.

"At this point, I'm sick of me," the 27-year-old joked in her acceptance speech, having spent so much of the ceremony on stage. "I could quit tomorrow and have the best career of my life."

Choosin' Texas was also named single of the year and song of the year, leading Langley to joke in an acceptance speech: "This song is the gift that keeps on giving."

Langley won six awards in total, including female vocalist of the year, music video of the year and album of the year for Dandelion.

She also performed her song Loving Life Again with a string quartet, and duetted with Miranda Lambert for a performance of Snakeskin Boots.

Choosin' Texas made history in September after spending 23 weeks at the top spot on the Billboard Hot 100 chart. It has now spent 28 weeks in total at the summit.

Following her win, Langley took to social media and said: "Hard to put this night into words and what it means.

"Thank you to my fans. Thank you for loving this record, thank you for coming to my shows, thank you for believing in my artistry.

"This year has been the most incredible journey, and I want to thank you for sharing in that with me. I love y'all."

Taylor Swift also performed at the CMA Awards for the first time in 13 years.

Her performance began with Swift walking backstage and featured cameo appearances from country stars including Brad Paisley, Little Big Town, Sugarland, and Brooks & Dunn.

Swift then sang her recent hit I Knew It, I Knew You, from the Toy Story 5 soundtrack, using a blue guitar with bedazzled clouds on it, in a nod to the animated franchise.

The singer also mixed in some of her 2006 country hit Our Song, while Keith Urban joined her on the banjo.

Swift's performance came after she was inducted into both the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame and the Songwriters Hall of Fame earlier this year.

Other winners on the night included Chris Stapleton who won male vocalist of the year, The Red Clay Strays who won vocal group of the year, and Brooks & Dunn with vocal duo of the year.

Meanwhile Stephen Wilson Jr won the new artist of the year award while Charlie Worsham won musician of the year.

The award ceremony began with a tribute to country music legend Dolly Parton, who died in August aged 80.

Ceremony host Lainey Wilson began the tribute by duetting with singer-songwriter Vince Gill on a rendition of Parton's I Will Always Love You.

item.title: Joanne Young was drugged and raped by strangers after her husband offered her online
item.description: The warning comes after four men are found guilty of abusing a woman who was drugged by her husband.
item.content:encoded:
Warning: This story discusses sexual violence and abuse

When Joanne Young awoke tied to her bed, she had no idea about the horror that had been unfolding while she was unconscious.

After hearing her then-husband Philip Young calling for someone else to "get down", she quickly realised another person was in the bedroom with them.

Unbeknown to Joanne, Young had advertised online for other men to abuse her. He then drugged her and invited a series of strangers into their bedroom to sexually assault her.

This had been going on for 13 years.

On Thursday, four men were convicted of a number of offences including raping and assaulting her. Her ex-husband had already pleaded guilty to a number of rape charges.

Young, a former Conservative councillor, and another man, Dean Hamilton, pleaded guilty to rape and sexual assault at a previous hearing.

The group came from a variety of backgrounds. One of the men worked on Ministry of Defence nuclear defence projects while another drove Red Cross trucks to Romania in the 1980s.

Speaking outside court after the verdicts earlier, Joanne said "silence is not an option if we are serious about preventing abuse" - you can read her statement in full here.

Her case has striking comparisons with the repeated rape of Gisèle Pelicot in France, with experts saying the crime was "deeply abusive".

Online, Young portrayed the abuse as a shared sexual kink known as "cuckolding". The photographs used in the adverts posted on sites like Craigslist and Grindr showed Joanne inanimate and tied to the bed.

James Foster, a specialist prosecutor with the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), said Young "would drug her so that he could then sexually abuse her and record that sexual abuse and also arrange for other men to attend the address to sexually abuse her".

One of the men who answered the advert was Dean Hamilton, 46, who admitted to raping Joanne and abusing her in 2015.

The other men who were convicted of sexually assaulting Joanne were Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, Richard Wilkins, 62, Norman Macksoni, 48 and Mohammed Hassan, 38 - the man Young told to "get down" when Joanne woke.

They told the court they believed they had the consent of both Joanne and Young and were told Joanne was pretending to be asleep - when in fact she was heavily sedated.

"But not once during any of this abuse did they ask Joanne Young what she wanted or show any interest in what her wishes were," Foster said.

The law states the sexual consent can only be given if the person involved "agrees by choice ... and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice".

Investigators are told to establish "what steps, if any, the suspect took to obtain the complainant's consent".

Professor Marianne Hester, emeritus professor at the University of Bristol, said Joanne "clearly" had no capacity to say no, adding a "women cannot consent if they are asleep".

"So it's the same if they are completely drugged. They cannot make the decision to agree to sex," she added.

Hester, who has researched gender-based violence for years, said those cases raise broader questions about attitudes towards women and sex.

"We have to question the men, the way men think it's okay to do sex and how they keep normalising, we keep normalising all these very abusive acts within sex and that's really problematic," she said.

Hester added: "We know that investigations have now started on certain websites and that individuals have been identified in a number of different countries who have been up to exactly the same kind of thing.

"So I think that there are potentially quite a lot more cases in the pipeline."

The case has also reignited questions about the role of websites used to facilitate abuse.

Lisa Sugiura, Professor of Cyber Crime and Gender at the University of Portsmouth, argued online platforms have a responsibility to address content that normalises violence against women.

"Often these sites are accompanied by image-based abuse and deeply violent language and rhetoric about women anyway," she said.

"You think, how are these forums allowed to act with impunity without oversight and accountability?

"Before we even get to the question of whether we should simply accept the word of a man claiming to speak on behalf of himself and his wife."

Data shows hundreds of similar potential crimes are currently being investigated across the UK.

The National Crime Agency said there was an "urgent need" to deal with the problem as an international issue.

NCA investigators have identified more than 270 individuals linked to one online forum and successor groups.

The CPS describes this type of offending as an emerging challenge for investigators.

"This particular type of offending, where a husband is drugging and abusing his wife and arranging for other men to abuse her, does seem to be a new type of offending," said Foster.

A spokesman for Wiltshire Police explained the extent of drug-rape offences was unknown because victims might not know they had been targeted.

He said: "While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly under-reported crime type.

"Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption. These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging."

Sugiura disagrees the offending itself is new.

She believes technology has made it easier to facilitate and conceal abuse that may have existed for years.

"The use of technology enables anonymity, it enables that division of identity, the protection of the respectable face offline, and these heinous deeds online," she said, adding offenders often operate within wider online communities where misogynistic attitudes are encouraged and abusive material is shared.

"These are not always isolated incidents," she said.

"They can be part of larger networks where people are swapping tips, encouraging one another and sharing material that is deeply abusive towards women."

"I think that there are potentially quite a lot more cases in the pipeline," she added.

  • If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, support and information is available at BBC Action Line

Follow BBC Wiltshire on Facebook , X and Instagram . Send your story ideas to us on email or via WhatsApp on 0800 313 4630 .

item.title: Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance
item.description: The visuals of the historic trilateral meeting may be the only lasting impression left by the summit.
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump went into his trilateral meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping with little on the agenda and no clear asks – and it appears that he left with little in return.

In the end, the visuals of the meeting – the "optics", as political wags like to say – may be the only lasting impression from the summit, billed by some as an historic "Yalta 2.0" meeting of great powers.

The pomp and the ceremony, in the end, may be what the US president wanted most. Trump, bruised by his Republican Party's drubbing in midterm congressional elections earlier this month, clearly relished the global spotlight during his three-day trip to Asia and the historic nature of the first-ever US-Russia-China trilateral meeting.

In an interview on Wednesday with Fox News, Trump noted his prominent seat at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) dinner on Tuesday and his reception upon arriving in China - "the fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people" – as evidence that the trip already was a success.

That might appear to be a low bar, but it's one that could satisfy the American president.

So far, however, the US has been remarkably silent following the three-party meeting.

While China was quick to release a joint communique detailing the discussions and Putin expounded during an hour-long post-meeting press conference, Trump has made minimal public comments, instead promising a news conference at the White House on Friday.

On his trip to China earlier this year and following his meeting with Xi at the APEC summit in South Korea last October, Trump spoke with the press early in his flight back to Washington.

For the moment, the White House is letting the joint communique, released Thursday after the three met, do the talking. But the document is mostly a vague endorsement of efforts to ensure "strategic stability and international security".

That, along with the visuals of three powerful men sitting in the same room to amicably discuss global issues, might offer some reassurance no catastrophic conflicts are on the horizon. But pledges of further "dialogue" and an acknowledgement that nuclear war "must never be fought" provide minimal substance beyond the rhetoric.

"In general, it's good for the leaders of the major global players to come together in various formats, even if the results appear to be modest at best," David Firestein, head of the Bush Foundation for US-China Relations, told the BBC.

A line about boosting "the production and supply of refined petroleum products" seems directed at Putin, given that nation's role as a major source of fossil fuels on the international market. And it was hard to miss the condemnation of the International Criminal Court – a recent target of American ire.

If there's one thing the leaders of the three major world powers can agree on, it's that multilateral global organisations that attempt to enforce international law shouldn't have the teeth to back up those efforts.

While in China, Trump called Putin his "friend", and praised his "outstanding personal relationship" with Xi after sharing a handshake and hug with the Chinese leader.

But once Trump returns to Washington, he is likely face a political environment where views of his Asia trip range from measured concern to outright criticism.

"I am concerned by how we are characterising our relationships with geopolitical adversaries. Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are not our friends," Republican Senator John Curtis of Utah said in a statement to the BBC on Thursday.

"Diplomacy is important, but it should never come at the expense of clarity about who our adversaries are."

Democrats, for their part, did not mince words.

"American security cannot be traded away for photo opportunities or personal aggrandisement," nine senators on the foreign relations committee wrote in a letter to the White House.

Trump is hardly the first American president to seek an international diplomatic breakthrough as a salve following domestic political setbacks. Democrats Bill Clinton and Barack Obama took overseas trips as presidents shortly after their party's own midterm electoral defeats.

In those cases, any boosts to their standing proved short-lived. And while Trump may have gotten the images he wanted from his Asian summit, the lack of substantive progress accompanying them likely means this trip also will be quickly forgotten.

Brandon Drenon contributed to this report.

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here . Those outside the UK can sign up here .

item.title: Crew unaware of risks before Mike Lynch's yacht Bayesian sank, say investigators
item.description: The vessel sank off the coast of northern Sicily, killing seven people including British tech tycoon Mike Lynch.
item.content:encoded:
The crew of the Bayesian superyacht did not know about critical safety risks that left it vulnerable in powerful winds before it sank off the coast in northern Sicily, killing seven people, British investigators say.

British tech tycoon Mike Lynch, 59, and his daughter Hannah, 18, were among seven people who died when the vessel sank on 19 August 2024.

The sinking of the Bayesian unfolded with "extraordinary speed" when a violent downburst of freak hurricane-force winds knocked it onto its side in less than 15 seconds, the UK's Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) final report said.

Safety information provided to the crew did not identify this type of risk, the MAIB said.

"It was very dynamic, very quick," said MAIB principal inspector Simon Graves. "The speed of events overtook the crew and prevented them from taking any other action."

The accident also led to the deaths of Morgan Stanley International bank chairman Jonathan Bloomer, 70, and his wife, Judy, 71; American lawyer Chris Morvillo, 59, and his wife Neda Morvillo, 57; and crew member Rick Thomas, 59.

Rob Loder, chief inspector of marine accidents said: "Our thoughts remain with the families and loved ones of the seven who lost their lives, and with all those affected by the loss of Bayesian. This accident developed with extraordinary speed."

Fifteen survivors escaped from the 56-metre (184ft) luxury yacht and managed to get to a life raft that had been launched by a crew member.

The marine investigation found that the Bayesian "had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised, because the yacht had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down".

In addition, "the extreme winds that night were also not explicitly forecast, so the crew had no warning of the risk", Loder added.

In the early hours of 19 August 2024 the Bayesian was anchored outside of Porticello port, on the north coast of Sicily.

With thunderstorms rapidly coming in, wind speeds went from 8 knots to about 70 knots (80mph) within minutes. The weather forecast had only predicted gusts of up to 27 knots (31mph).

The MAIB report stated that with no sails set Bayesian was vulnerable to being knocked over in severe winds.

It also found that any knockdown - where the boat was suddenly tipped sideways - would be "irrecoverable once the yacht passed the angle of vanishing stability", assessed in the study as being 73 degrees. Once the vessel passed this angle it could not right itself.

In addition, the centreboard, which provides stability when a ship is under sail, was raised. The report said the centreboard was not needed when the Bayesian was using its motors and was rarely lowered at anchor. The way the boat was loaded, and the angle of the wind, also contributed to the accident.

Inspectors said a "downburst of hurricane-force winds" was the most likely cause of the ship keeling over.

They happen when cold, dense air plunges rapidly, sending out violent winds across the surface.

The MAIB said that none of risks were covered in the UK training syllabus, nor in published guidance available to crew.

Once the vessel was on its side, it rapidly filled with water and sank.

As it heeled over, five people were injured, either by falling or by items falling on them and a deckhand was thrown into the sea, the report said.

As water started entering the yacht, two of the guests "used the furniture drawers as an improvised ladder to exit into the central alleyway", then climbed along the internal walls to get into the saloon.

The MAIB's final report into the sinking, published on Thursday, appeared to contrast with recent reports from Italy, where prosecution experts have reportedly blamed errors by the crew rather than problems with the yacht.

The investigation was carried out alongside a criminal probe in Italy, where captain James Cutfield, chief engineer Tim Parker Eaton and deckhand Matthew Griffith are under investigation over potential charges of multiple manslaughter and culpable shipwreck.

British investigators said that Italian prosecutors had restricted access to some witnesses and evidence.

"It is possible that the circumstances depicted in this report may alter following disclosure of evidence withheld by the Italian authorities," the report says.

However, the MAIB's Graves said he was satisfied with the British investigation.

"We are content with our investigation, the investigation that we've undertaken, and the information we've used to feed into it."

The report also found that alcohol consumption had not contributed to the sinking.

The MAIB report makes seven recommendations to four agencies. It calls for new regulations to be set for single-hulled sailing vessels, and new rules around life rafts.

It also urges collaboration between the Met Office and its global counterpart to improve information-sharing of severe weather forecasts with mariners.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency is also investigating the sinking.

item.title: India's religious make-up - what a new Pew study says about Hindus and Muslims
item.description: India will remain predominantly Hindu, though its Muslim population is projected to grow faster, according to a new survey.
item.content:encoded:
India will remain overwhelmingly Hindu for decades to come, but its religious composition is projected to shift gradually.

A new study by the Pew Research Center, projecting the world's religious populations to 2070, estimates that Hindus will make up 76% of India's population by then, down from 79% in 2020, while the Muslim share will rise from 15% to 20%.

The shift is rooted largely in differences in age and fertility: Indian Muslims are younger than Hindus and, on average, have more children.

The Pew projections place India at the centre of a wider demographic shift across South Asia.

Pakistan is expected to overtake Indonesia as the country with the world's largest Muslim-majority population, with India moving into second place. Bangladesh, too, is projected to see substantial growth in its Muslim population.

The study projects the religious composition of the world over the next 50-year period, drawing on data from 201 countries and territories, covering virtually the entire global population.

It tracks seven religious groups between 2020 and 2070, assuming recent demographic trends continue. Using census and survey data, it establishes each group's size and age profile in 2020, and factors in differences in fertility and religious switching.

The findings place India at the heart of a changing global religious landscape. The country is expected to have the world's second-largest Muslim population by 2070, after Pakistan, with about 334 million Muslims. Pakistan itself will overtake Indonesia as the country with the largest Muslim population, with an estimated 461 million.

Yet the projections offer little support for the more dramatic narratives sometimes attached to India's changing religious composition.

If current demographic trends continue, the Hindu population in the country is expected to grow by 176 million between 2020 and 2070, the report says. It will continue to account for more than three-quarters of the country's population.

Despite a sharp fall in India's overall fertility, Muslim women still have more children, on average, than Hindu women. Pew attributes the shift primarily to demographic momentum.

Indian Muslims had a median age of 24 in 2020, compared with 29 for Hindus.

Between 2025 and 2030, Pew estimates Muslim women in India will have an average of 2.3 children, against 1.8 among Hindu women.

"We expect religious change in India to be driven almost entirely by long-standing demographic differences between Hindus and Muslims: Muslims are younger and have higher fertility rates," Stephanie Kramer of the Pew Research Center told the BBC.

"The fertility gap has narrowed considerably – from more than one child per woman in 1992 to about half a child in recent years and is likely to keep shrinking," she said.

"But Hindu fertility is already below the replacement level, while Muslim fertility is projected to remain above it for another two decades." (A replacement level is one at which new births are sufficient to maintain a stable population.)

The projections are hardly surprising, says KS James, an Indian demographer at Princeton University.

"The fertility gap between Muslims and Hindus is well established and it means Muslim population growth is likely to remain faster for the next few decades. But fertility is declining across all religious communities and the gap is expected to narrow further," he told the BBC.

"Ultimately, they will converge," he says, adding that the projections do not point to anything dramatically different in India's demographic trajectory.

Demographers push back against claims, often amplified by Hindu right-wing groups, that Muslims will eventually outnumber Hindus. There is no evidence of any significant religious conversion driving population change in India, they say, and the projections do not support such "alarmist scenarios".

The wider South Asian picture is equally revealing, according to the report.

Pakistan's Muslim population is projected to more than double to 461 million by 2070, overtaking Indonesia as the world's largest. India will rank second, with 334 million Muslims, while Bangladesh's Muslim population will rise to 218 million. India and Nepal, meanwhile, will remain the world's only Hindu-majority countries.

There appears to be a global story behind these regional shifts.

By 2035, Muslims are projected to overtake Christians as the world's largest religious group, according to the report. By 2070, their numbers are expected to reach 3.64 billion, up from 2.02 billion in 2020.

Christianity, meanwhile, will have just under three billion followers. Muslims will account for 36% of humanity, compared with 26% today.

But the most dramatic transformation may be taking place thousands of miles west of South Asia, in Africa.

Christianity's centre of gravity is moving steadily away from Europe and the Americas towards sub-Saharan Africa.

The report says that if recent trends continue, more than half of the world's Christians are expected to live there by 2070, compared with 31% in 2020. Pew forecasts that the Democratic Republic of Congo will overtake the United States as the country with the largest Christian population.

The steepest decline is expected to occur in Europe. If current trends continue, by 2070 Europe will be home to 11% of the world's Christian population, down from 22% in 2020, the report says.

The US is projected to lose its Christian majority by 2065, although Christians will remain the country's largest religious group in 2070.

One reason for this changing religious landscape is the growing number of people identifying with no religion.

In UK and France, the "religiously unaffiliated" are projected to become the majority by 2070. South Korea is expected to follow suit.

Yet their share of the world's population is forecast to fall from 24% to 17%, largely because of a decline in China's population.

China accounts for about two-thirds of the world's religiously unaffiliated population. Its expected population decline will more than offset growth in secular populations elsewhere, the report says.

By 2070, there are other unexpected shifts.

The US is projected to become the world's fifth-largest Hindu population, with immigration driving much of its growth.

And Australia's unaffiliated population will overtake Christians as the country's largest group.

Buddhism, meanwhile, faces a demographic squeeze. Its population is expected to fall by more than half in China, Japan and South Korea, reflecting the ageing and shrinking populations of East Asia. Laos and Mongolia are projected to lose their Buddhist majorities.

There are, of course, caveats. These are demographic projections, not predictions of everything that might happen. Pew assumes that recently observed patterns of fertility, migration and religious switching - or conversions - will continue.

"There are many events that could affect religious group populations (including wars, natural disasters, epidemics and changes in economic or social circumstances) that are not analysed here," the report admits.

India's baseline also required projecting the 2020 religious composition from the 2011 census, because the subsequent census had been delayed

Still, the broad direction is unmistakable.

South Asia will remain indispensable to the world's religious story, not just because of India's enormous Hindu population but because of the growing weight of its Muslim populations. Africa will increasingly shape Christianity's future, while Europe and parts of East Asia become more secular.

Clearly, by 2070, the world's religious landscape may look markedly different, shaped less by conversion than by the uneven arithmetic of births, deaths and migration.

item.title: This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls
item.description: The meeting comes with challenges as there are things Xi does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.
item.content:encoded:
Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.

For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.

Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table.

And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets.

Ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics.

His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order.

But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.

Ukraine, the balancing act

First, China is not keen for the war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year, to be on the agenda.

This is a delicate balancing act for Xi who is aware his relationship with Putin may damage China's connections in Europe. The EU is a key market, especially now when the Chinese economy is heavily relying on exports.

However Xi also doesn't want the war to end in a way that will destabilise Russia, a key ally and neighbour.

Beijing is still trying to maintain that it is neutral in this war and has repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's full-scale invasion.

The US, especially under the previous Biden administration, and Europe have accused China of sending Russia components that it could use in its war in Ukraine, while also propping up the country's economy by buying oil and gas.

Xi wants to keep Putin close, but not too close because he also doesn't want Russia's problems to become China's problems.

China's growing nuclear arsenal

Donald Trump has already made it clear he wants the three leaders to discuss limiting the world's supply of nuclear weapons.

The US and Russia possess the world's largest stockpile of nuclear warheads. But China is rapidly expanding its own arsenal, which is raising alarm bells in Washington.

The last major US-Russian arms control treaty, known as New START, expired in February this year, triggering fears of an arms race. The agreement had set a cap to control the number of nuclear weapons in US and Russia's arsenal.

Trump would like China to be included in any new agreement, but Beijing has pushed back.

Xi's argument will be that his arsenal is considerably smaller than what Washington and Moscow own, and, therefore, it would be unfair for Beijing to be bound by their limits. China also believes it should have the freedom to develop its own nuclear capabilities.

This subject could complicate Xi's bid for China to be recognised as a leader on the world stage - because the US could argue that the status includes being a responsible nuclear power.

Will everyone stick to the script?

Xi will want to control the optics of this meeting, from start to finish.

Chinese officials like to nail down agendas with talking points and produce carefully choreographed speeches.

But in this unprecedented summit, Xi will have to live with two very unpredictable leaders.

Both Trump and Putin have their own agendas and the US President has already threatened to go off script.

There is a risk that they both dominate the meeting and Xi ends up looking like a host, rather than the architect of a major diplomatic moment.

Of course, Xi may be ready for this. It may even play into his hands.

The Chinese leader has been trying to portray himself as a stable global leader - at this summit he will be flanked by two men embroiled in wars they cannot seem to end.

So any unscripted moment could serve to highlight his preferred role as senior statesman.

Xi's problems at home

For all the attention, this meeting of three men with vastly different agendas is unlikely to yield any significant outcomes.

But the power it projects is important for Xi as he heads towards next year's Communist Party Congress, where he is expected to secure a historic fourth term as leader of the party and country.

He may hope to use this as propaganda at home, given the country is grappling with huge domestic challenges.

A country-wide property crisis has dented consumer confidence. Local governments are heavily in debt. Manufacturing has slowed and more of China's workforce has become dependent on flexible jobs with no pension or social security. One in five young people are thought to be struggling to find work. Frustration and anxiety about the future bubble up routinely.

Xi does not have to deal with elections, and the country has not seen major protests in decades. But he will be concerned about his popularity within the party elite as these problems - and the palpable frustrations they produce - grow.

At a time like this, a photo-op with Putin and Trump may offer him proof that his country's "century of humiliation" is over. China is no longer a rising power, he can argue - rather, it is increasingly shaping the rules of a new era.

item.title: Leasehold system set to be scrapped in England and Wales
item.description: The proposed Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill will also include capping ground rent at £250.
item.content:encoded:
The government is to introduce new laws to scrap the ownership rules for flats in England and Wales and cap ground rents at £250 a year.

Under the plans, which will not become law until at least next year, most new leasehold flats will eventually be banned and replaced with commonhold, where residents collectively own and manage their buildings.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook said the current leasehold system was "blighting lives" and was an "anachronism in the 21st century".

But the Residential Freehold Association says the plan is an "unprecedented abuse" of their rights, which will wipe billions from the value of pension funds, which have invested heavily in property.

The Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill, to be published on Thursday, is likely to contain further details on when the measures would come into force.

In order to become law, the bill would first need to be approved by both Houses of Parliament, a process that will take several months.

'Continuous torture cell'

The bill will also include plans to cap ground rent - the annual fee paid by current leaseholders to their freeholder - at £250 from 2028. That will then be reduced to a "peppercorn" rate - which is effectively nothing - after 40 years.

Fozia Malik lives in a one-bedroom flat in Oldham and says her ground rent will go up from £150 to £300 in January. That is alongside service charges of more than £4,000 a year.

Malik says her block of flats has been plagued by a number of problems, including fire safety issues and rising costs.

The managing agent for her building says the service charges are due to costs that are out of its control and high insurance because of fire safety issues.

But Malik says she would "never" buy a leasehold flat again, describing it as a "continuous torture cell".

When she bought her flat, Malik assumed the system would work in the same way it does in Pakistan, where she grew up, and in most other countries, where buying a home also means owning a share of the land it sits on.

However, in England, most flats are sold on a leasehold basis. That gives the buyer the right to occupy and use a property for a set period of time, but the freeholder retains ultimate ownership of the building and the land.

Systems based on shared ownership and collective management - such as commonhold - are already standard in many parts of the world, including Australia, New Zealand, the US, Canada and much of continental Europe. They give residents ownership of their home and a stake in the building's common areas.

Scotland does not have leasehold tenures, while Northern Ireland has just a handful of leasehold properties.

The government says its reforms are intended to bring England and Wales more closely in line with other other countries around the world, which do not have leaseholds.

It comes as more than 1,000 leaseholders have contacted the BBC over the past two years with complaints about the current system.

Risk of two-tier system

Campaigners have welcomed many of the reforms, but questioned what happens to the millions of people who already own leasehold homes.

While the legislation is expected to reshape ownership for new developments, converting existing leasehold buildings into commonhold is far more complicated. And it has led to concerns that current leaseholders will be left behind.

Giles Grover, from the campaign group End Our Cladding Scandal, says there is a risk the proposed changes will create a two-tier system of those buying new homes and existing leaseholders.

He began campaigning on behalf of flat owners following the Grenfell Tower tragedy. He says: "It's so complicated, will the measures that are being introduced actually benefit everyone?"

The government says the bill will make it easier for existing leaseholders to convert to commonhold, abolish forfeiture - so people cannot lose their homes over relatively small debts - improve transparency around service charges and crack down on estate charges.

Pennycook says it will transform "the experience of homeownership for existing leaseholders by giving them greater rights and protections and providing them with easy and effective escape routes".

However, the issue about how existing leaseholders can move into commonhold and how freeholders should be compensated remains unresolved.

A spokesperson for the Residential Freehold Association, which represents the UK's largest freeholders, says £18.7bn "could be wiped out from investments overnight".

The association says property investors, which often include pension funds, have invested £15bn in residential ground rents.

item.title: Van Gogh painting sells for record $190.4m after row over its Nazi history
item.description: Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Vincent van Gogh's life.
item.content:encoded:
Auction house Sotheby's has sold a painting by Vincent van Gogh for a record $190.4m (£144.8m).

The sale of Châtaigniers en fleurs ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom") shatters the renowned artist's previous auction record of $117.2 million set in 2022.

The historic sale in New York on Wednesday comes after an eleventh-hour agreement was reached to resolve a dispute regarding claims the art piece was previously sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Van Gogh's life. It is considered one of the most important works of art from that period to remain in private hands, according to Sotheby's.

It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.

The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.

Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.

Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.

"In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.

Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.

It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.

The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.

Four other owners then had the painting.

The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

item.title: Myanmar faces historic genocide verdict at UN court over Rohingya massacres
item.description: No state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.
item.content:encoded:
When the judges of the International Court of Justice read out their verdict in the seven-year-old genocide case filed by The Gambia against Myanmar on Thursday, they could make history.

In the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948, after the Nazi Holocaust, dozens of individuals have been successfully prosecuted for the crime of genocide, in conflicts such as those in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.

But no state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.

"It would be a judgment of landmark importance if The Gambia were to win this case," says Arsalan Suleman, the lawyer leading the case against Myanmar at the court. "It would give renewed vitality to the 1948 Genocide Convention and to the notion of international legal accountability for crimes committed by a state."

The mass expulsion of the Rohingya population of Rakhine State in August and September 2017 was without question a military operation of exceptional brutality.

I was among a very small number of journalists who witnessed the deliberate burning of Rohingya villages in Rakhine, and also the dreadful human suffering of the hundreds of thousands who fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.

Their accounts of killing, torture and mass rape by Burmese soldiers have been thoroughly documented by human rights groups and a United Nations fact-finding mission.

I have on many occasions interviewed ethnic Rakhine people about their animosity towards the Muslim population, and I have documented the systematic obliteration of what remained of Rohingya villages by the Myanmar state.

But the question posed at the UN's top court, the ICJ, is whether all of this amounted to genocide.

The ICJ was established in 1945 to help settle disputes between states, not to try international crimes. However, it was chosen to address the attacks on Rohingyas in Myanmar because there were few other avenues of redress for the victims.

Myanmar authorities have denied accusations of ethnic cleansing or genocide, saying they were only responding to terrorist actions by Rohingya militants with so-called military "clearance operations".

A UN report in 2018, based on hundreds of interviews, said the army's tactics were "grossly disproportionate to actual security threats". It said top military figures in Myanmar must be investigated for genocide in Rakhine State and crimes against humanity in other areas. Myanmar rejected the report.

As Myanmar was not a signatory to the International Criminal Court, it was not possible to file a case there against the officials accused of atrocities in Rakhine State.

Instead in November 2019 The Gambia, backed by the Organisation of Islamic Co-operation, filed a case at the ICJ, arguing that all states are bound by the Genocide Convention, so all have an interest in upholding it.

It accused the state in Myanmar, not just the military, of genocide.

This was a novelty in international law; a state not directly affected by an act, arguing that it had legal standing to make a complaint because it was indirectly affected by any violations of such an important convention.

Myanmar objected to this argument, but the ICJ judges ruled that The Gambia was eligible to file the case.

The case drew even more attention when the Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, who at the time headed the elected government in Myanmar, chose to lead the initial legal defence of her country at The Hague in person, for which she was widely criticised.

She had very limited influence over the actions of the Myanmar military in Rakhine State, but her refusal to condemn them dismayed many of those who until then had admired her courage and adherence to democratic principles.

Since she was deposed by a coup in 2021 and placed under arrest the defence has been led by a new team appointed by the military.

Historically, proving that genocide has been committed has been very difficult. Judges apply a high bar to this.

Typically, where there is no explicitly genocidal programme, like that of the Nazis, the judges require that the evidence presented at court must be such that the only reasonable inference from the actions of the defendants is that they had genocidal intent.

When Bosnia-Herzegovina filed a genocide case against Serbia at the ICJ in 1993, it took the court 14 years to conclude that while incidents like the 1995 massacre at Srebrenica did amount to genocide, there was not sufficient proof that the state of Serbia had genocidal intent, though it was found to have failed to prevent genocide.

Myanmar's lawyers and Aung San Suu Kyi have argued something similar.

Suu Kyi said that The Gambia's team mischaracterised a complex conflict and military operation, and that while she accepted that war crimes may have been committed against the Rohingyas, that is not proof of genocidal intent.

But Arsalan Suleman believes the weight of evidence his team gathered is enough to meet that high bar.

"What we presented to the court was the long history of discrimination targeting the Rohingya, and how that history, and the policies connected with it, provide a background to understand the government's language, rhetoric, propaganda, and policies that were part of the 2017 'clearance operations'," Suleman said.

"We discussed the 1982 citizenship law, and the tightening noose of discriminatory laws that restricted access to education, healthcare, livelihoods, and travel - all of which made life really impossible for the Rohingya and, we argued, was one of several indicators of genocidal intent."

What happens if the court does find in favour of The Gambia?

Myanmar would then find itself tarnished by having committed "the crime of crimes", as sitting on the same bench as Nazi Germany, the Rwandan Hutu militants and the Bosnian Serbs at Srebrenica.

That might seem a setback for Min Aung Hlaing, the general who now runs Myanmar, who above all was responsible for the military's operations in 2017, and who has been trying to improve his dismal international image in recent months.

There is no right of appeal against an ICJ verdict. However, there is also no penalty that follows an ICJ verdict.

The Burmese coup leader is focused mostly on rebuilding relations with neighbouring Asian countries, who are unlikely to pay too much attention to such a verdict, and much less on rebuilding relations with Western countries who do care.

But for the huge Rohingya diaspora this verdict matters a great deal.

"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of the Rakhine town of Buthidaung in 2017 and now lives in Canada.

"For the Rohingya, this trial is a moment of acknowledgement of our suffering after years of denial. The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades, not just this year."

He and other Rohingya activists hope that a ruling in favour of The Gambia will prompt more co-ordinated action by other countries to find a resolution which allows them to go home to Rakhine State, in safety.

More than a million are stuck in wretched camps in Bangladesh, barred from employment as international funding dries up.

But the obstacles to realising this hope are formidable.

Rakhine State has been ravaged by a conflict between the military and the insurgent Arakan Army, which now controls most of the territory. It is supported by the indigenous Rakhine population who are very hostile to the idea of the Rohingyas coming back.

Many Rohingya villages have been completely destroyed. And international support for them has faded over the years. Even an unprecedented genocide verdict at the world's highest court cannot change that reality.

item.title: Claude-maker Anthropic poised for stock market debut worth up to $1.5tn
item.description: Anthropic started just five years ago an is now one of the biggest names in artificial intelligence.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic is poised to hit a value of up to $1.5tn (£1.14tn) when its shares start trading on the stock market on Thursday.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the popular chatbot Claude said its shares will be priced at $83 each when it lists on the Nasdaq, a tech-focused stock exchange based in New York.

That price will make it one of the most highly valued companies in the world.
