item.title: Trump shakes hands with Putin and Xi ahead of historic talks in China
item.description: The three leaders will meet together for the first time on Thursday during a closely-watched summit.
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met for the first time in more than a year on Wednesday, as they prepared for landmark talks in China with Xi Jinping.

The US president was greeted off his plane by the Chinese leader as he arrived in Shenzhen for a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders, which will culminate in a closely-watched meeting between the pair and the Russian president.

After a carefully choreographed handshake and hug between Trump and Xi on the tarmac, the US president later greeted and exchanged pleasantries with Putin ahead of a reception.

Trump and Putin are expected to hold one-on-one talks on the sidelines of the summit on Thursday, in which the war in Ukraine could be discussed.

However the main focus during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (Apec) will be on the US-China-Russia talks on Thursday - the first time the trio of leaders have met together in person.

A full agenda has not been made public but there have been various hints about what could be discussed, including the wars in Ukraine and Iran, nuclear proliferation, trade tensions and developments in artificial intelligence.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin and Trump have not yet held a substantive meeting, and merely greeted each other on Wednesday.

Peskov also said that "no more than an hour" had been allocated for Thursday's trilateral talks between Putin, Trump and Xi.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has raised fears of a plan to end the war being discussed in the absence of representatives from Kyiv or Europe.

It is unclear whether China would want this issue to be on the agenda in Shenzhen, with Beijing talking more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".

China has officially remained neutral since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, rejecting accusations from Kyiv and its allies that it has been tacitly supporting Moscow, including by exporting dual-use technology used by the Russian military.

Wednesday's handshake was the first in-person meeting between Trump and Putin since August 2025, when the Russian leader travelled to Alaska for talks on the Ukraine war which failed to deliver a breakthrough.

Xi's personal reception for Trump at the airport mimicked a similar move by the US president when the Chinese leader visited Washington in September, a gesture Xi described as "special".

In Shenzhen, a red carpet was rolled out in front of Air Force One for Trump, with a cheering crowd, honour guard, military flyover and flowers presentation all in place to welcome him.

Chinese state-run news agency Xinhua quoted Xi as saying he wanted to pursue a "constructive strategic and stable relationship based on respect, fairness, and equality".

Xi's greeting will be seen as a diplomatic gesture designed to begin the week's talks with his American counterpart on a cordial note.

The south-east Chinese city the Apec summit is being held in is a booming area for manufacturing and advanced tech.

It comes against the backdrop of the ousting of Nvidia chief executing Jensen Huang, who admitted to having an affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of spying for Beijing - a claim dismissed as a "smear" by China.

Trump has pursued warmer relations with China but the incident points to ongoing tensions between the two powers.

Several hours before Trump's arrival, Putin landed in Shenzhen and held around two hours of talks with Xi, with whom he has pressed for closer economic and defence relations.

Xi said both countries would "move forward steadily and boldly" and that the relationship was "stable as a mountain, unshaken by storms".

item.title: Council wins legal fight against flags on lamp-posts
item.description: In her decision, Judge Emma Kelly says there was a "compelling need" to grant the interim injunction.
item.content:encoded:
Birmingham City Council has won a High Court injunction preventing unauthorised flags being attached to lamp-posts and other highway infrastructure across the city.

The authority sought the order after thousands of St George's flags and union jacks were put up by supporters of anti-migrant group Raise the Colours from summer 2025 onwards.

Council lawyers argued the displays created safety risks and fuelled tensions, while campaigners said the move would restrict freedom of expression.

Judge Emma Kelly said there was a "compelling need" to grant the interim injunction.

In her ruling, the judge said it would last until trial or further order of the court.

The order applies to Raise the Colours' leader Ryan Bridge; Ben Cullen, who is also associated with the group; and persons unknown from attaching flags to street furniture and highway infrastructure.

It also grants a power of arrest against Bridge and persons unknown, meaning police could arrest someone without a warrant if they are suspected of breaching the injunction.

The council said anyone who breaches the order could be jailed for up to two years, fined or have their assets seized for contempt of court.

The local authority sought the injunction after thousands of St George's flags and union flags were attached to lamp-posts and bridges in Birmingham from summer 2025 onwards.

Lawyers acting for the council argued the displays could pose safety risks, obstruct visibility and contribute to tensions and disorder. The application also referred to reported incidents of alleged intimidation, harassment and obstruction connected to flags being put up in the city.

The court heard that, on one occasion, a man suffered a broken leg when he was struck by a cherry picker being used while flags were being installed.

The case followed similar legal action in Oxfordshire, where the county council secured a permanent injunction against four named individuals over flags attached to lamp-posts and other highway structures.

Bridge opposed the injunction, arguing it would interfere with rights to freedom of expression and protest under the European Convention on Human Rights.

His barrister, Liam Wells, told the court the campaign amounted to political expression protected by the convention and argued the injunction would have a "chilling effect" on those rights.

In her ruling, Kelly stressed the order was not a ban on displaying flags.

"The interim injunction needs to be understood for what it is," she said.

"It is not the court nor the claimant 'banning the union jack' or the display of Pride flags or anything of the like.

"Whilst the interim injunction order will cover flags of all types, it is limited in scope to the restraint of unauthorised flags attached to highway street furniture or infrastructure, and to the restraint of associated conduct, within the administrative area of Birmingham."

She added that concerns the injunction would unduly restrict free expression were "unwarranted" and said she was satisfied it was "just and convenient" to grant the order.

The injunction covers all unauthorised flags attached to street furniture, regardless of the type of flag involved.

Birmingham City Council's cabinet member for equalities, communities and social justice, Jane Baston, welcomed the ruling and described it as an "important step" in tackling unauthorised attachments to public highways.

She said residents remained free to display flags on their own property and said the council's approach had been "proportionate and evidence-led".

Councillor Robert Alden, leader of Birmingham local Conservatives, criticised the authority's decision to pursue the injunction, saying it should focus on resolving the city's bin strike and improving basic services.

Campaign group Brummies United Against Racism & Hate Crime welcomed the ruling, describing it as "a welcome decision and long overdue".

A further hearing is due to take place in Birmingham on Thursday.

Follow BBC Birmingham on BBC Sounds , Facebook , X and Instagram .

item.title: Fiona the hippo undergoing care after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo
item.description: Zookeepers say she cannot have surgery but are providing fluids and supportive care to help her pass the hat.
item.content:encoded:
The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona is undergoing emergency medical care after swallowing a knit hat that slipped into her enclosure.

The Zoo said that Fiona had swallowed the hat about nine days ago and was asymptomatic at first, adding that she was "large enough that a small-ish hat should be passing through".

But a few days later, her appetite started to decrease, and the zoo staff were trying to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system.

Fiona rose to fame when she was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo and at first struggled to survive. Her story inspired an ice cream flavour as well as a character in Cincinnati's ballet.

Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, told US media that the hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.

"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.

Zoo staff have been providing a series of supportive measures like fluids and ultrasounds to help Fiona recover.

The latest ultrasound showed the hat passing through Fiona's small intestine, the staff said, adding that she is still a bit dehydrated.

"Surgery isn't an option for full-grown hippos and our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own," one of the zookeepers said in an update.

Fiona was born six weeks early to 17-year-old hippo Bibi on 24 January 2017.

At birth she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species.

The zoo said staff were "rooting for her and hoping that she proves to be as strong and resilient as she was at the beginning of her life".

item.title: Couple ordered to cut hedge after claiming it was not a hedge
item.description: They insisted the description of the boundary plants was wrong and instead claimed it was a mixture of 17 closely planted trees and shrubs.
item.content:encoded:
A couple has been ordered to reduce the size of their hedge after they claimed it was not a hedge at all.

Prof Angus Macdonald and Dr Patricia Macdonald received a notice from East Lothian Council after neighbours complained the trees and shrubs were overhanging onto their property, shedding branches, leaves and berries, and blocking out the sky.

The couple appealed to Scottish ministers and insisted the description of the boundary plants was wrong, claiming it was actually a mixture of 17 closely planted trees and shrubs.

But the Scottish government reporter stated the plants met the definition of a high hedge in Scotland and ruled in favour of the council.

In Scotland, a high hedge is defined as a row of two or more trees and shrubs which are taller than two metres above the ground.

The reporter said: "I am satisfied the shrubs and trees are a high hedge, which acts as a barrier to light and prevents the reasonable enjoyment of the neighbouring property."

The council ordered for it to be cut down and maintained at a maximum height of 2.5m (8ft) but excluded an ash and willow tree at either end of the boundary wall from any work.

In the appeal, the couple said the trees and ivy made a "significant contribution" to the visual amenity of the street which sits within the Musselburgh Conservation Area.

They said the structure of the trees and shrubs provides shelter from extreme weather, cleans the air of pollutants and helps to reduce high temperatures during summer.

"It has also provided considerable support for wildlife of every kind, including more than 50 species of birds, more than 10 species of butterflies and numerous species of bees and other useful insect pollinators," the couple added.

The reporter said the hedge would continue to contribute at a lower height.

They ordered the time to comply with high hedge notice be expanded to ensure it could be met outside of bird nesting season.

item.title: The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
item.description: The AI company behind Claude is about to sell its shares on the US stock market - making its founders very rich.
item.content:encoded:
In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.

The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.

Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at between $70 - $78 each.

If they go for the highest price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn each.

So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?

Dario Amodei

In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.

He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.

Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.

Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.

But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.

Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".

Daniela Amodei

Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.

She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.

Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.

She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.

The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.

Tom Brown

Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.

He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.

Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.

He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".

Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.

Jack Clark

Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.

Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.

He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.

Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.

Jared Kaplan

Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.

He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.

His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.

Chris Olah

Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.

But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum.

Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.

He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain.

The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.

Sam McCandlish

Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.

McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.

He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

item.title: Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries to be US Speaker of the House
item.description: The nomination sets him on the path to become the first black lawmaker to lead the chamber when Democrats take control of the House in January.
item.content:encoded:
Democrats in the US House of Representatives officially nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker, setting him on the path to become the first black lawmaker to lead the chamber.

The House will elect its new Speaker on 3 January, when the next term begins and Democrats will be in the majority.

His election to the powerful position - the Speaker is in line to succeed the president after the vice-president - is widely expected. Should he win, Jeffries will preside over his party's largest House majority in years and benefit from the Senate also being under Democrats' control.

Jeffries told reporters after the vote that the nomination was "a high honour and a distinct privilege".

As of Wednesday, Democrats will hold at least 257 seats in the House next year, which is well beyond the 218 needed for a majority. Seven races from the recent midterm elections are still uncalled.

Jeffries, who represents a district in New York, was re-elected as the party leader in a 251-11 closed-door vote on Wednesday. He has served as minority leader since 2023.

The Congressional Black Caucus, currently made up of only Democratic House members, noted the potential history-making moment when Jeffries takes the helm of the House.

"The American people, largely driven by turnout among Black communities, particularly across the south, have trusted us to make Washington work for them," said the committee's chair, Yvette Clarke, in a statement. "Now, it is our charge and responsibility to do all we can to deliver on their faith."

Despite overwhelming support in Wednesday's vote , Jeffries faced a handful of holdouts from new members in the party's left wing, who have said the party's sweeping victory in the midterm elections is a sign voters want change.

"While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes in this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of our leadership," seven incoming lawmakers, including fellow New Yorkers Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, said in a statement.

All congressional Democrats are gearing up for clashes with the White House once they officially take control in January.

President Donald Trump, a Republican, has signalled a willingness to work with Democrats on some issues, but has also pledged to use his veto power to reject legislation he does not like.

Trump's opposition could make it hard for Democrats to deliver on their campaign promises to address affordability and pass other reforms.

At a news conference following the vote on Wednesday, Jeffries pledged that House Democrats would "fight to lower the high costs of groceries and gas and housing", and "make healthcare affordable for every single American".

Though the party will have a large enough majority to weather defections on must-pass legislation, Jeffries will still have to navigate internal ideological divisions that have grown particularly sharp over US support of Israel and Americans' rising healthcare costs.

Many incoming Democrats, including members of the Democratic Socialists of America, won their elections by challenging the party establishment.

The Congressional Progressive Caucus, from the party's left wing, congratulated Jeffries on the nomination, adding they would "continue conversations with Leader Jeffries to ensure Democrats deliver a bold agenda for working people".

Along with shepherding legislation, Jeffries as Speaker will also have to manage the complex array of investigations that Democrats plan to launch into Trump, his family, and cabinet members now that they have regained control of the chamber's oversight powers.

Rounding out their party leadership team, House Democrats also elected Katherine Clark of Massachusetts as majority leader, Pete Aguilar of California as majority whip, and Joe Neguse of Colorado as assistant speaker.

item.title: Grand Theft Auto 6 is a masterpiece, say critics
item.description: Critics have their say as to whether GTA 6, the most anticipated video game of all time, lives up to the hype.
item.content:encoded:
After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.

Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?

According to the first reviews, it's a resounding yes.

Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100 - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.

Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.

Not everyone is enjoying the glowing praise - with some posters to online forums objecting to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype."

But there is no question the reviewers have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".

Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building.

"The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote, but he added "there are also nits to pick".

For The New York Times one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors.

Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action.

But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.

The graphics of the game were hotly anticipated and so far have not disappointed critics, with The Guardian describing Leonida, the setting inspired by Miami, as "so lifelike that at times it beggars belief".

And the relationship between the lead characters, Jason and Lucia, has also stunned critics.

"They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim," The Guardian's Keza MacDonald wrote, adding: "I found it impossible not to care for them".

Writing for Forbes, Paul Tassi said: "I can't say I've ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share".

The Washington Post said GTA 6 "raises the bar at every level", while Bloomberg's Jason Schreier called it a "masterpiece" in his five star review.

"It's hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here," he wrote. "There's nothing else like it.

"While playing this game, I often found myself wondering how it even exists."

Rockstar hasn't revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (£760m).

Gaming journalist Jordan Middler is one of the lucky few in the UK who got early access from Rockstar and tells BBC Newsbeat it is the "game of a generation".

He'd played for about 100 hours by the time he hit the credits and says he still has so much to do.

Middler did spot one negative though - he found the game can "slow down" because of how much is going on.

He also says it is "long overdue" that there is a female lead in Lucia.

"The way previous GTA games have dealt with women has been a boys' club approach," he says.

"Introducing Lucia and not making her some kind of token character, she just fits in completely... and she will quickly become a fan favourite without question."

Early nominations

The Game Awards - the most watched ceremony of its kind in the industry - gave players a teaser of the critical reception when its 2026 nominations were revealed on Tuesday.

And despite having not released at the time, GTA 6 was the most-nominated title.

It will be up for eight prizes, including game of the year and best music.

The nomination of Manni L Perez in the best performance category confirmed wide speculation that she is the actress behind main character Lucia in GTA 6 - a fact Rockstar hadn't previously officially confirmed.

The jury for the event is largely made up of gaming journalists around the world, who would have received advanced copies for review.

Some, though, have questioned how a game that has just been released has garnered such positive reviews and award nominations.

There is a view in some online forums that the hype around the game has got out of control as, with one poster commenting: "I think everyone's tired of hearing about this game - I don't even want to play it anymore."

It appears so far, however, that is likely to be very much a minority view.

Additional reporting by Jasmine Sandhar

item.title: Security flaw found in Java, world's third-largest programming language
item.description: The same tech start-up that discovered a PHP flaw used AI to uncover a critical software bug in one of the world's most popular computer language programs.
item.content:encoded:
A cyber-security firm has used artificial intelligence (AI) to uncover a critical flaw in the hugely popular computer programming language Java.

Tech start-up Calif - which recently identified a cyber-security flaw in another language, PHP - found the bug in Java's memory functions.

Java is a popular programming language used by nearly all of the world's top companies such as Apple and Amazon, as well as many banks, hospitals and governments.

It is meant to make the IT world more secure by managing your memory online, said computer scientist Professor Toby Walsh, which is why "this is such an unlikely and serious flaw".

The discovery comes after a string of serious technology issues, including a massive Microsoft outage.

On Tuesday, the US National Security Agency said its internal communications went offline on Tuesday due to a "scheduled routine maintenance".

The NSA did not specify whether its outage was linked to the identified Java bug.

Apple also reported multiple services suffered full outages due to an internal update, while a network failure grounded all flights in the US.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the incidents were related.

Java releases critical update

With the help of AI, Calif discovered a serious security vulnerability called Java4Shell, which allowed an adversary to remotely execute unwanted commands to Java's memory system.

In this case, the adversary was OpenAI's recently-released model GPT-6 Cyber, which is not yet available to the public.

But there are fears hackers could now identify the bug if the flaw isn't fixed.

Oracle, the owner of Java, has not acknowledged the bug, but released a "critical patch update" on Tuesday, which it said contained security vulnerability fixes.

At this stage it is unclear if any platforms or companies have been affected by the latest incident.

But the Java flaw remains a huge concern for cyber-security experts, who say overloading a system's memory is one of the most common ways for hackers to exploit or crash a system.

The BBC has contacted Oracle for comment.

Nearly every critical sector, including banking, national security systems, aviation and telecommunications, relies on Java.

First released in 1995, the programming language and computing system is now the "beating heart of the modern economy", Calif said in its investigation.

One of its main functions is to manage and protect memory for you, Walsh, a leading researcher in AI, told the BBC.

Any time you transfer information on the internet, receive a file from a user or need to log into an IT system with a password, the platform you are using is likely relying on a Java program.

The serious flaw could comprise "critical financial systems, customers and organisation's data," cyber-security expert Dr Pedram Hayati said.

In Australia alone, almost every bank uses Java for managing critical transaction data, Hayati added.

The latest incidents have exposed how nearly every critical sector - including national security systems, aviation and telecommunications - relies on legacy infrastructure online.

Earlier this week, thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, reported trouble accessing services.

The Java discovery follows a critical cyber-security flaw identified in the PHP programming language, also identified by Calif.

PHP is the code that websites like Wikipedia use to collect information and present it in a way you can read on the web.

Surrey Centre for Cyber Security Prof Alan Woodward said the PHP flaw affected some 30 million websites, leaving them vulnerable to malicious attacks.

At the time, website owners were urged to check if their sites were affected and, if so, they were told to install updates to patch the issue or consider going offline.

The PHP flaws went undetected for at least a decade, which Walsh said is similar to what has happened with Java.

"It's been hiding in plain sight for 12 years", he said.

"AI is now exposing more flaws much more quickly," Walsh said including ones that may have been so obscure and difficult that humans could not have discovered them alone.

Earlier in November, OpenAI president Greg Brockman announced his company was pivoting 25% of its staff to focus on cyber-security demands.

item.title: Jeff Bezos says he was 'heavily involved' in casting Robert Pattinson as new Bond
item.description: The Amazon chairman says he was originally "biased against" Pattinson "because he's already so famous".
item.content:encoded:
Jeff Bezos has said he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond.

Speaking at an event in California, the Amazon chairman said he was originally "biased against" Pattinson - who starred in many blockbuster films like Batman and the Twilight series - "because he's already so famous".

The role of 007 has typically gone to an actor who is not as well known at the time of casting. But Bezos said in screen tests, "it was so obvious he is James Bond".

This will be the first 007 film in the official series not under the creative control of the Broccoli family, who had overseen the franchise since the first movie in 1962. Amazon purchased MGM, which co-owns the franchise, in 2022.

"There was something special about Rob", Bezos said at Semafor Silicon Valley & The World Event on Tuesday.

Pattinson was unveiled as the franchise's seventh James Bond on Monday, taking over from actor Daniel Craig. He will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.

In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."

The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.

The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.

Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.

But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.

"We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on Friday," Bezos said.

There were five finalists who went through "real, old-fashioned screen tests", acting out three different scenes in full costume, with real sets and other actors, he said.

"By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance," Bezos added. "It was immediately un-debated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director … we all gravitated toward Rob."

The pick comes amid widespread Hollywood cuts and consolidation, with studios struggling to get people into cinemas.

Hollywood insiders have said Pattinson was viewed as a safe pick to bring audiences in, rather than taking a risk on a new actor who could grow with the franchise.

"Maybe he's boring. Maybe Hollywood would be passing up a chance to anoint a badly needed new star. But with so much at stake for everyone involved, that all makes him the obvious pick," Hollywood journalist Matthew Belloni, who predicted the pick, wrote in his newsletter.

The BBC's Regan Morris contributed to this report.

item.title: What's gone wrong at Britain's worst bathing site?
item.description: The BBC looks at why in a dry summer with few sewage spills, one bathing site failed so many water quality tests.
item.content:encoded:
The official sign on the banks of the River Tone at French Weir Park in Taunton advises people not to swim.

But that hasn't stopped Jo, Jenny, Sue and a second Jo from enjoying a regular dip together.

"People think, oh you're swimming down by the supermarket, that can't be very nice, but it's gorgeous," Jenny Hillier says, as the women huddle round with their coats and hot drinks after a bracing October plunge.

People have been swimming at the spot on the River Tone in the centre of Taunton for more than a hundred years.

But it is only since 2024 that French Weir Park has been designated an official bathing site, which means from May to September the water gets tested by the Environment Agency (EA).

Those tests regularly confirm what the women's senses have been telling them for a while - the water quality is poor.

"There are times when we've come down and we haven't got in, either because of the look or the smell," says Jo Macdonald. "We don't take risks. We don't put our faces in. We don't swim with cuts or anything."

"This summer I got quite poorly," Jenny says, explaining that she'd had diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle cramps.

"I'd swum and then within six hours I was unwell. I was poorly for probably about seven to 10 days and it was not nice. I think it was the river that day."

So why is she back swimming in it?

"There are germs everywhere, all over the place. You can catch Covid in Tesco," she says.

This summer French Weir Park failed its tests on 13 of the 19 days it was sampled. The BBC analysed data from all four regulators across the UK for 2026 and found French Weir Park's failure rate of 68% was the highest of all the bathing sites

The regulators look for two types of faecal bacteria – E. coli and intestinal enterococci – that originate either in human or animal guts and can make people ill if ingested.

So where's it coming from at French Weir Park? The local water company Wessex Water says it could have come from wildlife, agriculture, private septic tanks as well as its sewerage works.

We decided to take a closer look to see if we could work out where the truth lies.

The testing regime

Our wastewater treatment system is built on the assumption that faecal bacteria - from our poo - once discharged into nature will be rapidly diluted and perish.

The bacteria are known to have little impact on wildlife but they can make humans sick if ingested – so the rise in popularity of wild-swimming and testing of bathing sites have increased awareness.

As part of a BBC investigation we analysed the water sampling results from this summer across all the UK's 700 official bathing sites on the coast, in lakes and rivers.

We found that more than 10% of the UK's coastal sites and 37% of its inland sites failed to meet regulators' minimum standards across the summer.

That difference is likely to be because the sea acts as a more effective dispersant and can dilute and kill faecal bacteria quicker than a lake or river.

Of the 11 worst bathing sites in England in 2026, seven were on inland rivers or lakes.

Why are our rivers so dirty?

Poor water quality has historically been linked to raw sewage spills. These are much more likely after it has rained. So why, in a summer that was extremely dry, did bacteria levels remain high in so many rivers?

In Taunton the official testing data suggests there has been a constant flow of bacteria entering the river.

So the BBC carried out its own sampling near three wastewater treatment works upstream of the Taunton site. We found the treated liquid coming out of the nearest sewage works at Bradford-on-Tone had about 240,000 colony forming units (CFU) of E. coli per 100ml - that's a level about 250 times higher than that considered safe for swimming.

"The counts from just outside the treatment works in my experience were high for treated effluent", Dr Rob Morley from Index Microbiology told us at his laboratory near Bristol as he peered down at small dots of E. coli bacteria on a transparent plastic plate.

What was of particular interest to Morley were the results of the test on water samples we'd taken above and below the point where the treated wastewater enters the River Tone.

It showed 199 CFU of E. coli above, which is fine for swimming and 7,701 CFU just below, more than eight times the regulators limit.

"You can see where it's seeding the river with pollution," Morley says.

"If we were to look further down the river, we would expect the levels to get lower with the dilution effect. But that does quite clearly show the impact that treated effluent can have on the river."

We shared our findings with Dr Andrew Thompson, a fellow at the Institute of Chemical Engineers. He was involved in a 2024 report that warned high concentrations of bacteria and viruses were common, particularly in the summer when river levels are lower and could cause serious diseases if ingested.

Thompson told the BBC the levels of E. coli we found in the River Tone were not illegal, or even particularly unusual, because there are currently no laws or regulations about how much bacteria water companies are allowed to discharge in what the industry calls treated effluent.

Animal or human?

We also wanted to know whether analysing the E. coli samples from the bathing site could give us clues to where it came from.

With assistance from researchers at the University of Bristol, Morley arranged for e-DNA analysis to be carried out to identify whether the E. coli bacteria were more likely to be from a human or animal gut.

The answer, as is often the case with water quality, is complex. There were lots of different types of E.coli in the samples.

"Some were from humans, some were from animals and some were just generic from the environment," Morley says. "It definitely suggests that some of the E. coli is definitely coming from human origins, therefore potentially from that treatment works."

As with all of our testing, more needs to be done to reach firm conclusions.

Both the EA and Wessex Water are investigating what's causing the water quality in Taunton to be so poor. But sources at the EA told the BBC that constant flows of treated effluent is high up the list of likely culprits.

In response to our testing Wessex Water told the BBC its treatment works at Bradford on Tone was working normally and was meeting all its permit conditions set by the EA.

So could steady flows of treated effluent loaded with bacteria be behind many of the problems at bathing sites across the UK?

"All the sewage treatment works in the UK and in England have permits to protect the ecology and the wildlife within the river," says Jim Flory, a regional manager for the EA in the south-west.

"They've not set permits for bathing water regulations, which are all about protecting people who may want to be swimming, canoeing or using the water."

That has led to a system where a popular bathing site gets officially designated – the testing regime discovers it has high levels of faecal bacteria – and then a lengthy process begins to try to work out where the sources are and whether it's affordable to fix them.

Wolvercote Mill Stream in Oxford was the second inland river to get bathing water status in 2022 and since then the water has always been rated "poor".

In an attempt to improve things, banks of ultraviolet (UV) lights have just been installed at a cost of £4m upstream at Cassington wastewater treatment works to kill bacteria before they reach the River Thames. But there's no question of it being installed everywhere.

"The reality is it's expensive. We have to be sure we're spending money wisely," Tessa Fayers from Thames Water says.

UV disinfection has been installed at 160 of the nearly 7,000 wastewater treatment works across England – almost always as targeted interventions to protect either shellfish or bathing sites downstream.

Wessex Water said it had no plans to introduce UV disinfection at Bradford-on-Tone and that it would publish its conclusions on why the water quality is so poor in April 2027.

Sign up for our Future Earth newsletter to keep up with the latest climate and environment stories with the BBC's Justin Rowlatt. Outside the UK? Sign up to our international newsletter here.

item.title: British hacker who stole $11m through text message scheme jailed for six years in US
item.description: Tyler Buchanan, from Dundee, was a member of the notorious Scattered Spider group and began hacking when he was a teenager.
item.content:encoded:
A British hacker has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the US for conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies via text message phishing, and stealing more than $11.6m (£8.8m) in cryptocurrency from individual victims.

Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, started hacking as a teenager and was part of the collective of young hackers known as Scattered Spider, which has been blamed for a string of high profile cyber-crimes.

US prosecutors said the thefts had "severe, life-altering consequences" for victims and showed the growing threat posed by online crime groups.

The sentence brings to an end a years-long international investigation involving authorities in the UK, US, Spain and Canada.

Buchanan admitted taking part in a hacking campaign that began in 2021, when he was 19.

Working from his parents' home, he and other English-speaking hackers in the US and UK targeted employees at major technology and telecommunications companies.

It made them $8m in less than two years, according to US prosecutors.

Buchanan and his hacker gang sent out hundreds of SMS messages to the mobile phones of people who worked for large tech or telecoms companies.

The SMS phishing messages contained links to spoof websites designed to look like legitimate sites of victim companies.

The group used messages like "Hi, your account is due to expire - you need to log in to your work account here immediately or you will lose access to work apps".

The websites then lured the recipient into providing confidential information, including personal identifying information (PII), and account usernames and passwords.

The boys and young men did it on an industrial scale with Buchanan setting up a Telegram bot to collect all the victims' credentials as the duped workers unwittingly handed over their login details.

For some victim companies, subsequently stolen information included confidential work information, intellectual property, plus account access credentials, names, email addresses, and telephone numbers.

The group then used stolen information and SIM-swapping techniques to target cryptocurrency investors in the United States.

In the largest single theft, prosecutors said one victim lost $1.67m in December 2022.

Overall, authorities calculated that Buchanan and his co-conspirators stole more than $11.6m from victims.

Threatened with a blowtorch

Buchanan was also a victim of cyber-criminals.

In early 2023 his online identity and home address were leaked by rival hackers seeking access to his cryptocurrency.

Cyber security researchers and journalists reported that he was assaulted at his home and threatened with a blowtorch.

"TylerB and his group were highly sophisticated and organised but the violence he and others experienced was a sign of the troubling direction of these online communities of young hackers" says cyber security researcher Allison Nixon from Unit221B.

Buchanan then reportedly fled to Canada to escape further threats before returning home.

In April 2023, officers from Police Scotland searched Buchanan's bedroom after receiving a request from the FBI.

Investigators recovered a device containing the names and addresses of hacking victims, along with cryptocurrency seed phrases and account credentials belonging to at least one victim.

The following month, Buchanan left the UK again.

He was arrested on 31 May 2024 at Palma de Mallorca Airport in Spain while attempting to board a private flight to Naples.

After being extradited to the United States, he remained in custody before being sentenced this week.

In his November 2023 charge, Buchanan was named along with four American men and boys in their twenties and teens for alleged activity linked to the notorious cyber-criminal collective Scattered Spider.

They have all pleaded guilty too and are now serving time in jail.

Two other members of the Scattered Spider group were jailed in the UK in July for various cyber attacks including a disruptive one against Transport for London that caused £39m of damage.

item.title: Waymo pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways
item.description: The decision comes after California banned Waymo's driverless vehicles from operating on the state's highways following a series of traffic incidents.
item.content:encoded:
Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways, the company has said.

The decision comes after California banned Waymo's driverless taxis from state freeways following a series of recent traffic incidents.

California's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) cited an "imminent hazard to public safety" for the ban, noting an incident this month in which several driverless Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on US Route 101.

Waymo said it was working with state officials "diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations", adding that no injuries or collisions were reported following the incident on US Route 101 south of San Francisco.

California's DMV said Waymo's driverless taxis presented a risk "due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present".

In another incident earlier this month, footage widely seen on social media appeared to show a Waymo car trying to overtake patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing the pace of traffic on a San Francisco highway.

The California ban, which came into effect on 11 November, would remain in place until Waymo "demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions".

A Waymo spokesperson said: "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance."

Data on Waymo's website suggests that its cars, compared to human drivers, are involved in 95% fewer crashes resulting in serious injury.

Waymo currently operates driverless taxis in 15 US cities, but only offered freeway rides in a handful of those locations, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Miami.

The company's driverless taxis can continue to operate on regular city streets.

In May, Waymo recalled thousands of its self-driving cars in the US over a software issue that could allow vehicles to drive into flooded roads.

In the same month, multiple Waymo cars were spotted driving around a cul-de-sac in Atlanta, Georgia, in the early hours of the morning.

Have you been affected by the issues discussed in this story? Get in touch by using this link or the form below.

item.title: Democrats win Alaska Senate race two weeks after midterms counting began
item.description: Confirmation of Mary Peltola's victory caps of the party's rout of the Republicans in the midterms Senate election.
item.content:encoded:
Democrat Mary Peltola has won Alaska's hard-fought Senate race, completing a sweeping victory for the party in the US upper house in the midterm elections.

The win gives the Democrats a 56th Senate seat following a tumultuous and controversial election in Alaska, which featured alleged spoiler recruitment efforts and unprecedented court battles.

It took two full weeks of counting to call a winner in the 3 November poll due to the logistical challenge of collecting ballots from across the state's remote expanse.

It is the ninth Senate seat the Democrats have taken from Republicans in the midterms, giving the party control of the US Congress for the last two years of Donald Trump's presidency.

The Democrats also won back the House of Representatives, the lower chamber.

Peltola defeated the incumbent Republican senator, Dan S Sullivan, who is yet to comment.

In her victory statement, Peltola said the "status quo in DC is not working for Alaska".

She recalled speaking to "elders in tears about empty fish racks" and to parents in rural Alaska choosing between heating their homes and putting food on the table.

Peltola is the first Alaska Native elected to the US Senate, and is the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in Alaska since 2008.

Donald Trump won the state by 13 points in the 2024 presidential election, but defeat for the Republicans in this year's US Senate race in the state caps off a string of losses in the midterms for the president's party.

Many voters across the United States cited cost-of-living issues as a factor that affected how they cast their ballots.

Peltola's campaign had come under fire after the New York Times reported that her team worked with people who tried to recruit so-called spoiler candidates in an alleged attempt to confuse voters.

The alleged scheme led to a candidate named Daniel J Sullivan - a complete political unknown residing in a small coastal town who shared a name with the state's current US Senator and incumbent, Dan S Sullivan - contesting the race.

After legal challenges, state courts ruled that Daniel J Sullivan could remain on the ballot, and election officials distinguished them on election materials.

Peltola denied having knowledge of the alleged plot but her campaign swiftly came under fire, and both the US justice department and Alaska's Republican governor said they would launch investigations.

The Trump administration also filed a lawsuit attempting to stop the certification of the election results if the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan lost.

A federal judge, though, dismissed the case, following legal challenges from Alaska election officials as well as the Peltola campaign and voting groups.

Due to Alaska's ranked-choice voting system, voters confused about which Dan Sullivan was the incumbent could have simply chosen both men, listing them as their first and second choices.

If they did so, after the first round of voting was complete, tabulation would have re-allocated any votes from Daniel J Sullivan - who stood little to no chance of winning - to Dan S Sullivan.

Experts told the BBC that this process made it difficult for any potential spoiler candidate to have any impact on the results.

An analysis by BBC Verify found that even if every vote for Daniel J Sullivan had gone to the incumbent, Dan S Sullivan, Peltola would still have won.

The Democratic win in Alaska cements the party's majority in the US Senate, as the party now has 56 seats to the Republicans' 44.

The most senior Democrat in the Senate, Chuck Schumer, said Peltola had run "a pitch-perfect campaign devoted to the issues Alaskans care most about". Hailing the Democrats' final tally in the Senate, he said: "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago."

The Alaska seat was initially one of several toss-up races that appeared as a must-win for Democrats if they wanted to gain control of the US Senate. But by the time Peltola was called the winner, they had seats to spare.

With 99% of ballots counted, Peltola had slightly more than 50% of the votes, while Sullivan trailed on less than 46%.

Sullivan, a former Alaska attorney general and an ally of Trump, campaigned on his record of delivering energy and military investment for the state.

Peltola promised Alaskans a more independent voice in Washington.

"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," she said in her victory statement.

"I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families."

item.title: Irishman charged with destroying US military aircraft with axe
item.description: The $60m (£45m) plane was destroyed in an hours-long raid by an anti-war protester, according to the FBI.
item.content:encoded:
US officials have charged an Irishman with destroying a $60m (£45m) American military aircraft after he allegedly sneaked onto the tarmac of an airport in Ireland.

Daithi O'Corrain, 48, is accused of doing extensive research before he allegedly used chemicals and various tools - including an axe - to damage a US Air National Guard C-130 Hercules parked at Shannon Airport near Limerick.

American prosecutors have charged him with destruction of government property, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

O'Corrain is not currently in US custody, according to the Associated Press news agency, and it is unclear whether he has a lawyer who could speak on his behalf.

In filings unsealed by prosecutors in New York on Tuesday, agents from the FBI argued that the act jeopardised US national security. They say the plane was parked at the airport while en route to another country on a US military assignment.

"As alleged, Daithi O'Corrain carried out a deliberate, planned attack against a US military aircraft, causing tens of millions of dollars in damage and jeopardizing critical military operations," prosecutors said in a court filing.

"This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism," said FBI Assistant Director in Charge James Barnacle Jr, explaining O'Corrain "spent months researching the aircraft, acquiring tools and materials, and preparing to maximize the destruction he could inflict."

Officials say that the suspect planned extensively for the 11 April 2026 raid, and brought tools with him for the demolition, which took place over several hours.

He entered the plane by breaking a locking mechanism, officials say, then used straps to close the doors before covering the windows.

"O'Corrain then proceeded to inflict severe damage to the interior of the Aircraft by, among other things, cutting wire bundles and hydraulic lines within the Aircraft, crimping a liquid oxygen line within the Aircraft, destroying every gauge in the Aircraft's cockpit, and puncturing the Aircraft's air ducts," the US indictment says.

He also used gallium, a substance that can erode aluminum and steel, ball bearings which he poured in the fuel tank, and an axe which he used to puncture the exterior of the plane.

He was caught by airport crew, and filmed standing on top of the plane. He was arrested at the scene, and charged by Ireland's national police with causing criminal damages.

The US charges say that he had planned well, because he avoided cutting a line that would have risked causing massive explosion.

According to the Limerick Post, O'Corrain is from Cork City. Supporters have described him as an anti-war activist.

Shannon Airport is a key hub for US military personnel, and is frequently the scene of anti-war protests. It was used by President Donald Trump in September for his visit to Ireland.

US prosecutors note that there have been several breaches there in recent years by protesters, including in May 2025 when three people drove a van through a perimeter fence, and then again later that month when a US airplane was sprayed with paint, making it temporarily inoperable.

item.title: GTA 6: My wife and daughter have signed a 'do not disturb' contract
item.description: Painter and decorator Sean Little has booked the week off work to play the new Grand Theft Auto game.
item.content:encoded:
For Grand Theft Auto superfan Sean Little, a week off work to play the latest version of the blockbuster video game wasn't enough.

He knew that if he was spending seven days at home in Dumfries and Galloway, he would be expected to walk the dogs and pull his weight in the kitchen.

So the self-employed painter and decorator persuaded his wife and daughter to sign a "non-interference contract" giving him a week off Dad duties.

For a "signing fee", they have agreed to allow him to take over their living room and play GTA6 in peace.

"We're not allowed to ask him to do any sort of household chores," his wife Natalie told BBC Scotland News.

"We're not allowed to make any comments of how long he's been playing it for, any comments about him being lazy because he's not moved off the couch for hours.

"He gave me some extra housekeeping money so that I can buy sort of snacky food... he won't be cooking any meals.

"Literally he will be in here playing it and that's all he's going to do."

Sean is leaving nothing to chance. He's even bought paper plates so he's not asked to wash any dishes.

He says he pulled together the contract for his wife and 13-year-old daughter, Charlotte, as a joke and filmed it for his TikTok account.

But he admits there's some truth to it.

If they stick to their side of the deal it will ensure Natalie and Charlotte don't interrupt him, reveal spoilers or "set unnecessary household tasks".

And it outlines a series of banned phrases, which include:

  • You've been on that for hours
  • Are you seriously still playing that?
  • Can you just do this one thing first?

In return, there are financial incentives for Sean's family - he's paid £50 to Natalie and £20 to Charlotte, and increased his weekly contribution to family finances to £500.

"Probably people think I'm daft, but I mean, I don't know if they're even wrong, I don't even question them, and to be honest with you, I don't care," said Sean who lives with his family in Newton Stewart.

"I don't care what people think. My family are happy, I'm happy - as long as my bubble are happy, then who cares what anybody else thinks?"

'I'm still a teenager at heart'

He played the first Grand Theft Auto game when he was a teenager and has been a devoted fan ever since.

He compares himself to a Star Wars fan who watched the first film when it was released in the 1970s.

"If a new Star Wars film comes out in 2026, because they're 60 years old, they don't automatically stop being a Star Wars fan," he said.

"You don't grow out of being a fan of something."

Sean was in his mid-20s when GTA 5 came out and has been waiting 13 years for the new release.

"I've been excited for it for years, probably since finishing Grand Theft Auto 5 to be honest with you," the 38-year-old said.

"If it continues with the same kind of timeline, I'll be 51 when GTA 7 comes out - still a teenager at heart probably."

Sean has been working weekends, putting in 13-hour days and putting aside a bit of spare cash in preparation for his week off.

"I'm the same when I'm going to be having a holiday, except I'm just going to be sitting in my living room playing a game," he said.

So instead of a week off work, enjoying a holiday in somewhere like Benidorm, he'll be living the life in Vice City?

"Exactly, so much better by the way," he said. "I don't know if you've been to Benidorm but Vice, it is probably better to be honest. Sorry Benidorm."

item.title: Thomas Markle charged over child sex abuse material in Philippines
item.description: Markle is being held in custody in the US after one charge and has previously denied all of the allegations.
item.content:encoded:
Police in the Philippines have charged Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, with possession of and intent to distribute child sexual abuse material.

The charges were filed on Monday, Cebu province prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC.

Earlier this month, Markle, 82, was separately arrested and charged in the US with possession of child sexual abuse material. The FBI said agents, after searching storage units Markle rented, seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books, that they allege contained child sex abuse material.

Markle, who is in custody in the US, has previously denied the allegations. The BBC has contacted Markle's attorney for comment.

Elmido told the BBC that Philippine National Police had charged Markle Sr with "two counts of intent to distribute CSAEM [child sexual abuse and exploitation material], and one count of possession of CSAEM material".

Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.

Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.

Earlier this month, Markle Sr was arrested and charged in the US. He had initially been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida, but was taken back into custody last week after prosecutors alleged he removed his ankle monitor.

Meghan Markle has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.

In a previously shared statement after the allegations against her father emerged, Meghan wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."

She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

item.title: Pakistan's solar revolution has been so successful the national grid is crumbling
item.description: People installing their own solar panels has helped boost the solar share of Pakistan's electricity from 1% to 28%.
item.content:encoded:
Jewellery, glimmering silverware, sofas and an air-conditioning unit. Three months after his wedding, Faisal Shahzad's home in rural Punjab is bursting with gifts from his bride's family, as part of the dowry.

But the most prized possession is tucked under the bed: a 340W solar panel.

"In the summer we ran it from 08:00 in the morning until the evening," he says, adding they didn't need to use grid power at all during the day. "We ran our air cooler on it all day."

Pakistan has seen a boom in imported solar panels, which glisten from the rooftops of homes and hospitals; from farmers' fields to industrial complexes.

From 2018 to 2025, the share of electricity generated from solar energy in the country rose from 1% to 28%, according to Pakistan-based think tank Renewables First, with some seven million households now owning panels.

People used to gift motorbikes or other household items at weddings, Shahzad says. "Now they give a solar panel and an air cooler. It has almost become a must."

Alongside the solar panel he still uses the national grid to meet his energy needs, particularly as he lives in a house with his family and brothers' families, who often use multiple appliances simultaneously. But in a country where the average wage is just under 40,000 Pakistani rupees (£110; $145) per month, bills are becoming unaffordable, rising to 15,000-18,000 rupees.

This year, COP31 is pushing the world to move away from fossil-powered vehicles, boilers and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment. And while Pakistan has become a poster child for solarisation, the national grid system is experiencing knock-on eﬀects.

The power grid death spiral

The big pivot to solar wasn't driven by government policy but by individual Pakistani households. Most people we spoke to said they installed panels to escape soaring electricity prices from an often unreliable national grid.

Electricity tariffs have more than doubled in a few years, says Muhammad Hassan Dajana, industry liaison at Renewables First, while the cost of Chinese solar panels has "decreased by 93%".

"People have just found another way to be able to survive," says Energy Minister Awais Ahmad Leghari. "It's a very healthy thing. We have adapted to the situation. The people have reacted and responded in a very economically viable and efficient manner."

While the solar boom brings clear benefits, particularly for a country that imports huge amounts of fuel, there are worries too.

Pakistan needs to avoid the so-called utility death spiral.

When people buy less energy from the national grid, fewer customers are left to cover the fixed costs of maintaining it. That can force prices up - which in turn encourages even more people to switch to solar.

Over time, this can lead to a two-tier system in which those who can't afford to buy panels face ever-rising bills, while the national grid becomes an increasing burden on the state.

"You'll have a white elephant in the form of a state-owned enterprise that requires a lot of public funding to just stay afloat," says Dajana.

Pakistan's government says the costs are already being felt.

"In just the past two years, the exodus from the grid has cost the rest of the consumers more than $500 million [£378m] a year," says Leghari. "That's a very big burden."

The government doesn't want to pull people away from solar, he explains, but wants the grid to be more competitive to be able to offer better energy prices.

Private power producers, which feed into the grid, have been heavily criticised inside Pakistan for locking the country into costly, inflexible contracts. Producers themselves point to broader structural problems like poor grid maintenance as contributing to higher bills. Leghari says the government has renegotiated most of the contracts and is now focused on making the grid more efficient with better storage, less waste and more innovation.

Leghari wants the country to run on "up to 90% clean power" by the end of 2036 - including renewables and nuclear - with dependence on imported energy reducing from 26% to 4%.

Solar-powered business

But as the government tries to improve the grid, solar is still expanding with widespread adoption in industry.

Kohinoor Textiles Mills in Islamabad, which is powered by a sea of huge blue solar panels, is one example. Utilities manager Sabawoon Khan describes them as his "baby", pointing at construction work levelling the ground for more panels.

When the sun shines, the mills' hundreds of machines are powered entirely by solar energy, Khan says. The heavy-furnace-oil engines they once relied on sit mothballed in a warehouse.

But there are limits. When it's too cloudy or polluted, and during the night, the company takes more energy from the national grid. In the coming weeks, like other firms, it will start using industrial batteries which can store excess solar energy.

"We needed to reduce our energy costs and this was one way to do it," says Taufique Sayeed Saigol, the mills' CEO, who adds the plan is not to disconnect from the grid altogether.

"The state unfortunately doesn't have the resources so we can't really say that we blame everything on the state. We do some of the things ourselves."

Critics accuse the government of moving the goalposts on solar power. Previously, households could feed excess electricity into the grid and earn credits, which were then used to offset the cost of grid power when the sun wasn't shining. That policy changed earlier this year.

"Initially their policy was very helpful," says Arif Ehsan Malik, president of Faisalabad's chamber of commerce. "But then the policy changed. Now they have started purchasing at a lower rate and selling back at a higher rate."

Malik says that makes a big difference for small and medium businesses. Leghari counters that the costs of the initial model didn't add up; the electricity the solar producers put into the system was much cheaper than the electricity they ended up taking out of it.

"Those profits were coming at the cost of the rest of the consumers of the grid. Had we not changed those regulations, the rest of the consumers would have been burdened by at least 150 to 200 billion rupees a year, say, two years from now."

Despite admitting that the first wave of solar adoption was a "surprise" to the government, Leghari says he has no fear that solar could outrun their plans, saying it has been incorporated into their 10-year forecasts and the numbers leaving the grid have slowed.

Pakistan has big ambitions for solar; there are plans to open solar battery factories around the country and encourage more electric vehicles.

But it's also at a crossroads.

"There are two paths ahead," Dajana says. One is a future where solar and the grid work in parallel, demonstrating how a gradual energy transition can succeed. The other is where Pakistan becomes a cautionary tale, burdened with a costly, declining grid.

Shahzad's solar ambitions for his home in rural Punjab certainly have not slowed.

"We plan to get another 10-15 panels and install them on the roof, then connect a full system with batteries and back up.

"The plan is to be fully self-sufficient."

item.title: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as firm reports bumper results
item.description: The AI chip giant reported strong quarterly earnings on Tuesday after the dramatic exit of Jensen Huang.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia's quarterly sales doubled to top $100bn for the first time as the company insisted it has no plans to reinstate ousted co-founder Jensen Huang.

In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it is "business as usual" and told investors: "We've got this."

The company's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier, reaching $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading.

Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.

"The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said during a call on Tuesday with financial analysts.

The company's profits also doubled from a year ago. For the quarter, which covered the three months to 25 October, profit hit $65bn. Its revenue from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn in the same period.

Going forward, the company said its rapid growth is poised to continue, and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.

Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.

"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."

Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry.

"It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."

She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects".

"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."

The interim CEO also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China.

The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.

They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US.

Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped.

Despite board chairman Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analysts' questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.

He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection.

"With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new CEO will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."

Michael Monaghan from investment firm Founder ETFs is among those who want Huang back in the top job at Nvidia.

The Nvidia investor told the BBC that he is waiting to see the results of a thorough investigation into Huang's actions, instead of relying on "salacious allegations" made in the media.

Nvidia's strong earnings are "from the machine that Jensen built" and a company tends to lose "its shine and vision" after an iconic founder leaves, Monaghan said.

item.title: US National Security Agency's classified internal network reportedly goes offline
item.description: The National Security Agency says a "temporary degradation" affected some internal systems but that "mission-critical capabilities" were not affected.
item.content:encoded:
A highly classified network used by the US National Security Agency (NSA) for internal communications went offline on Tuesday for an unspecified period of time, according to US media reports.

The NSA - America's largest intelligence organisation - said it had experienced a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance" but that "mission-critical capabilities" were not affected.

The outage reportedly affected the NSANet network, which is how officials send and receive top secret or classified information.

It comes after a string of technology outages in the US in recent days that have affected flights, banks and other infrastructure.

"While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues," an NSA spokesperson said in a statement to the BBC.

"NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events."

It did not specify when the issue began, nor when it would be resolved.

The issue was not a cyberattack, multiple US news outlets reported.

Tens of thousands of people work at the NSA, which is responsible for collecting signals intelligence, overseeing cyber threats, and protecting US government communications.

Multiple sources told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that the agency was seeking to avoid having large numbers of employees log on to their computers simultaneously while the network was experiencing problems on Tuesday.

Sources familiar with the situation told CBS that operations at the NSA's headquarters in Fort Meade, Maryland, had not been affected but that some activities had been redirected to other facilities around the country.

Tuesday's outage follows a series of technological outages.

Last week, a massive Microsoft outage impacted schools, healthcare systems, businesses, courts and governments around the world - including the US and Canada - while a network failure grounded all US flights.

On Monday, thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, reported trouble accessing services.

Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems may have affected other banks and that it was not a cyber security incident.

item.title: Rubio says US not 'under systemic attack' after series of tech outages
item.description: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was "zero evidence" supporting theories online that recent outages affecting Microsoft, banks and flights are connected.
item.content:encoded:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed widespread concerns online that the series of recent tech outages in the past week are connected, telling reporters there was "zero evidence" of any link.

Rubio acknowledged that "people are fearful" the spate of outages, which included all flights being grounded in the US and widespread disruptions to banking, Apple and Microsoft services, could be linked or part of a plot.

"We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."

Cyber-security experts have said there is no evidence connecting the outages, and many of the issues appear due to updates to old infrastructure.

In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage, an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours, and issues for the National Security Agency, several US banks and Apple.

Every affected company or agency has said this was not a cyber-related incident.
