Rubio's comments came hours after US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also addressed the issue, telling Fox News the outages were not the product of a cyber-attack. He explained "lots of institutions" are patching or upgrading systems, which has caused some disruption.

Rubio was asked whether the Trump administration was concerned public fears could lead to stockpiling or a run on the banks.

Acknowledging those concerns, Rubio said the best way to deal with that is to share with the American people what the US government knows.

"Every indicator we have is that every single one of these events has an explanation or a cause that has nothing to do with a cyber-criminal, has nothing to do with a hostile actor or another country," he said.

Daily technology-related disruptions have happened since Thursday, when a Microsoft outage disrupted many of its services, including email.

The next day, the Federal Aviation Administration called for a nationwide ground stop lasting more than four hours.

On Monday a United Airlines technology failure delayed about 150 flights and a JPMorgan Chase software problem disrupted some banking services.

Apple users were impacted by outages affecting iCloud and Apple Pay on Tuesday. The company said the cause was not a cyber-attack but the outage was triggered by an an internal update.

A highly classified network used by the US National Security Agency (NSA) for internal communications also went offline for a period of time on Tuesday.

item.title: American soldier arrested by UK police on suspicion of spying taken into US military custody
item.description: The Metropolitan Police say he has been taken into custody by the US Military over suspected national security and espionage allegations.
item.content:encoded:
A US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia earlier this month has been taken into US military custody, British counter-terror police have said.

The serviceman has been identified as Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, BBC News understands. The 41-year-old - who has served in the US Army since 2008 - was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police.

Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC).

Counter Terror Policing said he is now in custody over suspected national security and espionage allegations. At the time of his arrest, Russia said they had "nothing to do with it".

British police previously said he was being held in London after he was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.

The day after Tyner's arrest, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he was "unaware" of what it was connected to.

"We have nothing to do with it, and it has nothing to do with us," he told reporters in Moscow.

Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said: "Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them [their American partners] to progress."

"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," he added.

FBI director Kash Patel said an army officer was in custody "as the result of an espionage investigation and the close cooperation" between the bureau, US Army and various UK partners.

"Together we worked to identify a potential threat to national security and take swift action," he said.

"This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk."

US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon said the case should serve as a "stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath" they all take.

"Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardising our collective defence, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served," he added.

item.title: Town's Seven Sisters tower blocks to be demolished
item.description: The landlord says refurbishment would have cost at least £269m, while replacing them was "affordable".
item.content:encoded:
A town's landmark tower blocks, which have dominated its skyline since the 1960s, are set to be demolished after years of uncertainty over their future.

Rochdale's Seven Sisters tower blocks, which contain 766 flats, will be replaced by about 600 homes, social landlord Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) said.

Residents began moving out of the flats in October 2025 following concerns about their long-term safety but a local campaign, previously backed by Rochdale Council, had appealed for the buildings to be refurbished rather than demolished.

But RBH said replacing the buildings was the "only realistic and affordable way" to provide suitable homes for residents.

Refurbishment would have cost at least £269m and would have taken 12 years, RBH said.

Some 78 households have yet to accept an offer of another home.

Previous building surveys have identified structural and electrical issues with the tower blocks, and problems with water pumps and roof damage.

RBH said it expected all remaining residents would be supported to move out by August 2027. One of the blocks, Mitchell Hey, has already closed.

RBH Chief Executive Amanda Newton said: "College Bank has been home to generations of Rochdalians, and we recognise the important place the blocks hold in many people's memories."

She said replacing the buildings was the "only realistic and affordable way" to provide homes.

Plans to demolish the towers were first revealed in 2017, prompting opposition from residents, and demolition was ruled out in 2023.

RBH subsequently said all options were back on the table.

The social landlord said the proposed 601 new homes could accommodate more people, despite being fewer in number, with at least 249 additional bedspaces.

RBH said it hoped some former residents could return to College Bank once the new homes were built, although this had yet to be agreed.

The redevelopment will require planning permission, and RBH did not give a demolition date in its announcement.

Listen to the best of BBC Radio Manchester on Sounds and follow BBC Manchester on Facebook , X , and Instagram . You can also send story ideas via Whatsapp to 0808 100 2230.

item.title: Carney looks to China as Trump tariffs squeeze Canada's car industry
item.description: The PM has suggested Chinese automakers could replace American ones in Canada - but some say that would not be easy.
item.content:encoded:
Canada's car industry has become one of the clearest stress tests for Ottawa as it grapples with US tariffs on the sector.

Now Prime Minister Mark Carney has signalled that he is looking to China, where he is on a visit for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit (Apec), as part of the solution.

But that avenue is not without controversy, and is once again drawing the ire of those close to Donald Trump.

While in Cambodia earlier this week, Carney told reporters that Canada could turn to European and Asian carmakers to save its auto manufacturing sector if a trade deal with the US could not be reached.

If Canadian auto workers are "not fully utilised in a North American context, that provides other opportunities.

"Canada's going to move forward either way," he said.

He went on to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in China on Tuesday for their second head-to-head in less than a year. The two talked of the importance of developing their relations, and Carney said they had agreed to further tariff cuts.

Neither side mentioned vehicles specifically, though analysts suggest the issue will have been prominent in their minds.

In January, Carney said that opening the door to China's electric vehicles (EVs) could result in investment into Canadian-owned companies and the creation of manufacturing jobs in the sector.

American tariffs on imports of Canadian-made vehicles have led to thousands of job losses in Canada and anxiety over the future, as 90% of cars made in Canada are shipped to and sold in the US.

At the same time, China has been eyeing Canada as a potential entry-point to the North American EV market. Earlier this year, Canada announced that it would let in 49,000 EVs from China at a low tariff rate, with plans to raise that quota gradually to 70,000 by 2030.

The move was a significant break from the US, which tariffs Chinese EVs heavily to protect domestic manufacturing.

Peter Navarro, Trump's senior counsel for trade and manufacturing, warned the prime minister against cosying up to China in a post on X.

"Are u really threatening to play China off the US? This is offensive in the extreme," he wrote on Monday. "You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive."

His comments were reposted by Pete Hoekstra, the US ambassador to Canada.

Chinese EV manufacturers like BYD and Chery have already been lobbying the Canadian government for market access.

Last week, Canada's Minister of International Trade Maninder Sidhu toured a Chery plant in China. He told reporters afterwards that Canadians could expect to see affordable Chinese EVs in Canada by early 2027.

These moves come as the toll of US tariffs on Canada's auto sector has become harder to ignore.

Stellantis, a multinational car manufacturer that made models like the Dodge Challenger in Canada, recently announced it would sell its assembly plant in Brampton, Ontario.

The facility had been idle since 2023 for a planned retooling, but what was supposed to be a temporary shutdown became permanent after Trump's tariffs.

The sale has led to speculation that a Chinese EV manufacturer could move into the facility, after Canadian media outlet CTV News reported, citing anonymous sources, that Stellantis was planning to lease back 25% of its plant to assemble "affordable" EVs.

The idea is unpopular with Ontario Premier Doug Ford. In a letter to Carney, he warned against opening the door for Chinese EV kits to be assembled at the Brampton plant.

China overwhelmingly builds its cars at home and ships them whole - or to be assembled in kits - overseas.

Lynette Ong, director of the China Governance Lab at the University of Toronto, said introducing Chinese auto manufacturing in Canada would be "controversial" due to fears that Canadian jobs could be lost and that the North American industry could be eroded.

"We want to make sure they're hiring Canadian workers, that they are helping train Canadian workers and that they are transferring the technology over," Ong said.

Carney noted there are "clear guardrails" in how Canada deals with China, including barring work on sensitive matters like artificial intelligence and critical minerals.

Canada has also eyed other partnerships. It is notably pursuing associate member status with the EU, and had signed a free trade deal with the Philippines earlier this week.

Just how much Canada is willing to embrace Chinese manufacturing, however, still depends on the outcome of ongoing US-Canada trade talks.

Progress has been made in negotiations, Carney recently said, but differences remain. It is unclear if Trump and Carney will speak on the sidelines of the Apec summit later this week.

item.title: William and Kate celebrate Earthshot Prize winners in Mumbai
item.description: The Prince and Princess of Wales were joined by sporting and acting stars for the annual environmental awards ceremony.
item.content:encoded:
The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize.

Five award-winners were named at a ceremony in Mumbai, India, and will each receive £1m to scale up their projects.

One of the winners was a country - with Bhutan being recognised for its environmental policies that help to safeguard water supplies for nearly a fifth of the world's population.

Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actor Rami Malek and Bollywood stars Alia Bhatt and Sonam Kapoor were among those who attended the ceremony, which saw performances from Take That and Bridgerton's Simone Ashley.

The annual event, founded by Prince William and now in its sixth year, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.

Prince William was joined by Catherine at the ceremony as the royal couple continued their first official overseas trip together in four years. Catherine's cancer treatment has limited the amount she has travelled internationally.

They arrived on the event's green carpet wearing outfits celebrating Indian fashion.

Prince William wore a bespoke Bandhgala, a classic Indian formal jacket, while Catherine was dressed in an Anarkali dress by Mahima Mahajan made from handwoven silk Georgette with traditional Banarasi gold detailing.

During his speech, Prince William said this decade was the moment when positive change becomes irreversible" and remarked that history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.

He added that "around the world, we are witnessing human ingenuity on a remarkable scale".

Separately, Catherine highlighted the "hope" represented by entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis.

The princess, who presented an award, also said: "Just as the natural world finds ways to adapt and flourish, so too can we, when we nurture new ideas and give them the opportunity to grow.

"The people we're celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come."

There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature; Clean Our Air; Revive Our Oceans; Build a Waste-Free World; and Fix Our Climate.

Five winners were chosen from a list of 15 finalists who attended Tuesday's awards ceremony.

Earthshot Prize 2026 - full list of winners

  • Protect and Restore Nature: Bhutan, the country that helps to protect the water security of 1.6 billion people across South Asia and has a national nature coalition that aims to revive forests and rivers by restoring 50,000 hectares of damaged land
  • Build a Waste-Free World: PFAS-Free France, a national campaign that helped secure landmark legislation banning 'forever chemicals' in France by 2030, and hopes to extend the ban to more major countries
  • Revive Our Oceans: Niue Ocean Wide Trust, the Pacific island's scheme that has safeguarded marine life by investing in conservation to fund the long-term protection of its vast waters
  • Clean Our Air: Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, a scheme rolling out up to one million electric rickshaws across India with the aim to drasitically cut one of the world's largest sources of on-road air pollution
  • Fix Our Climate: Ørsted, a global energy company that has cut its direct carbon emissions by more than 98% by transforming from being highly coal-intensive to a leader in offshore wind

The Earthshot prize, first held in 2020, was inspired by former US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely.

Tuesday's event also saw appearances on stage from Earthshot ambassadors Robert Irwin, the Australian conservationist, and Nomzamo Mbatha, the South African actor.

As well as Take That, there were also musical performances from a number of Indian artists including Shreya Ghoshal, composer and pianist Merlin D'Souza and all-female hip hop collective Wild Wild Women.

The dazzling awards night was brought to a close by musician and composer Shashwat Sachdev.

Earlier on Tuesday, William and Catherine drove in an electric rickshaw to meet the 15 finalists.

As William stepped from the vehicle, which is manufactured by prize winner Mahindra Last Mile Mobility and has a top speed of 55mph, he said: "It was quite good fun, really good fun."

The couple arrived in India on Monday for the three-day visit, which is expected to also include a meeting with India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday.

Their first engagement saw them play a game of street - or "gully" cricket - in Mumbai alongside Tendulkar.

item.title: School offers prizes to pupils for turning up to class on day GTA 6 comes out
item.description: Belfast Boys' Model school issued letters to parents, saying that the release of the game on Thursday coincided with GCSE maths exams.
item.content:encoded:
A school concerned about pupils not coming in on the day the highly-anticipated GTA VI video game is released has offered young people prizes for turning up for classes.

Belfast Boys' Model school issued letters to parents, saying that the release of the game on Thursday coincided with GCSE maths exams.

The school said that "activities such as playing Grand Theft Auto can wait until the weekend".

On Monday, the school added that pupils who attended school on both Thursday and Friday would be entered into a draw for a £70 gift card for either PlayStation or Xbox.

In a letter issued to parents, reported by The Nolan Show, the school reminded "all parents and carers of the importance of ensuring that students attend school on Thursday 19th November".

It also said that "all Year 11 students and some Year 12 students" would be sitting a GCSE maths exam on Thursday, the same day the game comes out.

"Good attendance is one of the strongest indicators of academic success," the letter added.

Mary Montgomery, who is principal of the school, said "the primary focus" of her letter was Thursday's Mathematics examination and "encouraging our boys to be in school and ready to achieve their best".

"The results at GCSE have been fantastic in recent years and we want to continue that success for the boys," she said.

"It also highlighted the launch of GTA as something which might entice some boys to stay at home. However, the games vouchers were a pupil-led incentive."

GTA VI is released on Thursday, 13 years after the previous edition and with an estimated development cost of more $1bn (£866m).

In 2013, the term 'GTA Flu' was coined in reference to the large number of sick days reportedly taken when GTA V was released.

On Monday, the school announced that all pupils in attendance on Thursday and Friday would be entered into a draw to win one of two £70 gift cards "for PlayStation/Xbox".

Anthony, a 15-year-old pupil at the school told BBC News NI he is "very excited" about the game.

He has already downloaded it and when it is released he is "going to play it a lot".

"I've been waiting a long time for this," he said.

"You can pre download it now, install it now and when the game comes out you can instantly play it."

Michael, who is 17, is also excited to play the new GTA game, adding he thinks the school's idea to incentivise attendance is a "really good one".

The idea for the draw, which came from the pupils, will mark International Men's Health Day and raise money for charity.

"This idea is a really good one because gaming and mental health coincide a lot with men as they can use gaming as escapism from personal problems such as school, work and exams," Michael said.

He added: "We think gaming can be used as a way to negate the problems and stress that arise from school, so we brought that idea for the vouchers to get more people into school."

He added that gaming can help the pupils "switch off and manage some of the stress around exams, which is important with GCSE modules this week".

Speaking to The Nolan Show, a former school principal Kathleen O'Hare said the decision to send the letter to parents was "very wise".

"The cult of this game is so large that parents will be put under extreme pressure at times," she said.

O'Hare added that it has been "proven" that missing a day of school "really does matter".

Pete Wray, a Ulster Unionist Party councillor who works with children, said "there is a sizable amount of young people that are in our education system and completely disengage".

"They take an odd day off, and once they've got one day off, they're anxious about going back because they know they're going to be behind, and that leads to more and more problems," he said.

Wray said he will be imploring young people not to miss school to play the game, but that he "completely understands how people can become engrossed in it".

What is GTA 6?

Considered one of the most highly-anticipated video games in history, the game is the latest in the long-running Grand Theft Auto series.

The game series, which has attracted controversy in the past over its depiction of violence and crime, is also the most expensive game ever made, with estimates putting development costs at more than $1bn (£866m).

The previous game in the series, GTA 5, sold nearly 230 million copies, making it one of the best-selling games of all time, which has generated billions of dollars in revenue for developer Rockstar.

GTA 6 will feature its first ever playable female protagonist in a 3D setting - Lucia - alongside her partner in life and crime, Jason, as a second playable character.

Like other GTA games before it, the sixth chapter is set in a fictional US state - this time in Leonida, which is Rockstar's version of Florida.

item.title: How the attack on Putin's prized Crimean Bridge unfolded
item.description: One of the key symbols of Russia's occupation of Ukraine has suffered major damage after a seven-stage attack by Kyiv.
item.content:encoded:
Stretching across the Kerch Strait in the Black Sea, the Crimean Bridge was always a symbol: for Russia, a prestige project cementing its claim to sovereign Ukrainian territory, and for Ukraine, a hated piece of infrastructure emblematic of Moscow's occupation of the Crimean Peninsula.

A key section of the double-arched, 12-mile-long bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said that the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".

But eight years after its unveiling, the bridge has now become material proof of Kyiv's ability to pierce through Moscow's military defences to hit even its most treasured and protected structures.

How did the seven-stage operation play out?

The attack on the strategic Crimean Bridge was carried out gradually to cut across several layers of defence, Kyiv confirmed on Tuesday.

For several weeks Ukraine's Security Service and its General Staff gradually destroyed air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets, and other designated targets, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

A significant strike had already been reported on 16 November, when drones hit the bridge at night. Traffic was paused briefly then reinstated, and although the arch over the road section was visibly damaged, the structure remained standing.

But that hit turned out to have been only the penultimate stage of a complex attack.

In the early hours of 17 November, the final strikes dealt a fatal blow to the weakened arch structure.

One verified video - filmed from a camera on board a Ukrainian-made Flamingo missile - shows the weapon approaching the main span of the bridge and heading towards the steel arches, with the footage freezing just before impact.

The Flamingo had potentially been modified to be controlled remotely, which improved its accuracy enough to strike the bridge supports, munitions expert Justin Bronk, from the Royal United Services Institute said.

The missile's "very heavy warhead" made it "more suitable" for attacking the bridge's reinforced concrete spans and supports, Bronk added.

Zelensky later confirmed that several types of missiles and drones had been employed in the attack, which led the massive road arch - weighing thousands of tonnes and measuring about 227m in length - to collapse into the strait.

Daylight images taken from the shores of Crimea to the north show a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was too dragged below into the sea.

This is clearly critical damage to the crossing. Far from just being a decorative feature of the bridge, the arch played a structural role, transferring loads and supporting the span and helping to ensure the stability of the entire structure.

The parallel arch supporting the railway section has remained standing, although it may also have been damaged. All traffic on the bridge was initially suspended, though trains were later allowed to resume running.

But the damage to the bridge's main span is "catastrophic", Colin Capriani, a structural engineer from Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, told BBC Verify. It was "very hard to envisage" how the bridge could be rebuilt given it is clearly well within range of Ukrainian weaponry, Capriani added.

Major attacks in 2022 and 2023 had already caused serious damage to the road spans of the bridge, but the structure survived.

The difference this time is "the most critical and vulnerable part of the bridge has been hit", said David MacKenzie of engineering consultancy COWI, adding that "although the wreckage of the bridge can be cleared fairly quickly, reinstating full road traffic will take over a year".

What effect could the collapse of the bridge have on Crimea?

Moscow uses Crimea as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles. From there it also carries out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplies its troops in southern Ukraine.

The attack comes after a summer of frequent strikes on Crimea, dictated by Ukraine's stated goal of cutting the peninsula off from Russia. At the time, Kyiv vowed to turn the Crimean Peninsula "into an island".

Now - although it is too early to speak of a complete blockade of Crimea – the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis has increased significantly.

There is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions. However, Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar, which has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.

Moscow can also still utilise the ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited - and anything on the Black Sea has become vulnerable to attack. Resupplying Crimea by sea is risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.

In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge - particularly its enormous arch - may have blocked the shipping channel. This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including the occupied cities of Mariupol and Berdyansk.

Away from the operational value of the damage to the bridge, the symbolic significance remains.

In 2018, Putin triumphantly drove over the bridge representing the unification of Russia and Crimea in a Russian-made truck. That section of the road now lies on the seabed.

Nearly five years since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Putin continues to wreak destruction on Ukraine's civilian population, but his most prized symbols of power are increasingly threatened by Kyiv's reach.

item.title: Russian military plane crashes killing all 19 on board
item.description: Russia's defence ministry says it preliminarily believes a technical malfunction was the cause of the crash in the Kemerovo region.
item.content:encoded:
A Russian military transport plane has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, the country's defence ministry said, according to state-run media.

The An-12 aircraft went down during a "scheduled flight" in an "uninhabited area" in the Kemerovo region, the ministry said in a statement.

The ministry added that it preliminarily believed a technical malfunction was the cause of Tuesday's crash. An investigation by Russia's aviation authorities is now under way.

Local Governor Ilya Seredyuk said an emergency response team "quickly extinguished a blaze" after the crash near the village of Yagunovo, and the area was sealed off by police.

Seredyuk, who visited the crash site, said "a helicopter and medical facilities have been put on standby".

The governor added that the "main task" now was to help investigators carry out their work.

He also posted a video showing firefighters combing through what looked like the crash debris, with a number of ambulances also seen standing nearby.

CCTV footage posted on social media appeared to show the moment the plane crashed, with a lighted object falling through the sky in the distance. An explosion then lit up the sky, but the crash was too far away to be seen.

The BBC and Reuters news agency verified the time and date of the footage, while Reuters also verified the location based on features of the scenery that matched satellite imagery of the area.

It was not immediately known whether the crashed aircraft had any cargo on board.

An-12 planes are widely used by the Russian military to transport weaponry and personnel, and also for search and rescue operations.

item.title: We couldn't afford a house alone, so we bought one with strangers
item.description: People who can't afford to get on the housing ladder are buying homes with someone they don't know.
item.content:encoded:
When Elizabeth and Tom Wilcox realised they could never afford to buy the home they wanted for themselves and their two children, they decided to take a leap of faith.

They'd find another couple with young kids, complete strangers to them, and propose that they go halves on a property and all move in together.

Based in Vancouver, which has long had some of the highest house prices in Canada, the Wilcoxes were desperate to buy a home that had a back garden for their children to play in.

"We wanted a house with a yard that could fit a trampoline, in a walkable neighbourhood, but we couldn't afford it," says Elizabeth, a project manager in the healthcare sector.

With a budget of C$1m ($700,000; £500,000) all they could hope for was a small apartment with a balcony at best.

That was when Elizabeth came up with the idea of buying with another family.

'We've saved thousands'

They placed an advert in a local estate agent's e-newsletter, but it took two years before they finally met a family whom they clicked with – Ashley Pullman and her husband and two children.

In 2023, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans co-bought a six-bedroom, detached house, complete with a back garden, for C$1.85m.

The two families split the deposit of C$250,000, and continue to go halves on the monthly mortgage payments of C$3,900. They also divide bills and other expenses equally, such as any necessary home repairs.

Elizabeth says the arrangement has saved both families "tens of thousands of dollars".

While there is no official data available for the number of people buying homes with people they previously didn't know, Parimal Gosal says he has seen a big increase in interest in Toronto as a response to high property prices.

Gosal is the founder and CEO of Husmates, an app and website that connects people in Canada's largest city who are looking to potentially buy a home with a stranger.

It can be seen as "a financial relationship, and that takes emotions out of it", he says.

It's unclear how common this phenomenon is elsewhere in the world. David Hollingworth, from British mortgage broker L&C, says while he hasn't come across it himself, he thinks it also happens in the UK, though is "very niche".

"I remember that before Covid-19 there was a matchmaking event in a London pub, like speed dating, for people looking to buy a house with a stranger," he says. "How successful this was I don' t know."

Three years on, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans say their living arrangement is still working out.

While each family has some private living spaces, such as their own kitchens, they share the big basement-level living room, which includes a home gym in one corner, and a shared freezer.

"If someone says they're in the basement to work out, we know not to go there for a bit, and it's never been an issue," says Elizabeth.

Ashley agrees that there are no problems. "Maybe it's arrogance but my husband and I felt like we were the type of people who could live with strangers," she says.

'We have house meetings'

Sabrina Bowman, a freelance business consultant in Toronto, has co-owned a home with two other housemates since 2018. When she signed on the dotted line and moved in she didn't know one of the other two people.

While Sabrina says she isn't comfortable sharing the exact financial details, she says they decided to divide up the deposit and mortgage payments based on each of their levels of income.

She says any household disputes can be addressed early with open discussions. "What is important to us is having structures to communicate about everything that happens in the home."

They have regular house meetings where they discuss chores, financial issues, birthday celebrations, and any disagreements.

"It's great to see people be honest about something they may not be comfortable about and for us to find a solution to that problem," Sabrina says.

In the case of both Sabrina's house in Toronto and the Wilcox and Pullman property in Vancouver, they have legal agreements in place in case someone wants to sell up and move out.

For both homes, reasonable notice periods are specified, and for Sabrina's, the departing housemate is required to give those remaining the first opportunity to buy their share.

Toronto real estate lawyer Tanya Walker says such legal assurances are vital. "You need something legally binding instead of a bunch of emails and Facebook messages that can be too messy to collect if a dispute comes up," Walker says.

Back in Vancouver, Elizabeth says that neither family has a timeframe for how long they will live in the house. "All of us are really happy with the set-up and location so it would be hard to move.

"I can't put a price on how it felt to watch the kids jump on the trampoline for the first time, or run in circles on our patch of green grass."

item.title: Pretending to be in New Zealand, booking leave and buying consoles - the lengths fans are going to for GTA 6
item.description: Sensor Tower estimates the game has already made $1.18bn from pre-orders across PlayStation and Xbox
item.content:encoded:
Grand Theft Auto fans have waited 13 long years for the latest edition of the game to be released - and going to extreme lengths to be ready for its launch.

GTA 6 will be released at midnight on Wednesday - and Victoria Evans, from West Sussex, is not leaving anything to chance.

She has her alarm set for 0500, and has a day off booked. She says she put the game's release on her leave request form which was approved, she told BBC News, despite the fact her boss "doesn't know what GTA 6 is".

She's far from the only one. For the game's launch day, HR software company BrightHR looked at absence data from more than 1.2 million employees from 70,000 businesses across the UK.

It found GTA was mentioned in 4.6% of time-off requests by employees. Throughout November and December, it said an estimated 83,000 days had been booked off for the game.

And booking leave is only one of the ways fans are making sure for the big day. Others are buying a new console to play it on or even pretending they're halfway around the world to get early access.

Big demand

Market intelligence firm Sensor Tower estimates GTA 6 has already generated $1.18bn (£894m) from 12 million pre-orders - although Rockstar has not confirmed this.

Despite the option to preload the 212GB game, Jennifer Holmes, chief executive of the London Internet Exchange, said several UK internet providers including BT and Virgin Media had "increased capacity in anticipation of higher demand" ahead of launch.

Gamers have long been known to book time off work for major releases.

When Red Dead Redemption 2 launched in October 2018, social media users were sharing plans to take the day off, with one analytics firm reportedly finding more people talking about calling in sick for it than any other game that year.

Similar conversations took place ahead of Cyberpunk 2077's release in December 2020, with fans discussing taking several days off to play.

Some places have decided to lean into the trend for GTA 6 by offering incentives around the game - including the US Army's 3rd Infantry Division based at Fort Stewart, Georgia.

It gave some active-duty soldiers a four-day pass to play the game when it is released in November, as long as they sign a reenlistment contract for a minimum of two years between 1 August and 12 November.

"The idea was to have a unique incentives programme that connects to what soldiers are interested in," public affairs officer for the division, Lieutenant Colonel Angel Tomko confirmed to the BBC in August.

"There are 130 soldiers eligible within the battalion, and 20 have selected this incentive as part of their reenlistment," she said at the time.

Allow Instagram content?

‘accept and continue’.

Moving to New Zealand

Aside from taking time off, some gamers have also been discussing a technical loophole which could give them valuable extra hours of play before it officially unlocks in their country.

Because GTA 6 will release at midnight local time in all regions, New Zealand will become one of the first places where it is available, due to it reaching midnight earliest because of its position near the international date line.

This has led to some investigating ways to "trick" their consoles into thinking they're based in the island country when they are in fact thousands of miles away.

According to Google Trends, searches for the "GTA 6 New Zealand trick" have surged by more than 5,000% in the UK over the past month.

Games journalist Vic Hood said many gamers would be looking to play earlier to "get in on the action as soon as possible", as well as to prevent spoilers.

"As New Zealand is 13 hours ahead of the UK, that's 13 hours of gameplay that has time to spread across the internet and potentially spoil some key story beats and in-game surprises," she said.

"Took an extra day of paid time off when I found this out," one fan posted on Reddit on the trick.

It also means gamers would be playing the game at the much nicer time of 11:00 GMT, rather than having to stay up all night.

But another Xbox user shared caution on Reddit, noting that while the loophole had been exploited for many years for other game releases, GTA 6 "might be the game where Microsoft finally does something about this 'exploit'" - which could include banning players.

GTA 6's developers Rockstar and publishers Take Two Interactive have not commented on the loophole, and neither have Sony nor Microsoft.

Louise Wooldridge from Ampere Analysis said both Microsoft and Sony had "rules governing regional accounts and purchases" for the Xbox and PlayStation, adding that Sony's were "slightly more restrictive".

Players who choose to use the workaround could therefore risk breaching those terms and conditions and potentially face restrictions on their accounts or lose access to their digital games.

Some gamers will have to wait even longer than their console-playing counterparts to get their hands on GTA 6, as the game will not be available on PC at launch, similar to previous GTA releases.

"Spare a thought for the PC users who will have to live vicariously through others' YouTube videos and Twitch streams," gamer Stephen Finn told the BBC.

A PS5 now costs from £520, while the more powerful PS5 Pro is nearly £790.

Despite the hefty price tag, for some the temptation to join the community in playing what many have called the biggest game launch of the year, if not decade, has been too great.

Reddit posts and videos, such as one by US YouTuber isoish, show fans buying consoles specifically to play the game.

"So, the only game I'm going to have on here is GTA," the content creator said in the video.

"The whole PS5 is for GTA 6."

After more than a decade of waiting, it seems some fans are determined not to waste a single minute of GTA 6's release - no matter the cost or extra effort.

Sign up for our Tech Decoded newsletter to follow the world's top tech stories and trends. Outside the UK? Sign up here.

item.title: Nigerians among 12 suspects arrested in $4.5m Canada luxury car theft syndicate
item.description: Canadian authorities say they have recovered 96 luxury vehicles destined for West Africa.
item.content:encoded:
Canadian police have arrested 12 suspects, including eight Nigerians, in an investigation into an alleged car theft syndicate.

They are accused of stealing luxury vehicles and shipping them to West Africa.

Police in Peel, Ontario said they had recovered 96 high-value vehicles concealed in shipping containers. The vehicles, valued at $4.5m (£3.4m) were destined for export via Canadian ports.

The trafficking of vehicles from North America and Europe to African countries has been a long-standing concern for law enforcement agencies.

The suspects face 231 charges, with arrest warrants issued for others. Police say some of the accused may face deportation after their criminal proceedings are concluded.

The arrests followed months of what police described as an "extensive auto theft investigation".

The investigations began in March in partnership with Canada's border agency after police identified a warehouse allegedly being used to store stolen vehicles.

Investigators believe the network was led by five people who coordinated the theft, transportation and export of the stolen vehicles, with the others playing supporting roles.

"Together, investigators linked the network to loading sites, container movements and the transportation of stolen re-VINed vehicles," the police said in a statement.

Re-VINing is the illegal practice of altering the Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) to conceal its identity and make it harder to trace.

Canadian authorities have described organised vehicle theft as a growing threat, saying it was linked to wider criminal networks.

"Organised auto theft is a predatory business model run by transnational syndicates that terrorise families and fund broader criminal enterprises," Peel Regional Police Deputy Chief Nick Milinovich said.

Last year, Interpol said more than 100 luxury vehicles stolen from Canada and European countries had been recovered, exposing a network involved in trafficking stolen cars to West Africa.

In a separate operation the same year, Ghanaian security authorities recovered 43 luxury vehicles stolen from Europe and North America.

They attributed the success of the operation to improved cooperation between national and international law enforcement agencies.

item.title: Woman who accuses Russell Brand of rape says prison message 'upsetting'
item.description: Mia Latter spoke to the BBC after the jailed comedian claimed he was innocent of offences against four other women, in comments on a podcast following his convction.
item.content:encoded:
A woman who has made allegations against Russell Brand has said she finds it "upsetting" and "really shocking" that he was able to claim he was innocent from prison, following his conviction for rape and sexual assault.

Speaking after the comedian's wife Laura read out a message from him on their Sunday Service show on YouTube, Mia Latter told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she found it "appalling" to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".

"I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she said.

Latter, 37, who has alleged she was raped by Brand when she was 16, was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and he denies her claims.

Brand is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being found guilty at Southwark Crown Court of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, involving four women.

In recent years he has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following, including in the US. In the message read out by his wife on their show, Brand said: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

Latter said the broadcast "was really shocking to me... it was appalling, frankly, it was upsetting to watch".

She said the woman who gave evidence in the trial "got their verdict, and for him to say, 'I'm innocent, I'm not guilty' - well, you are, you're a convicted rapist now. There's no arguing with that".

Downing Street said on Monday it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said that "prisoners are rightly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims".

Latter said she was 16 when she met Brand, who was 30 at the time.

She was one of six women who made allegations against him as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation in 2023. None of the women were involved in his recent trial.

In an interview with the Sunday Times this week, Latter said Brand told her to keep their relationship secret from her school friends and claimed that he referred to her as "the child" in front of his entourage.

She has waived her right to anonymity in order to campaign for a staggered age of consent to be introduced in the UK that would make sexual relationships between 16 and 17 year-olds and adults illegal.

Latter told the Sunday Times the Crown Prosecution Service decided not to include her as part of Brand's criminal trial but police wanted her to be part of "subsequent" proceedings. She told the paper that she would not continue with the criminal process so she could focus on her campaign.

Latter told Today a staggered age of consent could have stopped her relationship with Brand "dead in its tracks".

She said: "It would have 100% made a difference because my parents tried to stop the relationship.

"They tried to prevent me from seeing him... But if it had been a criminal offence for him to be having a relationship with me, none of the subsequent abuse would have ever happened because they would have been able to stop the relationship dead in its tracks."

Latter also told Today that she and the complainants in Brand's trial had been accused of being "money hungry".

She said she had initially been reluctant to speak out because "I knew that the audience that he'd cultivated over the past few years would come for me".

"It's a criminal trial, there's no money.

"Me talking to the Times, me talking to you, me doing any interviews, there's no money, there's not a penny. We're just doing this in the pursuit of justice."

But Latter said Brand had been "monetising all these platforms" during his trial by continuing to make videos that appeared with advertisements on social media.

item.title: Gujarat riots gang-rape survivor 'heartbroken' after bail for two convicts
item.description: Bilkis Bano has spoken of her "pain, shock and disbelief" at the top court order and vowed to fight back.
item.content:encoded:
The article has details that some readers may find disturbing

A pregnant Muslim woman who was gang-raped and saw 14 family members murdered during the 2002 Gujarat riots has spoken of her "pain, shock and disbelief" after two of her rapists were recently granted bail.

Bilkis Bano said in a statement that she heard about the top court order through press reports and vowed to fight back.

The freed men are from a group of 11 convicts - part of a Hindu mob - serving life terms for the attack on Bano.

All the men were also freed in 2022 after a Gujarat government order. That decision, and the celebrations as they left prison, caused global outrage. In 2024, the Supreme Court overturned the order.

In a short three-page order dated 28 October, the Supreme Court granted bail to Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya and suspended their sentences while their petition challenging a 2017 Bombay High Court order is being heard.

The judges explained that the early release was because the two convicts "have been under incarceration for a period of more than 17 years" and "that one of the appellants has a severe handicap".

On Tuesday, Bano's lawyer Shobha Gupta told the BBC that the news of Joshi and Modhiya's release had left "Bilkis heartbroken".

"She has to restart her battle for justice. She had no information that this case was coming up in the Supreme Court. What is troubling for us is that every time something like this happens, we worry that it could affect her faith in judiciary."

Gupta said it was difficult to understand why the convicts were being released because "it's not a routine criminal case, it's a case that shocks the conscience of the world, of entire humanity".

The attack on Bano and her family was one of the most horrific crimes during the Gujarat riots, which began after 60 Hindu pilgrims were killed in a fire on a passenger train in the town of Godhra.

Hindu mobs attacked Muslim neighbourhoods, blaming them for starting the fire. The riots continued for three days and more than 1,000 people died, most of them Muslims.

When rioters attacked Bano's village and started setting Muslim homes on fire, she and 16 relatives went on the run. She was 19, had a three-year-old daughter and was pregnant with her second child.

They were attacked on the morning of 3 March 2002 by a group of men "with swords and sticks", she'd told me in 2017. Her three-year-old daughter, she said, was snatched from her lap and killed.

Her attackers were her neighbours, men she had seen almost daily while growing up. They tore off her clothes and several of them raped her, ignoring her pleas for mercy.

Her cousin, who had given birth two days earlier, was raped and murdered and her newborn baby was killed too.

Bano survived only because she lost consciousness and her attackers left, believing she was dead. Two boys - seven and four - were the only other survivors of the massacre.

Her fight for justice has been long and nightmarish. The first arrests were made only in 2004 after the Supreme Court called in federal investigators and transferred her case to Mumbai, saying that courts in Gujarat could not deliver justice to her.

In her statement released on Monday night, Bano spoke of "fresh tears of pain, shock and disbelief".

"I still cannot believe that once again, for the second time, an order has been passed by the Supreme Court without calling me up and without hearing me," she said.

"For 24 long years, I have stood up to fight for justice... again and again. Yet today, I find myself losing the very justice I had fought so hard to win.... And I am scared of losing faith in justice, yet again."

Bano vowed to "fight this order... for my children, who do not deserve to live haunted by fears and scars for the rest of their lives".

"I do this for my three-year-old Saleha who deserved to live and whose memory demands justice. I do this for women everywhere. Because no woman, no survivor, no citizen should have to endure this eternal test of belonging and equality, and fight for justice for the rest of her life."

Prime Minister Narendra Modi was Gujarat chief minister at the time of the riots, and was criticised for not doing enough to prevent the carnage. He has always denied wrongdoing and has not apologised for the riots.

In 2013, a Supreme Court panel also said that there was insufficient evidence to prosecute him. But critics have continued to blame him for the riots happening on his watch.

item.title: Putin's Crimea bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
item.description: Ukraine says the attack took weeks to plan, while the Kremlin vows to rebuild the strategic bridge.
item.content:encoded:
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.

Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge - also known as the Kerch Bridge - has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Russia's war effort.

A Kremlin spokesperson insisted the bridge would be rebuilt "better than before".

Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges, both important crossings over the Dnipro River, were closed after Russia targeted the Ukrainian capital overnight.

Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.

The damage reported on Tuesday appeared to be far more severe than previously, with a large arched section of the bridge apparently destroyed.

Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.

Zelensky said the overnight strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".

He said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and a Russian-backed official said some rail services were operating.

The bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2018.

While Ukraine has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Putin.

The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.

Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".

For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.

Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.

Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water.

Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services were damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.

Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.

Strikes on the busy Northern and Southern Bridges will cause major disruption to people's daily lives.

Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkasy region, according to local officials.

The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.

The collapse of the arched section of the Crimean Bridge has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.

However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.

This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.

There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.

Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.

In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel.

This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdiansk.

Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

item.title: China is hosting the world's leaders in its AI wonderland. Here's what they won't see
item.description: Drive away from Shenzhen's tech-flecked skyline and you will run into the challenges confronting Xi's China.
item.content:encoded:
At 27, Huang Shihua is living the Chinese Dream.

He works as an engineer for a leading humanoid robot company in Shenzhen. The sprawling south-eastern metropolis is touted by China as the origin story for a high-tech future powered by artificial intelligence, robotics and home-grown innovation.

Drones soar across the sky to deliver your dinner, driverless taxis play relaxing music as you journey to your destination, and robots don't just hand you a cappuccino - they explain the origin of your coffee beans.

"We have created a miracle in Shenzhen," Huang says, surrounded by humanoid robots making coffee and playing chess. "Many young people from across China, full of passion and dreams, have flocked here."

Now they all spend their days figuring out ways to make robots smarter.

The Chinese call Shenzhen the "city of dreams". The moniker suits it: one of China's wealthiest, it is close to Hong Kong and the place where the country's explosive growth took off decades ago.

Its manufacturing inventory mirrors China's rise: cabbage patch dolls, then TVs, later iPhones, electric vehicles, drones and now the robots, which are drawing Huang and a new generation of Chinese ambition.

The "miracles" these young engineers are chasing are central to Xi Jinping's bold vision for China. So where better to show it off than Shenzhen, which will be centre-stage when US President Donald Trump, Russian leader Vladimir Putin and others arrive for a global economic summit this week.

And yet there is another side to this flashy, coastal city, a side that they will not get to see. Drive away from towering skyscrapers towards Shajing and Songgang, once the source of much of the world's electronics, and you will run into the challenges confronting Xi's China.

"Everyone feels life is hard," one construction worker tells us. "Lots of factories have relocated and workers lost their jobs."

China remains exceptionally good at making things - and Shenzhen is proof of that. But the city also holds the evidence for what ails the world's second-largest economy. The property crisis is not over, denting confidence in the future. This is one of China's most expensive cities but even here, our taxi driver tells us, his house is now only worth a third of its original price.

A weak property market and sluggish consumer spending mean many households are buying less. Factories are increasingly relying on exports while many manufacturers have cut production, downsized, automated or moved elsewhere in search of cheaper labour.

The result is a growing number of workers turning to temporary jobs in the gig economy, often with lower pay and fewer benefits.

"Shenzhen is not a magic place," says one delivery driver in his 40s, unwilling to give his name.

"Some say there is gold everywhere in Shenzhen, but it's not like that anymore. It's not a city where you can come and thrive. If you don't work hard, you won't have anything."

The BBC spent several days in Shenzhen exploring these two very different sides of China's progress: on the one hand is the dazzling promise of AI, and on the other are the anxieties of workers who worry if there will be room for them in the future it creates.

Wednesday is sandwich and bubble tea day in the offices of DexForce Technologies.

The elevator is packed with young engineers and developers headed to the right floor for the free carbs and sugar that will fuel their afternoon. They jostle past their creations en route: human-sized, yellow robots whose limbs fill every available corner.

"I believe that in a decade, robots will be able to better serve humanity by taking on highly repetitive or even dangerous tasks," Huang says. That could be anything from serving coffee to working in mines, and they are being trained for all of that in this laboratory for the future, where machines flail, jerk or lurch into motion as they learn to behave.

To him, "Shenzhen is another 'America'. Because, much like in the US, many young people have been able to realise their dreams and earn the wealth they desire."

This is what Xi wants to hear as he pushes China to lead the world in advanced tech. Shenzhen has indeed long been a place for seeking opportunity but Huang and his colleagues want to do much more. They don't simply want to continue China's manfuacturing supremacy. They want to transform it.

Beyond making "our lives more convenient and comfortable", Huang sees AI as helping "the entire world become one family - a global village. AI has the potential to foster equality and the prospect of AI-driven equality is, to me, the most exciting possibility of all."

Smiling enthusiastically, he explains how he hopes that robots can help emerging economies across Africa and South East Asia catch up by reshaping their production lines too.

This tech-charged optimism, which is everywhere in the building, jars with the uncertainty elsewhere in Shenzhen, where robots are nowhere to be found. Yet. But that's just the first of the differences.

In Huang's side of the city, tech and finance workers stroll to the office after a morning workout, sipping coffee that probably cost more than 30 yuan ($4.50; £3.40).

On the other side, scooters whizz through streets piled high with goods being shuttled between factories as vendors sell whole breakfast plates of spicy noodles for under 3 yuan.

Outside one of the city's tallest skyscrapers, 50-year-old Ms Lu has a phone to her ear and a pen in her right hand while grabbing a bag with her left from a delivery driver.

She shouts four key numbers at her co-worker: instructions for another Chinese woman who is waiting to take the delivery up the elevator to someone sitting at their desk.

This is the lunchtime rush outside SEG plaza, home to 70 storeys of thousands of tenants. Lu used to be one of them. "I ran a small business on the second floor. I sold circuit boards," she says. "But it's getting so hard to do business these days and the rental fees got higher."

Often likened to China's Silicon Valley, Shenzhen has seen rents soar with the influx of new capital, squeezing out smaller, more traditional businesses. At 50, Ms Lu couldn't find another job until the delivery drivers came to her with a plan.

The wait for the elevator can take half an hour – wasted money for a driver trying to fill as many orders as possible. So Ms Lu became a new layer in the ever-evolving gig economy.

"The delivery drivers bring food here to the building entrance. We pick it up and take it upstairs. The drivers pay us 2 yuan per order," she explains, always on the move. Delivery drivers earn between four to eight yuan per order, so Ms Lu gets a decent cut of their earnings.

"The lunch peak time only lasts two or three hours… if they use our service, they can get more orders done, and we can earn some money as well. But the market is bad. These days I only earn around 200 yuan per day."

An estimated 200 million Chinese workers, roughly 40% of the urban labour force, now depend on some form of gig work. Many delivery drivers in Shenzhen tell us they chose temporary work because there are fewer opportunities at factories than before.

"We need to adapt to the situation we find ourselves in," one driver told us, "rather than waiting for it to adapt to our needs." A group of them are waiting outside the gates of an e-cigarette factory to make industrial deliveries.

Others nod in agreement. Another driver says he has little choice: "I have two children to raise and I can't stop working. I don't have time to think about anything else."

Permanent jobs often require contributions to social security and pension, which reduces take-home pay. But gig work means more cash in hand and flexibile hours.

"Most workers prefer jobs with a fixed, shorter-term duration. It allows them the flexibility to resign and leave whenever they choose; they have no desire to become permanent employees," says job agent Li Xiaohe.

Increasingly, he puts up boards on pavements advertising temporary factory jobs that pay around 22 yuan an hour for assembling small electronics.

Although agents also appear to be in a shrinking pool, with several former shop fronts shuttered: yet another sign of the downturn in traditional manufacturing.

"Our business is perhaps not as optimistic as it once was," Li admits. "We can feel the effects of Shenzhen going through a transformation."

That transformation is hard to miss.

Drones buzz above the lush grounds of a purpose built "talent park" along the city's waterfront, dipping and darting as they deliver meals to a dedicated platform. Phones held high, tourists capture them landing with their lunch.

"This is amazing. The technology is just great. I wish we had this back at home," exclaims one Canadian tourist. Our coffee order - for a five-yuan delivery - arrives in just over 15 minutes, the drone landing seamlessly so I can pick up my order.

"I heard that many years ago, Shenzhen was a fishing village," says Anle, who is visiting from Vietnam. "Ha – no more fishing village," he laughs as he orders milk tea to be delivered by drone for him and his wife.

For all the ingenuity on display, it feels more like a demonstration of what is possible rather than a mundane reality. The deliveries, which are only possible in certain locations, stop at 20:00 local time. The driverless cars, which need a separate app to order, are also a novelty – they even offer you a massage when you are on your way.

At night, in the glow of a thousand dancing lights, the drones take on a different role. They fly above the park warning people to behave and not cause trouble.

Far from the glittering skyline, workers gather around plastic tables outside restaurants serving cheap hotpot and seafood skewers.

There are more expensive restaurants along the street, but they too have taken a hit. One owner told us business is down by more than 70% as workers are hesitant to splurge on dinner.

Many of them have spent decades here, including 58-year-old construction worker Mr Wu. He arrived in Shenzhen from Sichuan in the 1990s not long after China opened the city up to foreign businesses.

He was among millions of migrants from poorer provinces who came to work on production lines or build skyscrapers. They are still coming.

All the people we spoke to came from elsewhere. They often labour up to 14 hours a day and live in shared dormitories, sustained by the prospect of stable work and decent pay to send home to their families.

For these workers, the Covid pandemic, when Chinese manufacturing hit a record low, appears to have been the first turning point.

"After Covid, our salary dropped by at least a third," Mr Wu recalls, after which wages never fully recovered.

"I will continue to work," he adds. "As long as you keep working, you will have an income. More salary or not? It doesn't matter. As long as you keep working, you will have an income. If the economy slows down, we all slow down. If it grows, we all get better."

For all these decades, Shenzhen lived up to its bargain: work hard and your life would improve.

But now, in a city that is being redefined by automation and AI, that old promise feels less secure.

item.title: Imran Khan seeks urgent medical care fearing he 'may not return alive'
item.description: Pakistan's ex-prime minister, who has been in prison since August 2023, says he has been denied justice.
item.content:encoded:
Pakistan's jailed former PM Imran Khan has appealed for urgent medical treatment, saying that his and his wife's health has been deteriorating.

"At 74, this unrelenting state is taking me to a place from which I may not return alive," the cricket star-turned-politician wrote in a letter published by his lawyer Salman Safdar.

Authorities in Islamabad maintain that Khan gets seen weekly by doctors, who have assessed that he is of "satisfactory" health.

Khan, who faces more than 100 charges, has been in prison since August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year. Khan argues the cases against them, ranging from corruption to selling state gifts, are politically motivated.

Concerns over Khan's health have grown louder in the past year, with his family claiming he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.

In his letter, Khan wrote that doctors have told him he is "highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest", and that his heart has already "suffered damage".

He also expressed concern for Bushra Bibi, whom he says suffered a detached retina in April and underwent surgery in secrecy. Khan said he fears she may lose her sight without further surgery.

"I have fought impossible legal battles in countless cases, and I have not stopped. But the system has stopped giving me justice," he wrote.

He said that he is being held in solitary confinement for up to 22 hours a day, where he is allowed neither visits by his family nor access to books and television, and that this has "taken a heavy toll" on his mental health.

He also claimed he had only seen his lawyers four times over the past year.

"I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," he wrote.

Pakistan's parliamentary affairs minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry disputed these claims, saying Khan is "provided with all facilities in prison, including food of his own choosing".

"[He] is currently the most well-accommodated prisoner in Pakistan," the minister told reporters.

Authorities also say Khan was taken to a government-run hospital for an eye injection a week ago, where doctors deemed him "clinically stable".

Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.

His arrest in May 2023 sparked large-scale, violent protests by supporters, who ransacked the corps commander's residence in Lahore, smashing chandeliers and making away with furniture, paintings, and even peacocks, among other things.

At least eight people died in the protests and the army were called in to quell the violence.

Even behind bars, Khan remains a force in Pakistani politics.

Thousands of his supporters took to the streets in early October in a dayslong march, demanding his release. Authorities later ordered a crackdown on protests and imposed a state of emergency in Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Former international cricket captains have made several appeals in recent months to Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, insisting that Khan be given proper medical care.

item.title: Robert Pattinson to replace Daniel Craig as James Bond
item.description: The 40-year old is best known for his role in films including Twilight, The Batman and The Odyssey.
item.content:encoded:
Robert Pattinson, the British actor known for films such as Twilight and The Batman, has been confirmed as the next actor to play James Bond.

The announcement was made by Amazon MGM Studios in a social media post on Monday, with a picture showing Pattinson in character as 007.

The 40-year-old becomes the seventh actor to play the famous fictional spy and will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.

In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."

The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve and written by Steven Knight, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.

In his statement, Pattinson said he was "deeply grateful" to the film's creative team "for their belief in me".

"To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement," he added. "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Daniel Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.

The next 007 film will be the first since long-term Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson stepped back and Amazon took creative control of the franchise, after acquiring the series' parent company MGM.

By the time the 26th Bond film is released, it will have been seven years since the last - 2021's No Time To Die - the biggest gap in the franchise's history.

Director Villeneuve is best known for films including the Dune trilogy, Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival and Blade Runner 2049, while writer Knight is known for TV hits Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer and Locke.

Pattinson has already worked with Villeneuve on Dune: Part 3, where he stars as a new villain, Scytale. The film is released next month.

In a statement reacting to Pattinson's Bond casting, Villeneuve said: "Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey.

"We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond.

"He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."

Pattinson's casting was also welcomed by Buckingham Palace, with a post on Instagram sharing the news and adding: "Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond."

Australian actor George Lazenby, who played James Bond in the 1969 film On Her Majesty's Secret, posted a video on social media welcoming Pattinson to "the most exclusive club in the world".

"Remember to enjoy yourself... Let's see if you'll have 'this never happened to the other fella' moment," Lazenby said.

"All the best mate."

Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.

But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.

Producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman said the "legacy of James Bond is in great hands with Robert Pattinson".

"His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times."

At 40, Pattinson is one of the older actors who was thought to have auditioned for the role of Bond.

Reports last week suggested Pattinson's deal committed him to playing 007 for three films, rather than the four that had reportedly been discussed with some of the other actors, but that has not been officially confirmed.

Robert Pattinson shot to fame as Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire,

He went on to play vampire Edward Cullen in Twilight, the hugely popular film series based on Stephenie Meyer's best-selling novels.

Pattinson starred opposite Kristen Stewart in five Twilight films in total, which collectively made more than $3bn (£2.2bn) at the box office worldwide.

He has gone on to star in other major films such as 2022's The Batman and Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, released earlier this year.

But he is also respected within the industry for how many roles he has taken in smaller movies - often independent, experimental or arthouse films.

His other credits include The Lighthouse, Mickey 17, Life, The Drama, Good Time, The Rover, Bel Ami, Primetime, Tenet and The Lost City of Z.

Pattinson follows in the footsteps of only six actors to have played James Bond in the official film series – Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig.

Craig appeared in five Bond movies in total, starting with 2006's Casino Royale, and spent 16 years as the secret agent created by author Ian Fleming.

In a statement, Fleming's estate said they were "delighted to welcome Robert Pattinson to the James Bond family".

The next film will mark a new era for the franchise. Amazon purchased MGM for $8.5bn in 2021, which included the rights to distribute James Bond.

Then in 2025, long-time Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson agreed to sell creative control of the franchise to Amazon MGM.

Before that, the franchise had been under the Broccoli family's control since 1962's Dr. No, when Sean Connery first starred as Bond.

The Broccoli family preserved the integrity of the character and brand for decades, resisting spin-offs and licensing that some industry experts now expect to see following Amazon's takeover.

item.title: Trump says Alaska voters chose the wrong Dan Sullivan. What does the data show?
item.description: Votes are still being counted in the Alaska Senate race, with Democrat Mary Peltola ahead of Republican incumbent Senator Dan S Sullivan.
item.content:encoded:
Almost two weeks after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterm elections, votes are still being counted in the race to elect a senator in Alaska, with Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ahead of her Republican rival - Senator Dan S Sullivan.

This Senate contest has drawn scrutiny after another Dan Sullivan entered the race earlier this year - with ballot papers listing both the incumbent Dan S Sullivan and a Daniel J Sullivan Jr.

Republicans have said this could have confused voters, prompting an unsuccessful legal challenge and President Donald Trump claiming votes for "the fake Dan Sullivan" were supposed to be for "the real Dan Sullivan".

US media has not forecasted a winner in the race - the last Senate seat still without a winner after the 3 November election.

But with 97% of the vote counted, even if Senator Dan S Sullivan's votes were combined with Daniel J Sullivan Jr's votes, this would still not overcome Peltola's lead.

Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, which means voters can vote for five candidates in order of preference. If no candidate reaches more than 50% of the first preference votes, then voters' other choices will be used to decide who wins.

BBC Verify has analysed voting data showing voters' second choices. It shows that over a third of voters who put Daniel J Sullivan Jr first left their second choice blank.
