item.title: Prince Harry praises war veterans on surprise visit to Ukraine
item.description: He has been showing support for injured veterans in Ukraine and praising the country's resilience.
item.content:encoded:
The Duke of Sussex has received an enthusiastic welcome in a surprise visit to Ukraine to support injured war veterans, meeting Ukrainian competitors taking part in his Invictus Games.

There were emotional scenes as he was applauded by injured service men and women in Lviv, where he told his audience: "You're going to win the war."

Prince Harry spent two days at events for veterans, with a press blackout for security reasons until he had left Ukraine, as the country continues to face missile attacks from Russia.

Ukraine has more than 150,000 injured war veterans and the prince visited projects supporting their treatment and rehabilitation.

"Ukraine now is experiencing elements of war that no other country has experienced before," he said - with technology advancing in areas such as drone warfare, but also in protecting cities and providing treatment.

A mobile phone app is where Ukrainians look for air raid warnings, telling them the direction, timing and type of any incoming missiles.

At the Superhumans Center near Lviv, Harry was shown how growing numbers of injured veterans receive groundbreaking treatment.

International experts used to come to help Ukraine, he said, but "now that has flipped," with Ukraine having the greater expertise with trauma injuries to share with others.

That included an innovation for Mykhailo Damaskin, a Ukrainian air assault forces veteran, who was so seriously injured in fighting in Kherson he was never expected to walk again.

In an experimental treatment he had a spinal cord stimulator implanted in his back, which allows him to walk, but has to be re-charged every 12 hours. He cannot feel his feet and controls his steps using his eyes.

He needs to be plugged in and charged up to be able to move - and jokes that he is "like a demo model of a Tesla".

"My goal is to go to the Invictus Games. I promised my father before he was killed that I'd be part of the team to represent Ukraine internationally.

"I'll prove to every guy with spinal cord injuries that life goes on after injury," said Mykhailo.

At the Superhumans Center Prince Harry sat at the bedside of Konstiantyn Vlasenko, who was airlifted from the front line by a drone last month in a rescue that was a first of its kind.

He had been alone for more than 200 days and had stayed at his position, despite losing both his feet.

In a moving encounter, Prince Harry told him he represented the spirit of resilience of Ukraine.

And he described the injured veterans as "role models", promising his audience: "The rest of the world will continue to support you."

Along with all the determination, it was an inescapably poignant sight too, with so many families and children at the medical facility visiting the growing numbers of badly injured war casualties.

At a noisy sports centre, Prince Harry arrived to watch a wheelchair rugby match taking place, with some thunderous collisions between the players.

He was welcomed by the competitors in what he has called his Invictus "family" and soon the visit turned into something approaching a group hug, with Harry disappearing into a sea of selfies and handshakes.

He was presented with a T-shirt remembering prisoners of war held by Russian forces.

And he later had a chance to play one of the events at the Invictus Games, a tennis-style competition called pickleball.

Watching was Ivan Voinov, who has lost a leg and suffered head injuries, but who is using sport to help his rehabilitation - including learning to dance again.

He said that dancing was his way to be together with his wife again, which meant so much to his recovery and recovering his identity.

At an Invictus awards ceremony during the visit, Prince Harry was greeted with choruses of "Harry, Harry, Harry", getting a rock star welcome.

"Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth, I feel encouragement," he said, having returned for a fourth trip here during wartime.

He promised that "when the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games".

There have been 400 wounded service men and women in Ukraine taking part in trials for next year's games, being hosted in Birmingham.

The sports events are an attempt to encourage rehabilitation and to recognise the resilience of people overcoming their challenges.

Prince Harry told a gathering of new Invictus members of a "cultural shift" from people being socially awkward about seeing injured veterans to wanting to show respect.

"These people have so much to offer," he said.

"Recovery cannot wait for the war to end, The scale of need in Ukraine is huge, and wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans need the chance to rebuild their lives now," said Rob Owen, chief executive officer of the Invictus Games Foundation.

item.title: Steering failure preceded New Orleans cruise ship collision, says NTSB
item.description: Preliminary findings by National Transportation Safety Board investigators suggest the tanker suffered a "steering casualty" before colliding with the cruise ship on Friday.
item.content:encoded:
The tanker that struck a cruise ship docked in New Orleans on Friday had a steering failure, officials said, citing preliminary findings into the collision.

It remains unclear what caused the "steering casualty" on the Atlantic Asphalt cargo vessel, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said in a media briefing on Sunday.

The collision left 32 people from the stricken American Heritage riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one was unaccounted for.

The NTSB said there are many different things that could be classified as a steering casualty, and they are "looking at all of them".

The tanker was upbound on the Mississippi River as it moved toward the east bank of the river just before the collision, said the NTSB, based on findings from the vessel's voyage data recorder.

Minutes before the crash, investigators said audio consistent with the ship's warning system was broadcast, along with commands to deploy the vessel's anchors and emergency ship handling orders.

"We are aware that there was an issue with the steering on board and causing the rudder to remain at a starboard position, causing the heading of the vessel to veer towards the east bank," investigator-in-charge Bart Barnum said during the news conference.

The exact issue with the steering has yet to be determined, he added.

A preliminary report from the NTSB is expected in 30 days.

Calls about the collision began around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday, when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans chief Melanie Montroll said after the incident.

There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the port authority.

Passengers began getting off the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping onto its side.

Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help while officials shut down traffic in the Mississippi River during the rescue effort.

The American Heritage had been finishing an eight-day cruise calling at destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi along the waterway.

item.title: Brand moved from Wandsworth to category C prison, his wife confirms on podcast
item.description: The convicted rapist has been moved to HMP Littlehey, which houses sex offenders.
item.content:encoded:
Russell Brand has been transferred to a category C prison, his wife Laura has confirmed, in her first public comments since he was jailed.

On Monday, the comedian was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Over the weekend, Brand was transferred from category B HMP Wandsworth in London to HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, which houses men convicted of sexual offences.

Laura Brand returned to the couple's podcast on Sunday, saying that she had spoken to her husband in prison and he "is OK and is praying". Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following among believers, including in the US.

HMP Littlehey, a category C training prison, is one of the largest prisons in Europe for men convicted of sexual offences.

It held more than 1,200 prisoners as of January 2025, according to data from the Independent Monitoring Board.

Before Brand's move to the prison, a source close to the disgraced comedian said he was doing "remarkably well considering the circumstances" at HMP Wandsworth and that he had been moved from isolation to a main wing.

A member of staff at Wandsworth said there had been "much excitement" among the inmates about Brand's arrival, with some slamming on cell doors and shouting out his name. They added that there had also been some anger displayed about his crimes.

Staff at other prisons told the BBC Brand's fame, combined with the nature of his crimes, could make him a target for other inmates.

In the couple's podcast, released on Sunday, Laura Brand can seen sitting on a sofa in what looks like a conservatory. She is holding a Bible with a candle burning in front of her.

The couple had continued their YouTube podcast during Brand's trial. They often read snippets of the Bible and discussed religion.

On Sunday, Laura told their followers: "We trust his [God's] plan and everything he is doing just now, even though it's painful and obviously will take some getting used to."

During the show, Laura played an episode she said had been recorded before her husband was jailed.

It featured the couple singing to the American folk singer Woody Guthrie before praying together.

Towards the end of the podcast, Laura returned on her own to read a message from her husband, in which he said he was not guilty for the offences he had been jailed for.

He called staff at HMP Littlehey "strong", "kind" and "dedicated", and he asked people to support his "treasured wife and family".

Male prisons are organised into four categories ranging from A, the highest security, to D, the lowest security open prisons.

The HM Inspectorate of Prisons says Category C prisons, like HMP Littlehey, are for prisoners who "cannot be trusted in open conditions" but are not deemed as much of an escape risk.

According to the Ministry of Justice, most prisoners are housed in Category C prisons, which provide training to help them resettle into the community upon release.

item.title: Trident submarine returns home after record-breaking undersea patrol
item.description: Defence Secretary Wes Streeting was at HM Naval Base Clyde to welcome the crew after the longest deployment at sea for a British vessel.
item.content:encoded:
A Royal Navy submarine carrying Trident nuclear missiles has returned to its Scottish base after a record-breaking 217 days spent submerged on patrol.

The 140-strong crew of HMS Vengeance have spent the tour in almost total isolation beneath the surface after setting out from Faslane, near Helensburgh, Argyll and Bute, on 12 April.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting was at HM Naval Base Clyde to welcome them home after the longest deployment at sea for a British vessel.

The typical patrol length for the UK's Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines has more than doubled in recent years, with six-month durations now routine due to a shortage of seaworthy vessels.

Crew members could be seen standing on HMS Vengeance as it travelled up Gare Loch earlier, accompanied by some smaller Naval support vessels and tug boats.

The vessel was encrusted in marine growth and some of its sound-absorbing tiles were missing.

HMS Vengeance was expected back at Faslane last weekend, but that was reported to have been delayed when the submarine replacing it on patrol had to return to base to fix a technical fault.

The head of the navy, First Sea Lord Gen Sir Gwyn Jenkins, praised the dedication of submariners in keeping Nato safe at a conference last week in Oslo, but said the UK must do better at maintaining the fleet.

Streeting said it "doesn't sit lightly" with him that crews were being asked to serve longer than intended.

He said: "It makes me feel even more indebted to the crew for the service they've given to the country, for the commitment they show, the dedication, the professionalism, the expertise.

"I think the whole country can be extraordinarily proud of our submariners and of our nuclear deterrent."

Since 1969 the UK has always had at least one ballistic missile-armed submarine patrolling at sea in order to provide a "nuclear deterrent".

The logic is that if Britain was under nuclear attack, it could launch a retaliatory strike on the aggressor, a concept known as mutually-assured destruction.

The four 492ft (150m) long Vanguard-class submarines can carry up to 16 Trident missiles, each capable of delivering multiple warheads which are several times more powerful than the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima in 1945.

In order to avoid detection the submarines remain submerged and in radio silence throughout the patrol because a transmission could give away their position.

But they can ascend to shallower depths and receive encoded messages via a floating wire antenna or communications buoy.

Crews have little contact with the loved ones apart from the "Familygram" - a 120-word message that arrives weekly, and they are not permitted to reply.

Messages are vetted and bad news from home can be withheld if it might jeopardise the operational effectiveness of a crew member.

Depending on the sea state they may be able to listen to radio bulletins.

Most of the crew work in shifts of six hours on, six hours off and sleep in narrow bunks, sometimes nine to a cabin.

Submariners returning from long patrols are said to find the outside world smells strange or even overwhelming because they have become so used to filtered air.

Their distance perception could also be affected by living in such a confined space for so long and they are advised not to drive for a few days while they adjust.

The Vanguard-class boats were commissioned in the 1990s with an expected service life of 25 years but are now expected to serve for up to 40 years before the first Dreadnought-class submarines start replacing them in the early 2030s.

Streeting said that program was "on track" and that it was important to get those vessels out "as soon as possible".

Patrols used to typically last three months but in recent years this has stretched to six or more because at least one of the boats has been out of action for refit or repairs.

A major overhaul of HMS Vanguard at Devonport Dockyard in Plymouth dragged on for seven years before it returned to service in 2022.

HMS Victorious is currently in dry dock undergoing a £560m "deep maintenance" that began in 2023, leaving only Vengeance, Vigilant and Vanguard operational.

The previous record for a Royal Navy continuous undersea patrol is reported to have been set by Vanguard in April when it returned to Faslane after 205 days away.

The patrol lengths of Russian or Chinese submarines are not known, but most navies are believed to send their vessels out for far shorter durations.

item.title: Charlotte Church closes wellness retreat after five 'beautiful' years
item.description: Church previously said she blew "pretty much all my life savings" on the £1.5m home.
item.content:encoded:
Charlotte Church will close her wellness retreat after five "beautiful years", the company has announced.

The Dreaming, based in Rhydoldog House near Rhayader, Powys, offered retreats aimed at helping people reconnect with nature and spirituality.

The singer-songwriter bought the former home of fashion designer Laura Ashley in 2021, with its renovation later featuring in a Discovery Channel documentary series.

Last month, the team at the retreat announced it would be "pausing" operations to "reassess" what it should offer.

But it has now confirmed it is shutting down.

In a statement on social media, the team said they had hoped it would be a "period of hibernation, rather than an ending," but have come to realise it is the "end of our journey with The Dreaming".

"What a beautiful, wild and wonderful few years it has been," the post added.

According to documents filed to Companies House in March 2025, there were five employees at The Dreaming.

"We've shared stories, made friendships, held space for one another and found moments of stillness in a world that so rarely allows us to slow down.

"Thousands of you have found your way to this little corner of the Welsh hills, each bringing something of yourselves, and each leaving a little something behind. You have made The Dreaming what it is."

Last month the business said it was in the process of "germinating new dreams for the future" and was set to "hibernate".

Earlier this year, Church said that The Dreaming was a response to the pressures of contemporary life.

She said: "I am really passionate about what we do, because I believe more than ever the world and the people of the world are in dire need of being held through some very difficult times.

"There are some very difficult transitional times for us as human beings on this Earth.

"This is also due to the excesses in which society is so much based around, capitalist values and ideologies, meaning there is then less around care, people, community, nature and belonging. We are crying out for these things, every single one of us."

Church previously confessed she had blown "pretty much all my life savings" on the £1.5m, seven-bedroom property.

The house, with origins in the 15th Century, belonged to textile, fashion and retail entrepreneur Ashley and her husband Bernard and was owned by the family until his death in 2009.

A planning application for the retreat in 2021 said Church wanted to transform Rhydoldog House into a carbon neutral wellbeing and healing retreat with four log cabins in the grounds as tourist accommodation.

Since opening, The Dreaming hosted more than 3,000 guests and offered a "pay what you can" scheme starting at £1 per night, as well as free stays for NHS workers.

item.title: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history'
item.description: The Ukrainian president says restrictions are still in place and making it difficult to stop Russian attacks.
item.content:encoded:
A crucial US satellite internet service is still operating too slowly and affecting Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

"We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said.

The issue over the speed of the Starshield system - a military-grade Starlink service owned by Elon Musk and provided to Ukraine by the US government - has been rumbling on for weeks.

Zelensky said he had asked officials "to work as closely as possible" with the US government and Musk's company. "It is important to be on the right side of history," he said. The BBC has asked the White House and Starlink for comment.

Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of missiles and drones in Ukraine airspace.

The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.

Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back".

It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented.

The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.

Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher.

On Sunday Zelensky said Ukraine was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones targeting electricity substations because "restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there".

"Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161km/h (100mph) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds'," he posted, referring to the drones that follow an Iranian design.

On Friday Zelensky said speed limits of around 100mph had been enforced on the network since Monday, but only in Russian-occupied areas and not the whole of Ukraine.

"It already has political implications. If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporary occupied territories as not ours," the New York Times reported him as saying.

Ukraine has also been beset by a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors used to defend against Russian missiles - a situation that Russia has exploited to intensify strikes on Ukrainian targets.

Overnight and into Sunday morning Russia hit energy infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and the Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr, and Kirovohrad regions, Ukraine said.

It also struck railway infrastructure in the Dnipro, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions.

Scores of people are said to have been hurt in those attacks, as well as two in the Donetsk and Kyiv regions.

Two people were killed in an attack on an infrastructure facility in Chernihiv Region's Mena, governor Vyacheslav Chaus said.

Multiple strikes were also delivered on energy facilities across the region, he added on Telegram.

Ukraine meanwhile said it had carried out strikes on a petrochemical plant and an oil refinery in the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk.

"On the night of November 15, units of Ukraine's Defence Forces reached Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan," the military said on Telegram.

"Two enterprises that feed the Russian war with raw materials and fuel came under attack."

Other Ukrainian strikes killed one person in Taganrog, an industrial port city near the border, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said.

In the occupied Luhansk region a lorry driver and an elderly woman were also killed, Leonid Pasechnik, the regional leader installed by Moscow said.

Meanwhile Estonia has announced it will shut its border crossing points with Russia from 1 December following a suspected sabotage attack on a defence company.

Eight people were detained over an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.

The Estonian authorities say they had been ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence service to try and carry out the attack. Russia has not commented.

"Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.

item.title: Thousands of US flights still cancelled or delayed two days after grounding of planes nationwide
item.description: The US transport secretary says that normal air-traffic operations may not be restored until Monday.
item.content:encoded:
Thousands of US flights were cancelled or delayed on Sunday as the US air-traffic control system continued to recover from a technical failure that led to a rare national ground stop.

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said normal operations may not be restored until Monday.

"We have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time," he told the BBC's US partner CBS. More than 5,000 flights were delayed and 2,000 cancelled on Sunday.

President Donald Trump urged Congress on Sunday to approve more money to modernise the air-traffic control system. The grounding of all aircraft scheduled to depart the US on Friday caused chaos at airports across the country.

More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the FAA announced at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) that flights would be grounded until further notice. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.

In the aftermath, 8,500 flights were delayed and another 8,000 cancelled, according to FlightAware.

The stoppage left passengers stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to their gates. Others were stranded in airports, sleeping on the floor and desperately trying to get in touch with their airline. The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.

The ground stop was lifted after about four and a half hours, but the impacts continued over the weekend.

On Saturday, airlines cancelled more than 5,900 flights and more than 7,000 others were delayed.

Investigators are still working to determine the root cause and who is at fault, but Duffy said the administration decided to ground flights after failures in a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate.

The transport secretary said a computer router installed as part of an upgrade from copper wire to fibre started sending out faulty signals.

He said on Sunday that the router - a piece of equipment which directs traffic across the network - was installed in El Dorado, Arkansas, and "flooded our network".

Duffy said that issues will continue to arise until the US makes major modernising changes to its air control system. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said.

"Let's not lie to each other," he said on NBC's Meet The Press. "We have to make investments into a network that has been neglected for decades."

In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump urged US lawmakers to allocate the money, saying "we can get it built quickly and efficiently".

"It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS! We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs," he said.

Experts say the US uses antiquated technology for flight communications.

Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".

He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."

item.title: Judge blocks Trump closure of 'Trash Island' Washington DC golf course on Sunday
item.description: The temporary order is part of a months-long challenge to the US president's plans to upgrade East Potomac Golf Links into a championship course.
item.content:encoded:
A federal judge has temporarily blocked the US government's closure of an historic golf course and park in Washington DC.

US District Judge Ana Reyes has been overseeing a months-long challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links, which he said would be closed from 15 November for extensive renovations.

Reyes has said President Donald Trump cannot close the park nor its golf course, but added that his administration was not required to actively manage either.

Trump, an avid golfer, has said his plans to upgrade the 106-year-old course will create "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World". The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

Declaring the current course "Trash Island", he announced in October that it would be renovated over 15 months to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments" - despite the ongoing litigation.

Reyes said in a 30-page decision issued on Saturday that the Trump administration's justifications for the proposed course closures were pretextual and that the government had violated at least two federal laws "to meet an arbitrary deadline".

"The government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely," Reyes wrote.

She said the closure "runs counter to the public interest in utilising national parkland", adding that the government had not "plausibly identified any harm it would suffer from a temporary restraining order that preserves the status quo pending further proceedings".

Her order will last until 28 November.

A coalition of advocacy and legal groups opposing the closure and renovation said they are "grateful that the court has stopped the government from unlawfully closing East Potomac Park and depriving people of this priceless piece of American history and wonderful recreation space".

"Our laws prevent this administration from acting without a fair and public process, and today's order will stop the government from ignoring those laws," said the coalition, which represents the plaintiffs and includes Democracy Forward and the Democracy Defenders Fund. "We are eager to continue to argue this case in court."

The legal dispute dates back to February, when the DC Preservation League and others sued over redevelopment plans for the park.

The historic course, which sits two miles (3km) south of the White House, is one of three public courses run by the National Park Service (NPS) in the nation's capital.

The legal fight then escalated in October when the NPS began to cut down hundreds of trees without notifying Reyes until 15 hours before work was set to begin.

After the trees were cut, Reyes ordered the Trump administration to stop tree removal until at least 26 October and give her three business days' notice about making any other permanent changes.

Despite the work stoppage, Trump announced that the course would be closed for 15 months from 15 November to accommodate for the renovations. He also shared a rendering of the course redesign.

"The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous and disease-infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall," he said in a post on Truth Social.

Reyes has since separately opened an inquiry into whether justice department attorneys had "made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated ethical rules".

That included whether giving late notice to the court about the renovation plans had been "done in bad faith", and whether the attorneys failed to correct previously false statements or withheld information.

She said she would carry out the inquiry with a special master, an independent third party.

item.title: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
item.description: Han Won-seok, 34, confessed to using a hidden camera and AI to get a near-perfect mark on the significant test.
item.content:encoded:
A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.

Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated.

The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation.

Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance.

"I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday.

"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating."

When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam.

He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly.

"It seems that because of me, other successful candidates are being suspected," he suggested.

The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting after Han admitted cheating.

The South Korean president's policy chief Ha Jun-kyung said new measures would be introduced to prevent cheating and warned "past crimes" would be "tracked down and apprehended to the very end".

Those found to have used AI to cheat in the tax accountancy exam will have their qualification revoked and will be banned from retaking the test for five years, the government said.

The scandal comes just days before the east Asian nation's annual college entrance exam, a crucial hurdle for students.

Han said he had only cheated to try and earn money and get a job that would make his parents proud of him again.

Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency told Korean news agency Yonhap on Sunday that it was looking into the case.

"We received a written confession through the test taker's lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam," it confirmed in a statement.

It added that the case had now been assigned to investigators.

Because of the significance of the national exams, instances of cheating are not uncommon in South Korea, and cases involving the use of AI have become more prominent as the technology becomes more sophisticated.

Last month, two college applicants were reported to have used AI glasses to try and cheat their entrance exams at two Seoul universities.

Education ministry data also says there were four cases of cheating through AI glasses at middle and high schools in the past 12 months.

item.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
item.description: The Nvidia scandal has raised questions over whether advanced AI chips ended up in China, despite US restrictions.
item.content:encoded:
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.

Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.

It said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".

It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".

On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.

Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".

The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.

Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.

Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced chips to China.

While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.

Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate".

China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

item.title: Fifth Canadian soldier dies from injuries caused by large fire at military base
item.description: Pte William Douglas Dal Bianco died from his injuries on Friday, a month after a fire that tore through CFB Wainwright.
item.content:encoded:
A fifth Canadian soldier has died from injuries he suffered when a grass fire swept through a military training area last month.

Four people were killed initially and dozens were injured when the fire, which ignited during a live fire training exercise, spread rapidly through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright carried by strong winds on 17 October.

Pte William Douglas Dal Bianco, who had been receiving medical care in Ontario, died on Friday, the Canadian Armed Forces said in a statement.

Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote on X: "Canadians are holding Private Dal Bianco's loved ones, and all those still grieving in the wake of this terrible tragedy, in our hearts."

The Canadian Armed Forces said that 24 military personnel were still in hospital receiving treatment, while 14 had been released as of Saturday. Thirty-eight military personnel had been injured in total.

Members of 1 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group had been conducting live-fire training at the base, in the province of Alberta, when the fire broke out.

Military officials said at the time that the fire spread across a kilometre in a matter of seconds, taking many of those on the base by surprise.

Firefighters battled the blaze through the night, while nearby hospitals became inundated by injured personnel and staff.

Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime".

An investigation found that the fire was likely sparked by a grenade launcher being fired on the base's grenade range, officials said.

Firefighters on the base had known about the fire but could not tackle it because it was in a danger area that could contain unspent explosives.

Canadian Chief of the Defence Staff Gen Jennie Carignan said the nation's armed forces were "heartbroken" by the loss of Dal Bianco, while Defence Minister David McGuinty offered his "deepest condolences" to his family, friends and colleagues.

"No words can ease the pain of losing a loved one, and my thoughts remain with all those affected by this tragedy," he said.

"We remain committed to supporting the families and the Canadian Armed Forces community during this profoundly difficult time, and to honouring Private Dal Bianco's service, dedication and sacrifice to Canada."

item.title: Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack
item.description: It marks the second attack on the country in three days and comes as the US and Iran remain locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz.
item.content:encoded:
Iran launched a drone attack against a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second attempt to target the country in three days.

The country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted the US air defence radar facility at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain using six drones.

Bahrain's military said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed the Iranian air attacks "before they could achieve their objectives".

It comes after Iran fired drones at Bahrain on Friday, its first attack against Gulf countries since September.

The US and Iran are locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows through it but shipping has been restricted since the outbreak of war in February.

Iran insists that it should control the strait and has been attacking what it calls "unauthorised" traffic, while the US military is providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the strait to keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states.

As sirens sounded across Bahrain on Sunday the interior ministry called on citizens to head to their nearest safe location.

Bahrain's foreign ministry said: "The Kingdom of Bahrain condemns in the strongest terms the continued brutal Iranian attacks on its territory and holds Iran fully responsible for their consequences."

In a statement on the strikes shared by Iran's state broadcaster on Telegram, the IRGC said: "The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response."

Earlier this week, the IRGC claimed that it struck a US early warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday.

The US military has denied the claim, stating that the IRGC launched two one-way attack drones towards Bahrain and both were shot down by US forces. It added that there were no injuries or damage.

Earlier in the week the US carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials told CBS, the BBC's US partner.

The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.

Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a naval blockade of Iranian ports.

Iranian negotiators had been discussing with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US meets seven conditions, reportedly including the lifting of the naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

However this week Donald Trump said that the US was no longer interested in a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered Vice-President JD Vance, who had been involved in efforts to restart negotiations, to focus on domestic US politics.

item.title: Staggered age of consent to be discussed after Brand case, minister says
item.description: A woman who alleges she was raped by the jailed comedian when she was 16 is campaigning to see relationships between 16-and 17-year-olds and adults made illegal.
item.content:encoded:
A discussion over a staggered age of consent is to take place, the work and pensions secretary has said, as the government faces calls to change the law following the case against Russell Brand.

Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Pat McFadden said that "appalling" stories of "abuse of power by powerful men" have emerged this week.

A woman who alleges she was raped by jailed comedian Brand when she was 16 is now campaigning to see the law changed so that relationships between 16 and 17-year-olds and adults would be illegal.

Questions over a staggered age of consent have "been raised and will be discussed" McFadden said, adding: "[I] can't tell you what the conclusion of that would be, but the last week has certainly put that up in lights."

Adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds, under UK law.

Mia Latter, who has waived her right to anonymity, told the Sunday Times that she wants the age of consent to be staggered.

Latter is one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.

She was known by the pseudonym "Alice". Brand denied the allegations at the time and none of the six women were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.

At Southwark Crown Court on Monday, Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half-years imprisonment after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, involving four women between 2004 and 2009. He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.

Latter said she was 16 when she met the comedian, then 30. She told the Sunday Times: "I think people were so struck by my story because of the age difference and the clear imbalance [in power].

"I don't want to criminalise teenagers having sex with each other.

"If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to.

"But...if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offence."

Layla Stone, founder of the campaign group Close the Consent Gap, said bringing in a staggered age of consent was about addressing a "power imbalance" in relationships involving 16 and 17 year-olds and adults. She urged ministers to commit to such a change.

Stone, a child protection social worker, told the BBC that 16 and 17 year-olds were seen as children in "every single framework of the law" and "we don't believe [they are] old enough to consent to having sex with much older adults".

Close the Consent Gap is proposing that 16 year-olds would not be able to have a sexual relationship with anyone older than 19, and that someone aged 17 would be prohibited from a relationship with anyone older than 20.

Further allegations of sexual misconduct in the entertainment industry came in the same week Brand was convicted.

ITV News and the Guardian published a story alleging that comedian David Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

One woman said she now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.

Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour when he was a judge at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room.

Walliams said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

The Metropolitan Police said on Friday it has launched an investigation into Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences", after the ITV News and the Guardian story. The Met said that the allegations it is investigating are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian but that it was "also proactively reviewing that reporting".

Speaking to Sky News, the work and pensions secretary said: "I do think that between Russell Brand, David Walliams, what's been put out there, people are looking at these issues in a new light."

Helen Whately, the shadow work and pension secretary, told Kuenssberg that it was worth debating a change to age of consent laws.

Whately said she has teenage daughters and would be concerned if they brought home a man many years older than them.

"I think any parent would look twice," she said, adding: "Let's have the debate."

Anna Edmundson, director of policy and social change at the NSPCC charity, said 16 and 17-year-olds can be particularly vulnerable to grooming by some adults and laws have been changed in recent years to prevent more people in positions of trust from having sexual relationships with children of such an age.

She said "other laws are failing to prevent them from being sexually exploited", adding: "Even though they are over the age of consent, young people are still entitled to be protected from harm."

item.title: Ex-Met Police inspector lied about wife's death in Barbados
item.description: Warren Arter faced claims of sexually exploiting crime victims - his wife was found in a blood-stained room.
item.content:encoded:
Warning: Contains graphic details of Rebekah Arter's death - and references to coercion and sexual abuse

A former Metropolitan Police detective, investigated for sexually exploiting vulnerable crime victims it was his job to protect, later lied about the death of his wife in a Barbados hotel room, BBC Panorama has learned.

Warren Arter first met his wife Rebekah after she reported domestic abuse to the Met. He then abused her for more than a decade. Her death two years ago has never been properly investigated.

Panorama can reveal failures by Barbados authorities to preserve evidence and interview hotel staff about Arter's suspicious behaviour before and after Rebekah's death, aged 47.

Despite a request from her family for assistance, the Met did not send detectives to the Caribbean island.

The Met told the BBC it took this decision because no allegation of criminality had been made.

Rebekah's family, speaking publicly for the first time, have told Panorama the Met failed her. The cause of her death is still not known with a coroner in the UK recording an open verdict.

We have also spoken to hotel staff who were called to the room in June 2024 after Arter rang reception to say his wife had collapsed.

Interviews with the staff, police sources - plus Arter's erratic communications following Rebekah's death - reveal:

  • Arter gave conflicting accounts - telling staff and Rebekah's family she had choked, fallen and banged her head, or he had woken up and found her dead
  • Evidence was not secured, vital forensic tests were not taken and Rebekah's organs were inexplicably "chopped up" by a pathologist in Barbados
  • Four days after Rebekah's death, a senior Met boss from its Gold Command was briefed about the incident in light of Arter's alleged offending - but it did not lead to officers travelling to the Caribbean island

Arter, 54, took his own life in HMP Wandsworth, days after he had returned from Barbados and been arrested for allegedly abusing another woman.

Rebekah had been escaping an abusive relationship when Arter investigated her case in 2006. The detective then pursued a relationship with her and moved in not long after.

Three years later, he was placed in charge of a unit in south-east London investigating rape cases.

Arter was later suspended by the Met and investigated over his conduct towards eight alleged victims by its watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) - but was never convicted.

Over the seven years he was suspended, Arter continued to receive his full detective inspector salary, before being dismissed in 2023 for drug offences.

All this time, he subjected Rebekah to sexual and domestic abuse, coercive control, and drugging, which the BBC has seen video evidence of.

Panorama has now spoken to several members of staff who were working at the luxury O2 Beach Club in Barbados on the night of Rebekah's death. All say Arter behaved suspiciously.

Two of them entered Arter's hotel room after he had called to say his wife was unwell. Both say it was immediately clear Rebekah was dead.

Andrew, a security guard, says he had to prevent Arter from going to a nearby street party, before emergency services arrived.

"So I'm asking him, why do you need to go when you have a bigger issue here?"

Andrew says Arter responded: "Oh, I just need to clear my head."

  • Watch Panorama: The Predator in the Police on BBC iPlayer from 0600 on Tuesday 17 November - or on BBC One at 21:00 that evening (not in Wales and Northern Ireland)

Arter then began crying "crocodile tears" and conducting performative CPR despite Rebekah's lips being blue, according to Andrew, who says Arter's explanation of what happened kept changing.

Initially, Arter told Andrew she had fallen near a chest of drawers - but her body was some distance away, near the kitchen. When police arrived, Andrew says he heard Arter tell them he had found her like that.

There was no sign of Rebekah having a head injury, Andrew says, despite bloodstains on the bed, the wall and the living room area.

Arter recorded a video of the room and sent it to family and friends in the UK.

"It looks like chocolate but it's blood," he can be heard saying.

Andrew says he told Arter to phone family in the UK - and then heard him tell them that she had been unwell.

"He was just trying to find the right story that fits and none of them added up," says Andrew.

The security guard says he told Barbadian police officers what he saw and gave a statement but was never formally interviewed.

Panorama has seen some of Arter's messages and spoken to Rebekah's friends and family who were contacted by him shortly after her death.

They reveal that Arter provided other possible causes of death - that Rebekah had "choked" or that her drink had been spiked.

These accounts are contradicted by Rebekah's daughter-in-law, Lacey, who says he told her they had both been asleep for 18 hours and he had woken up and found her dead.

"He was outright lying. He was forgetting what he was telling people," says Lacey.

Arter was briefly detained by Barbadian police but released a short time later.

One of the police officers who attended the room that night refused to share information with Panorama without payment. He still had a photograph of Rebekah's dead body on his phone.

Police in Barbados did not respond to our request for comment.

Other hotel staff members have told the BBC they were concerned about Arter's treatment of Rebekah during their stay.

Security supervisor Kenneth says Arter appeared "controlling" and "didn't allow Rebekah to do anything on her own". Rebekah also frequently appeared to be "intoxicated", he says.

A third member of staff, who worked on the front desk, says staff suspected Arter was "drugging" Rebekah.

Panorama has seen a video, filmed by Arter on his phone when she was still alive, which shows Rebekah clearly intoxicated. She is wearing the same clothes that she is pictured in after she died.

  • If you are in the UK and you have been affected by any of the issues in this story such as sexual abuse and violence , information and support is available at BBC Action Line

In the early hours of the morning after her death, during the staff member's night shift, Arter approached the hotel front desk to ask when Rebekah last had a massage in the hotel spa.

She says his question struck her as bizarre and felt like he was trying to get his story straight.

Meanwhile, back in the UK, Rebekah's son, Elliot, and his wife, Lacey, were becoming increasingly concerned after visiting the home she shared with Arter.

Inside, they say they found a variety of drugs and hidden CCTV cameras that Arter had rigged up in the house.

They also discovered photographs of Rebekah naked and bruised, involved in sexual acts, seemingly taken without her consent.

Four days after Rebekah's death, they went to Bexleyheath Police Station, the same station where Arter once led rape investigations, to report her death to the Met and raise concerns about his possible involvement.

"The front office staff said, 'Oh well it's happened in Barbados, it's a Barbados issue' - and tried to brush it off at first," says Elliot.

"The moment I gave Warren's name, it was like chaos - we had sergeants coming down to the front desk," says Lacey.

"But it really wasn't about Rebekah, it was more about Warren," she says.

That evening, an officer briefed a Gold Commander within the Met, a senior boss who decides how to respond to incidents. The Met did not send detectives to Barbados.

UK police forces can be asked to help investigate a death of a British national overseas - usually at the request of local police where the death occurred.

Under Foreign Office guidance, the case for such involvement is strengthened when families request assistance and there are credible concerns about the circumstances of the death, as there were in Rebekah's case.

The Met told the BBC it made immediate efforts to obtain information in order to assess whether to travel to Barbados but decided it would not be appropriate without an allegation of criminality.

An inquest in the UK later found that Rebekah's organs had been inexplicably "chopped up" into small pieces by a pathologist in Barbados.

This served no medical purpose and destroyed vital evidence, according to a UK pathologist who examined her body after it had been repatriated.

The inquest also established that key toxicology and histology tests - to look for signs of disease, injury or other changes in the body - were not conducted.

The coroner, Andrew Harris, said this raised the prospect of "deliberate concealment or obstruction of further investigation".

He also said that while bloodstains on bedclothes may be consistent with vomiting, he could not accept the cause of death determined by Barbadian authorities, aspiration pneumonitis - inflammation of the lungs - and delivered an open verdict.

He concluded that Rebekah's death likely involved intoxication and said unlawful killing could not be ruled out.

The inquest did not, however, consider Arter's alleged sexual exploitation of several other women whose cases he had investigated, to be within its scope.

Police in Barbados have previously said no marks of violence were found on Rebekah's body and there was nothing to suggest anything untoward - adding that they did not order toxicology tests because they believed she died from natural causes.

A week after Rebekah died, Arter flew back to the UK where he was arrested at Heathrow in connection with alleged sexual offences against another woman whose case he had investigated as a police officer in 2010. He was found dead in Wandsworth prison three days later.

In response to the BBC, Metropolitan Police Commander Simon Messinger said: "Our thoughts at this time remain with Rebekah Arter's family, who understandably have questions about the circumstances of her death.

"We would urge any victim survivors of rape and sexual offences - no matter how long ago a crime may have occurred - to reach out."

Elliot says his two young children will never know their grandmother.

"My daughter, my son - they're never gonna actually have any memories of her," he says.

"For the rest of my life, I'm never going to know how she's passed away."

If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noel directly and securely through encrypted messaging app Signal on: +44 7809 334720, by email at noel.titheradge@bbc.co.uk

item.title: Alleged Russell Brand rape victim wants age of consent law changed
item.description: Mia Latter, who says she was 16 when she met the convicted rapist, wants a staggered age of consent.
item.content:encoded:
• Warning - this story contains graphic content

A woman who alleges that she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity and is campaigning for a staggered age of consent in an interview with the Sunday Times.

Mia Latter was one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation. She was known under the pseudonym 'Alice'. Brand denied the allegations at the time.

None of the women in the 2023 media investigation were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.

Reacting to the proposal, Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh said it would be a "massive step" to change the age of consent law, but that it "deserves proper consideration and scrutiny".

Speaking to the Sunday Times, she added that it was "disgusting" that a culture existed in the 2000s that "normalised and celebrated" celebrities having relationships with teenagers.

On Monday the entertainer was sentenced to 10 and a half years for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.

The Sunday Times reported that Latter had initially described the allegation about Brand to them as a sexual assault and that is how they reported it in their 2023 investigation.

Latter, 37, "now calls this allegation rape", the paper said.

Latter said she was 16 when she met Brand, who was 30 at the time, when she was on her way home from a shopping trip. She said Brand was working at MTV.

She told the paper: "I think people were so struck by my story because of the age difference and the clear imbalance [in power],"

She said Brand told her to keep their relationship secret from her school friends and claimed that he referred to her as "the child" in front of his entourage.

It was towards the end of their relationship that Latter was allegedly orally raped by Brand, according to the Sunday Times.

Latter said that she was now campaigning for the introduction of a "staggered" age of consent that would prohibit relationships between 16- and 17-year-olds and adults.

"I don't want to criminalise teenagers having sex with each other," she told the paper. "If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to. But … if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offence."

She also told the paper that she would not continue with the criminal process so she could focus on her campaign.

In her interview with the Sunday Times she said that the CPS decided not to include her as part of Brand's criminal trial but the police wanted her to be part of a "subsequent trial".

A Met Police spokesperson said: "Officers launched an investigation in January 2026 after receiving an allegation of rape.

"Detectives sought advice from the Crown Prosecution Service to determine how best to proceed, and officers were advised that further information was needed before a charging decision could be made.

"This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence."

A spokesperson for the Crown Prosecution Service said it would "continue to work closely with investigators to provide advice and make sure cases progress as quickly as possible".

item.title: Israel kills Hamas commander in strike on Gaza camp, officials say
item.description: Both Hamas and IDF officials confirm the death of Samir Abu Younis, commander of the Rafah Brigade.
item.content:encoded:
A senior Hamas figure who helped plan and oversee the 7 October 2023 attack on Israel has been killed in an Israeli airstrike, officials in Israel and Gaza have said.

Samir Abu Younis, the newly appointed commander of the Rafah Brigade, was killed on Saturday in Al-Mawasi in the southern Gaza Strip, according to Hamas's Al-Qassam Brigades military wing.

A local Hamas official confirmed Younis's death. The Israeli military said it had targeted him and that prior to the strike "steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians".

Eyewitnesses in Gaza said four missiles struck a tent in the Al-Waha camp, which shelters hundreds of displaced people in Al-Mawasi, causing a fire to break out.

A medical source at Nasser Hospital in the southern city of Khan Younis said three injured people had arrived there, as well as a dead body.

The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) and Israel's security agency, the ISA, confirmed in a statement on Telegram that it had "eliminated" Younis.

Describing him as a "central figure among Hamas's senior figures", it said he had "acted with the aim of trying to restore the strength of the brigade and the Hamas terrorist organisation".

It added: "Younis directed the brigade's terrorists to advance and carry out terror attacks against Israeli civilians and IDF troops."

Al-Qassam Brigades wrote on Telegram that Younis had "participated in numerous high-profile operations and resisted enemy incursions", and was "one of the most important commanders involved in planning and overseeing the 7 October attack".

It described his killing as a "cowardly assassination".

Younis, 53, had been in his position since 15 September, following the death of the brigade's previous commander, Nael Abu Obeid.

He joined Hamas' armed wing in 1991 and held several senior operational roles before becoming commander. His funeral will be held on Sunday afternoon in Khan Younis, Hamas said.

The Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed an 251 others taken hostage, triggered the most recent war in Gaza.

Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in the Palestinian territory, the health ministry there says.

Though a ceasefire was reached last October, Israel has continued occasional strikes it says are targeting remaining Hamas militants, which it argues it has the right to do under the terms of the ceasefire agreement.

item.title: Judo champion shakes up French presidential race with surprise candidacy
item.description: Teddy Riner is one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, and one in five voters say they could support him.
item.content:encoded:
Apart from an overwhelming urge to pin one's opponent to the floor of the house, there is no obvious connection between politics and the world of top-level judo.

That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race.

The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.

But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances.

Riner is, after all, one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, regularly topping the polls for embodying the nation's "values". He is a proven winner, with five Olympic golds and 11 world championships under his belt, as well as a successful career in business.

More than 28 million people have watched his election broadcast on Instagram and X, shot with proper presidential decorum against a backdrop of books and a French flag. Some 22% told an Ifop poll within 24 hours they "could" vote for him.

Actors and television personalities have become presidents in other countries. The ex-leader of Liberia – George Weah – was formerly a professional footballer.

So why not a judoka in the Élysée Palace?

"Anyone who thinks that being out of the political in-crowd disqualifies Riner from running for the Élysée would be very wrong," says Guillaume Tabard of Le Figaro.

"But [Riner] too would be wrong if he thinks not belonging to the in-crowd is all it takes."

For now the whole of the French political world has decided to take the Riner candidacy seriously – or at least to pretend to. That is partly because he is such a popular personality that mocking his political hopes could easily rebound badly.

But it is also because the state of French politics – outside of the burgeoning forces of the hard left and hard right – is one of total disarray.

The centre-ground is floundering, with no candidate yet emerging who can inspire anything like the sense of mission of hard-right leader Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the hard left, who for now look set to face off in the final round of the presidential election in May.

So when a popular figure like Riner enters the race - proclaiming himself "neither left, nor right", wanting to "unite the country" and "put money back in people's pockets", railing equally against "racists" and "yobs who scare people off our streets" – politicians have to take note.

It is perfectly possible, probable even, that Riner's campaign will fizzle out after a brief period of hype, and that the judoka will after all be a joker in the pack. But it is also possible that it won't, in which case the pre-election arithmetic will need a hasty readjustment: and it won't be the centrists who are smiling.

Thus far, Riner has shown himself a master of the codes required for this kind of out-of-nowhere candidacy, the first of which is to press home the message: "Don't Worry! I'm NOT a Politician!"

In this day and age in France, anyone who smacks of the "system" is automatically downgraded in voters' eyes, so it is important to emphasise that you are only running for office because, one, you have experienced real life (unlike those loafers in Paris); and two, you have discovered that there are solutions out there for the country's many problems. Solutions that are invisible to those same blinkered apparatchiks.

All this Riner was able to express in last Monday's social media broadcast by using sophisticated rhetorical devices.

"People say I am a fool for wanting to run for the presidency," he said.

"Am I a fool? Well, if refusing to see France sink under the weight of debt; refusing to see mothers and fathers grit their teeth every time they do their weekly shop, and tremble with fear when their kids go out on the street… if all that means being a fool, then yes call me a fool."

It was a promising oratorial start for the sportsman, and certainly attracted the viewers.

But if he is serious – and Riner says he never does anything half-heartedly - that's not how he became an Olympic champion – then the hard work begins now.

What does Riner actually want to do? Who will be on his team? Where does he position himself on the all-consuming matters of the day: pension-reform, investment in education, the cost of living, public debt, the rise of populism or Russia's war in Ukraine?

In short, how does he intend to transform his undeniable popularity as a sporting figure into a political mandate?

Broadly, Riner appears to be on the right on economic matters and law and order, but being black and of Caribbean background he is also very strong on racism. When he says he is anti-extremism, he is referring mainly to Marine Le Pen.

In other words his pitch is somewhere in the centre, and against the extremes.

The trouble is, this is already an extremely crowded area, with important figures like ex-prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal signally failing to take off.

Currently there are a dozen or so candidates in the area between centre right and centre left, stretching from the Socialist-backed Raphaël Glucksman to the Republicans' Bruno Retailleau on the right.

The latest possible addition is Christine Lagarde, who steps down as head of the European Central Bank next February.

The addition of yet another contender will dilute their polling numbers even further, making a second-round qualification for Mélenchon more likely.

So no wonder the leader of France Unbowed (LFI) seemed so happy about Riner's decision to run. "We know how it goes: neither right nor left means not left," Mélenchon told reporters on Friday.

The only other politician who seems genuinely pleased, rather than putting on a fixed smile, is President Emmanuel Macron, who said Riner was a "great champion" and that politics "did not belong to the professionals".

That could be explained by the president's cool relations with his former prime ministers, Philippe and Attal, both of whom are doing all they can to distance themselves from their unpopular one-time boss.

Riner said he viewed Macron's praise as a "poisoned chalice", telling reporters on Saturday that he was "not the president's envoy, I'm not a Macronist".

Politics and judo have very little in common, but of the two, as Riner will soon discover, the more vicious is not the one that is fought out hand-to-hand after mutual acknowledgement on the tatami mat.

In Japanese, judo actually means "the gentle way".

If he starts looking like a serious candidate, Riner must know his life will be turned upside down, not just his physical form.

In politics you do not bow in respect to your opponent. You give him a metaphorical headbutt.

item.title: Nigeria cautions against travel via Ethiopia's main airport due to altitude
item.description: The foreign ministry in Abuja says 6 Nigerians with underlying health problems have died this year while transiting through Addis Ababa.
item.content:encoded:
Nigeria's government has cautioned its citizens, in particular those with medical conditions, against travelling via Ethiopia's main airport due to its altitude.

The foreign ministry in Abuja said 16 Nigerians with underlying health problems had died this year while transiting through Addis Ababa.

The city sits at an altitude of 2,334m (7,657ft) above sea level, making it one of the highest capitals in the world. Bole International Airport is a major hub for travel between Africa, the Middle East and Asia, serving millions of passengers a year.

Nigeria said those with cardiovascular and respiratory conditions were at an increased risk.

The Nigerian foreign ministry did not disclose the identities of the travellers it said had died, nor the cause of death.

It urged anyone with a health condition exacerbated by high altitudes to "exercise caution" when planning a journey via Addis Ababa and "obtain appropriate medical guidance" before doing so.

The ministry stressed that it did not want to discourage Nigerians from travelling through the Ethiopian capital.

Visiting an area at a high altitude can be dangerous for people with heart and lung diseases, as the air is thinner and so less oxygen can get into the bloodstream, experts say.

This means the heart has to work harder to get enough oxygen to different parts of the body, which can sometimes lead to heart failure among those with existing conditions, according to the American Heart Association.

The lack of oxygen at high altitudes can cause adverse effects such as dizziness, fatigue and shortness of breath among healthy people - which can cause complications for people with lung disease, studies show.

item.title: New Orleans port files $1m lawsuit over 'miracle on the Mississippi' tanker collision
item.description: The lawsuit filed by New Orleans officials also requests that the tanker involved in the collision with the cruise ship be seized and sold to pay for damages.
item.content:encoded:
The Port of New Orleans is suing the owners and managers of a tanker that crashed into a cruise ship docked in New Orleans on Friday.

The port is claiming the tanker is at fault for the collision that saw more than 100 passengers being rescued from the Mississippi River and caused more than $1m (£756k) in damage, according to court documents.

The collision left 32 people from the stricken riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one was unaccounted for. Officials hailed it as a "miracle on the Mississippi".

The exact cause of the crash remains under investigation, but US Coast Guard Capt Melanie Burnham said: "There seems to be some type of a loss of steering."

The paddlewheel cruise ship, American Heritage, was left on its side and partially submerged in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel Atlantic Asphalt on Friday afternoon.

The court documents added that the port terminal "was significantly damaged" in the incident.

The tanker, the M/V Atlantic Asphalt, its owner Nave Shipping SA, and its management company, Thome Ship Management Pte Ltd, are all named in the federal court lawsuit filed on Friday in the Eastern District of Louisiana court.

Officials are still investigating the full extent of the damage from the crash, as well as the cause, but the lawsuit says the port is looking for money to cover cleanup, inspections, repairs and other expenses.

The lawsuit requests that the tanker be seized and sold to pay for the damage. It also alleges that the collision "occurred as a result of the negligence, gross negligence, fault or carelessness" of the ship and operating companies.

It alleges that the tanker and companies failed "to use all available means to avoid the risk" of colliding with the riverboat.

Nave Shipping is a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation. BBC has contacted the China State Shipbuilding Corporation for comment.

Thome Ship Management has also been contacted. The firm said in a statement on Saturday that the crew of the Atlantic Asphalt were safe and accounted for.

"OSM Thome is fully complying with the local authorities as they carry out the necessary investigations," it said.

There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the port authority.

Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help while officials shut down traffic in the Mississippi River during the rescue effort.

The American Heritage had been finishing an eight-day cruise calling at destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi along the waterway.

item.title: PC sacked for speeding 75 times in two months
item.description: Jake Lay-Flurrie demonstrated "a repeated failure to follow the rules", says Essex chief constable.
item.content:encoded:
An Essex Police officer has been sacked after he was caught speeding 75 times in two months while on duty.

PC Jake Lay-Flurrie, who was posted in Braintree, drove at more than double the speed limit on five occasions between August and October 2025.

He was described as a "passionate and well-regarded officer" acting "with good intent" during a misconduct hearing in Chelmsford.

However, Chief Constable Rachel Nolan said Lay-Flurrie demonstrated "a repeated failure to follow the rules".

Each instance involved a marked police car. He also used the emergency lights, despite not being qualified as a response driver.

He was caught out by telematics equipment fitted inside the vehicles and was sacked on 6 November, having been found to have committed gross misconduct.

"Being a committed, proactive and otherwise well-regarded police officer does not excuse a repeated failure to follow the rules," Nolan said.

"No officer should believe that getting to an incident more quickly is more important than driving lawfully and safely."

item.title: Sotheby's auction of $180m Van Gogh challenged over claims it was 'sold under duress'
item.description: Sotheby's says it will work with the heirs of a family who had previously owned the artwork to try and reach a solution.
item.content:encoded:
Auction house Sotheby's says it is working to resolve a dispute over the intended sale of a painting by Vincent van Gogh.

Châtaigniers en Fleurs, which carries an estimate of $180m (£136m), is due to go under the hammer in New York on Wednesday.

But representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family - earlier German owners of the work - say it may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

Sotheby's say its own "extensive research" has not established this, but say they will work with the family to try and reach a solution.

"Sotheby's takes provenance and restitution matters extremely seriously and has undertaken extensive research into the ownership history of Châtaigniers en fleurs," Sotheby's told the BBC in a statement.

"We are aware of the concerns recently raised by representatives of the Fischer heirs and have been in dialogue with them regarding the painting's history.

"While our research to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress, we recognize the importance of engaging thoughtfully and constructively with the family and are committed to working toward a mutually satisfactory resolution."
