item.title: Australian teen missing in bush for six days rescued alive
item.description: The 17-year-old's mum has joked that he is "grounded for life" and "never leaving the house again".
item.content:encoded:
A teenager missing for six days in dense Australian bushland has been found alive.

William, whose surname has not been released, disappeared last Friday while on a camping trip with a friend in bushland about 180km (112 miles) east of Melbourne, Victoria.

Extremely cold overnight temperatures had left authorities concerned for the 17-year-old's welfare. Police dogs, divers and helicopters had been involved in the search.

He was located on Friday morning and reunited with his relieved family, who said he was uninjured but "grounded for life".

Rescuers winched William to safety, and fed him a doughnut and a bottle of water, before he was taken to hospital for a check up.

The boy's mother, Elizabeth Barkley, told reporters the teenager had "only a few scratches" and seemed fit and healthy.

"He's doing fine, everything seems to be fine, he's in perfect health," she added.

"He just stayed in one spot and waited to be rescued and I'm just over the moon he's alive."

Joking, she added: "He's never leaving the house again."

Police have said officers were emotional to have found the teen alive.

"It doesn't happen all the time," Victoria Police Acting Inspector Jason Benbow said. "I'm sure he's got a story to tell us soon, which we're very keen to hear," he added.

item.title: Trying Tourette's device was the best day of my life
item.description: Katie is one of many that say a device developed by researchers in Nottingham helped calm her symptoms.
item.content:encoded:
When Katie was just a child, her tics were so relentless they left her bedridden with a sore throat for two weeks.

The now 15-year-old says living with Tourette's affected her ability to sleep, eat, and caused her to miss school.

But a wrist device developed by researchers in Nottingham helped her calm down in an "instant".

Katie recalled trying it on for the first time, and said: "It was absolutely life-changing. It was like the best day of my life."

Tourette's syndrome is a neurodevelopmental condition with symptoms usually starting in childhood.

Katie, from Hertfordshire, said she first started to experience symptoms aged seven.

She said: "It was constantly moving, constantly making sounds and then I was kind of getting looked at like, 'why are you doing that?'

"I used to make snorting sounds, but it was constant all the time, so I'd give myself a really bad sore throat and then be in bed for two weeks.

"I think I became quite sad a lot of the time."

Katie's mum Julia said it was "heartbreaking" to see her daughter struggling.

"You feel helpless. You feel you don't know where to turn really," she said.

It was not until she read about a wrist device - developed by the University of Nottingham - that Julia felt hopeful for her daughter.

She and Katie learned more about the device, and came to Nottingham to try it in December before it was available to buy.

Katie said when she turned it on for the first time, the effect was "instant" and she became "really calm".

"And I remember on the drive home, I just cried the whole way home because I was like, 'I want it now'," she said.

Katie was among the first people to use the Neupulse device.

It works by delivering electrical pulses to the median nerve at the wrist, which trials have shown can change the activity in the parts of the brain involved in movement control.

They found that rhythmic stimulation can reduce the frequency and intensity of tics.

In 2023, a clinical trial of 121 people in the UK found they experienced, on average, a reduction in tic frequency of 25% while using a prototype of the device.

That year, it was also tested by the singer Lewis Capaldi, who has Tourette's, prior to a gig in the city.

The university added Capaldi was impressed by the effects of Neupulse and was eager to try it out again in the future.

The device was developed by the university and its spin-out company Neurotherapuetics Ltd, which secured £1m in additional funding to commercialise the device.

According to the Tourettes Action charity, there are two versions of the device: Neupulse-C - which is available as a consumer wellness device - and Neupulse-M, which is intended to be marketed as a medical device specifically for the treatment of tics and Tourette's syndrome, but it has not yet received regulatory approval for this purpose.

Neupulse-M is still going through the regulatory approval process. It is hoped that if regulatory approval is obtained, the device will be considered for NHS use.

The charity added the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) had identified the technology as "promising", and had requested further evidence of its long-term benefits before making recommendations over NHS adoption.

The university said "thousands" of the devices had been sold so far.

Prof Stephen Jackson, who has led the research, said seeing the impact on users of the device had been "a dream come true", and hoped it would be available on the NHS "in the next year or so".

He said: "We are working diligently and as hard as we can to get regulatory approval for the Neupulse device as a treatment for Tourette's.

"It's been provisionally evaluated by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, but they were unable to recommend it for use in the NHS until we have the regulatory approval. That's something we're working towards."

In 2025, NICE added: "Our committee will meet again to appraise the clinical and cost effectiveness of the technology and publish new guidance."

According to Tourettes Action, more than 300,000 people in the UK have the condition, which is incurable.

Jackson said: "We've had people saying they managed to get through their wedding vows without ticking.

"People saying they've been able to travel through the airport and travel on airplanes without ticking."

Among the users is 15-year-old Ollie, from Cheshire, who started making involuntary neck movements nearly two years ago.

"I just suddenly cracked my neck, and then about 48 hours after that, it was constant movements," he said. "It was incredibly sudden."

Ollie's dad, Alex, said daily tasks - including sleeping, eating and drinking - became "incredibly difficult", and said he and Ollie's mother were "at a loss... just watching our son deteriorate".

"There's a period of it where I didn't leave the house for about a month," Ollie said. "I didn't hang out with my mates.

"Reading and writing became really hard. I was out of school for six, seven months as I'm getting into GCSEs."

They heard about the device from the film I Swear, a drama based on the life of John Davidson, who is a Tourette's campaigner.

The family initially thought Ollie had Tourette's syndrome, but he was later diagnosed with Functional Neurological Disorder (FND) - a neurological condition that affects how the brain and nervous system work.

At that point, he said he came close to telling his parents "probably don't bother with this device", because he did not think it would work.

Alex said a few months ago, his son called them when he turned it on for the first time.

"You could hear that he was crying on the telephone because it had worked and his neck movement had stopped," he said.

Ollie said: "It's like a light switch. I remember my hands were quite shaky when I was calling my parents because it's like getting part of your life back."

They both said the gadget had been "life-changing".

Emma McNally, CEO at Tourettes Action, said users she had spoken to had given the device "nothing but praise".

"Some people have said it's helped them to go to places that they've not been for a long time, such as the cinema or a library.

"Other people have said it's helped them when they've been in a tic attack to help them come out of that to calm the tics and make them feel more relaxed," she added.

Mylo, 17, from Buckinghamshire, was involved in the clinical trial of the device in 2023 when he was 13.

He was recently given a device as a gift.

When he switched it on for the first time, he said he "instantaneously" felt the need to suppress his facial tics "going".

"As soon as it comes on, I can feel it," he said.

"I feel different... I feel new almost, which is strange. It's going to be such a big difference."

The device has recently been tested in early trials for people with Parkinson's to see if it can be used to reduce tremors.

Prof Jackson said the university was also looking to launch a UK-wide clinical trial to look at both anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

item.title: 'No light, no water, no heat': Ukrainians struggle with blackouts as Russia hits power grid
item.description: For parents in parts of Ukraine, trying to lead a normal family life with just a few hours of power each day is taking its toll.
item.content:encoded:
Daryna Kulchytska is a mum under pressure. A single parent in a seventh floor flat in Kyiv trying to feed two lively kids and ensure they do their homework. But Daryna also faces the added strain of a deadline she can't even be certain of.

All she knows is soon the lights will go out, the sockets will lose power, the wi-fi will drop, and the taps will run dry. Tonight, the electricity has kept flowing an hour longer than advertised, but Daryna's still racing to serve dinner and finish her own work from home.

"The last few days it was only four or five hours we had power, but it's not at the same times. For two hours we have electricity, then for eight hours we don't."

As peace talks continue, with US envoys meeting the Russian and Ukrainian leaders on Thursday, Ukrainians are facing a rolling schedule of planned power cuts because of intensified Russian attacks on their energy grid. Ukraine has responded by striking Russian oil refineries.

Officials are concerned that life will quickly become unsustainable for millions of Ukrainians if power supplies cannot be maintained for at least four hours per day. Some privately warn that's close already, as some families are living with outages of up to 20 hours in Kyiv.

The power cuts were introduced earlier this year than last winter, and they're already lasting longer - making homes like Daryna's darker and colder. She's wrapped in layers of clothing and a heavy coat - the temperature is dropping, indoors and out.

Just before 7:30pm, there's a click and that's it - darkness until dawn.

The lift doesn't work, the water will stop flowing because electricity is needed to pump it to their flat. So the torches and LED candles come out and Daryna, her son Kyryll and daughter Olena gather for a card game of Uno before an early night.

Twelve-year-old Kyryll, speaking perfect English learned during two years living in the US, is frank about the disruption.

"There's no light, no water, no heat, no electricity. And no fun. All the fun got sucked out with the electricity," he says. "We have a lot of board games. We have a whole shelf, but we've played them like a hundred thousand times already."

Many families sit in the shadows as blackouts sweep entire neighbourhoods, smothering homes and streets in darkness.

"You look outside and sometimes you see nothing. You have a big city around but you see nothing because there's no light," Daryna says.

Kyiv has been worst hit - its metro trains and trolleybuses at times brought to a standstill. Nationwide, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians have gone without power in recent weeks.

We saw why on a visit to one of Ukraine's largest power stations, barely standing after a recent ballistic missile strike - the most powerful and devastating attack of Russia's campaign against Ukrainian energy targets.

The enormous plant - which we've been asked not to name for security reasons - has been reduced to a pile of twisted metal and broken pipes, its turbines buried in rubble, taking the site completely off line.

Volodymyr Kovalenko was on duty in the control room keeping the plant working when the missiles hit at 3am.

"It was a very powerful attack. We'd never experienced anything like it. We'd had strikes before – part of the roof had collapsed, it was pretty grim. But this time it was particularly severe."

Kovalenko, who followed in his parents' footsteps and has worked at the site for 25 years, says the damage is heartbreaking, though he's confident it can be repaired.

But the work is being hampered by air raids every 15-30 minutes – seven times during our four-hour visit. Each warning of drones and further missiles forces teams to down tools and dive for cover, though during our visit all were shot down or flew on towards other targets.

If there isn't time to reach the site's main shelter, the workers hide in the foundations of its towering chimneys.

"It's very difficult," says Vadym Bobyr, who is leading the recovery effort. "You've mentally prepared yourself to do a particular job, and then… the air raid siren goes off, and you have to get out as quickly as possible."

The 39-year-old, who has worked here half his life, is dwarfed by the mangled ruins and daunted by the challenge of rebuilding the plant.

"It's emotionally difficult, because we've already repaired all this, got it running again, and now it's happened all over again. It hurts, but we keep working and getting things done."

As we speak there's another alert - an incoming Banderol cruise missile.

The workers dart through the maze of passages and pipework but there isn't time to reach a shelter - one of the plant's thickest walls will have to do for cover. The missile was eventually intercepted 5km (3 miles) away.

Energy workers are at enormous risk. Since August there have been almost daily attacks on power facilities, claiming several lives every week. And it's getting more dangerous.

On the edge of the site, with the latest threat over, a team returns to reinstating the power lines feeding the national grid. But they won't be carrying electricity from the shattered plant before the end of this winter, at least.

President Volodymyr Zelensky says Ukraine still has enough generating capacity to meet electricity demand - the problem is getting it to homes and businesses when so many power lines and substations have been hit. Russia is using "waiter drones" that cling to pylons and cables and go undetected until Russia decides to detonate them.

Maxim Timchenko, CEO of DTEK, Ukraine's largest private energy company, said Russia was already putting the degraded electricity grid under even greater pressure than last year, and that overstretched air defences were unable to protect all of Ukraine's critical infrastructure.

"What is different is the scale of attacks and the different types of weapons used in these attacks. This is what is the difference - they've doubled in power and in scale".

He said rebuilding the damaged power station would take at least until next summer, because workers under sustained attack were limited to only one or two productive hours per day.

"We are fighting for survival of not only the whole country but ordinary people, especially during winter," Timchenko says.

Kovalenko echoes the sense of mission about trying to keep the lights on. "Energy is the foundation of everything - people's lives, the state. Nothing can function without it. I've dedicated my entire life to this".

Many are choosing to leave the capital, or Ukraine altogether, to avoid months of bitter cold. Daryna, Kyryll and Olena know the winter has barely begun.

"It's the worst feeling," Kyryll says. "When I get home from school, I'm tired. I lay in my bed. Bam! Air alarm. Bam! No lights. Bam! A lot of homework. Bam!"

When the children are in bed Daryna confides her thoughts of moving to somewhere safer, or warmer. She's torn by the desire to stay at home - close to friends and relatives - and the worry of how unbearable life may become.

The strain is damaging her mental health, she tells me, and she fears the impact on Kyryll and Olena, who suffers nightmares. Still, Daryna remains defiant despite the darkness.

"I don't want to live without light. But actually people in Ukraine say, OK, without light, but without Russians. Yes, we're scared, we're scared a lot. But better for us to be without power, but [also] without Russians."

Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko, Kamila Hrabchuk and Daniel Wittenberg

item.title: Missing 11-month-old baby rescued after being buried alive in a crate in South Carolina
item.description: Officials say the child was found close to his father's home on Tuesday, a day after he was taken, and is being cared for in hospital.
item.content:encoded:
An 11-month-old baby has been rescued in South Carolina after officials say he was buried alive in a crate by his father.

Koah Sharpe had been missing since Monday when he was taken by his father, Michael Comer, 25, according to the Lexington County Sheriff's Department. Comer was arrested on a burglary charge on Monday evening but his son was not with him.

The baby was found on Tuesday "buried alive" and "clinging to life" not far from his father's house, Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said at a news conference. It is thought he had been there for 24 hours.

The child is now in hospital receiving care, Koon said, adding he was hopeful he would make a full recovery.

Police are still deciding what further charges to bring against the father.

The search for baby Koah began on Monday after his father took him from his mother's house.

Comer's mother was watching the child and had left her son alone with him briefly, Koon said, when he left abruptly with Koah.

Comer was seen travelling to multiple locations without the baby and was later arrested in Lexington County without Koah. A search party of 100 police and fire department officials were then sent to search for the child, the sheriff said.

He added that when they asked Comer where his son was, he "did not have much to say" about his whereabouts.

Koon said that rescuers searched the woods near Comer's house and saw some "freshly disturbed dirt". As they began to dig, they heard a baby crying - something the sheriff described as "the most joyful sound you ever heard".

"The race was on. Everybody was getting down there trying to get him out," Koon added.

He said the crate was wrapped in a towel that probably provided enough air for Koah to survive for as long as he did, while the cold weather kept him from getting too hot.

"The crate was, probably, I'm guessing about a two-foot [61cm] by two-foot dog crate. So, I think, once that crate hit the ground, he was probably up at least a foot from the top of that crate to the top of the ground," Koon explained.

Of the parents' relationship, the sheriff said there were "obviously some issues". Comer had previously pleaded guilty to domestic violence charges, court records show.

Comer's mother, Patricia Comer, told NBC News that Koah's mother had full custody of him but allowed her to supervise while her son watched him. She said her son had watched the baby before unsupervised without any problems.

"Honestly, I'm his mother, and I never expected this from him," Patricia Comer said.

item.title: Author says there were 'real concerns' about David Walliams within publishing industry
item.description: The comedian denies allegations of sexual misconduct, inappropriate behaviour and abusing his power more than 10 years ago.
item.content:encoded:
Author Chloe Combi has said she had heard rumours that there were "real concerns" about David Walliams's behaviour within the publishing industry more than a decade ago.

Combi told BBC News she had heard there were allegations about his "behaviour around young female staff" and says she was told in 2015 to warn schools that he was "not an appropriate booking".

An investigation by the Guardian and ITV News alleged that Walliams has been accused by several women of sexual misconduct, inappropriate behaviour and abusing his position, which he denies.

HarperCollins, which published Walliams's best-selling children's books, dropped Walliams last year after an investigation into his behaviour.

In response to the Guardian and ITV report, a spokesperson for HarperCollins said the company had decided not to publish any new titles by Walliams and that it took "employee wellbeing extremely seriously".

Walliams told ITV News and the Guardian that he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

Combi said she was getting invited to events such as book launches around the time one of her own books was being published, and was also running a scheme to bring "high-profile and inspiring writers and speakers" to talk in schools.

At an event in 2015, Combi said she got speaking to someone "quite senior" in publishing, who warned her about Walliams.

"We were talking about [the scheme] and possible writers who might be good for the project to work well with teenagers," Combi said.

"She gave me some great recommendations and said to me: 'Whatever you do, don't invite David Walliams, and FYI if you are speaking to head teachers or teachers, please inform them that he's not a good booking, not an appropriate booking for a school'."

Combi continued: "I obviously asked why, and to be honest I had already heard quite a lot of rumours because those worlds are quite small and contained.

"One of the things she said was that there had been real concerns about his behaviour around young female staff."

  • If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

Asked whether concerns about his behaviour was an open secret, Combi replied: "Yes definitely... and I'd heard it from people who worked in publishing, fellow writers, people kind of in celebrity and TV circles."

Combi said she never met Walliams herself, and said her information had come from "a number of people I was speaking to".

HarperCollins in September announced it would no longer be publishing his back catalogue.

The allegations against Walliams include:

  • One woman alleges she met Walliams at a fan event when she was 15. She says he groomed her and they had sex when she was 17
  • Another woman alleges she met Walliams for a coffee when she was 15, before going back to his house where he allegedly tried to lift up her shirt and commit an act that she now describes as a sexual assault
  • A woman who worked as a model in her teens accused Walliams of grooming her. A different woman who also worked as a model said Walliams tried to kiss her while showing her around his home
  • The investigation claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another
  • Other women allege inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room

In his statement to ITV News and the Guardian, Walliams said: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

Earlier on Wednesday, media minister Ian Murray said there is a "cultural problem" in the industry that needs to be "stamped out".

Giving evidence to the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee, Murray said he was "deeply saddened and also angry" to see the prevalence of abuse by men in the media industry.

Meanwhile, Minister for Women and Equalities Bridget Phillipson paid tribute to the "bravery" of victims who have shared their experiences in recent days.

Speaking in the Commons, she said: "Women and girls should never have to shrink our lives or ambitions because of outdated, misogynistic attitudes, and the appalling testimonies we have heard in recent days underline how much further we have to go."

Phillipson later said the government would "go further" on restricting the use of non-disclosure agreements, telling Sky News: "We cannot have a system where rich and powerful individuals, rich and powerful men, are able to silence women, buy their silence and stop things coming to light."

She said that she believed injunctions were being misused, and that her colleagues at the Ministry of Justice were looking at how the government can intervene to ensure this did not happen.

Comedian and podcaster Deborah Frances-White told BBC Radio 4's The World at One that young women are "definitely" still being exploited in the comedy industry.

She told the programme that perpetrators understand consent but they just enjoy the power that comes with ignoring it, adding: "The thrill is in the contravention of consent."

Asked whether she recognised the picture Russell Brand's conviction and allegations against Walliams had painted of the comedy industry, she said: "Yes, entirely."

She described an industry where she was asked to meet male producers in darkly lit rooms "walking a tightrope", having to make them feel attractive and avoid being assaulted as they influenced future employment opportunities.

She said these events are "definitely still going on" and that she is in a WhatsApp group with female comedians who share their experiences with each other.

Comedian Lucy Beaumont told Sky News that she was one of the people who spoke to the Guardian about allegations raised with her about Walliams.

Beaumont said she had been approached by a young TV worker who alleged inappropriate behaviour while working with Walliams on another show.

"This young person's job was to take young girls - he didn't think that they were children... he definitely knew that they were over 16 - he had to take them to Walliams's dressing room," she alleged.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Wednesday, Labour MP Jess Phillips said the behaviour alleged "needs to be stopped".

"What is described in the David Walliams story is an absolute modus operandi, a target group of women of a certain age, the kind of women who don't have the same amount of power as if you were doing this to a 35-year-old woman who might have a bit more about herself in the world," she said.

item.title: Missing sculpture returned with an apology and £100 charity donation
item.description: Police were investigating the suspected theft of the scrap metal bird from Eden Court Theatre in Inverness last month.
item.content:encoded:
A sculpture which disappeared from an art exhibition in a suspected theft has been returned with an apology and £100 donation to a charity.

Police were called after the scrap metal bird made by artist Helen Denerley vanished from Eden Court Theatre in Inverness last month.

It was due to be sold following the exhibition for the Scottish Mental Health Arts Festival to help raise money for Centred.

The mental health charity said the bird had "found its way home" along with a note of apology and a "generous donation".

The sculpture has an estimated value of £850.

Alana Kotrys, marketing and fundraising executive for Centred, said: "When we first realised the bird was missing, we said that we didn't know the full story and wanted to approach the situation with kindness and understanding.

"We're really pleased that things have ended this way."

She added: "Thank you to whoever returned the bird and made the donation.

"Your kindness means a lot, and it's a lovely reminder that there's always room for understanding and a positive way forward."

Denerley, who is best known for her large metal giraffes sculptures on Leith Walk in Edinburgh, was also pleased by the outcome of the appeal for the return of the missing piece.

She said: "Everyone I have told about the bird's return has had such a positive reaction.

"Thank you to the person who returned it."

item.title: Hegseth and team reprimanded by Army guard at solemn war memorial
item.description: The guard told the defence secretary and his companions to maintain an atmosphere of "silence and respect" during a Veterans Day visit.
item.content:encoded:
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and members of his team were admonished by an Army guard at the Arlington National Cemetery after he and his entourage appeared to violate the solemn war memorial's rules for decorum.

A video of the Veterans Day observance event shows Hegseth, his wife and senior advisers laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

The Army sentinel on duty then steps towards Hegseth and his group and yells: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."

Rules on etiquette at the cemetery dictate that visitors speak quietly and do not engage in disrespectful or disorderly conduct.

The tomb, which is one of the country's most sacred war memorials, marks the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in World War I.

A service member from the 3rd Infantry Regiment stands watch over the Tomb 24 hours a day and has done so since 1948.

"While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum," Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement.

"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored—and will always honor—the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe."

Earlier, President Donald Trump, Vice-President JD Vance and other top officials attended the annual wreath-laying ceremony at the cemetery.

During his speech at the ceremony, Trump offered his gratitude to uniformed service members who have fought for the country. He also touted what he sees as his administration's success in the Iran war.

"Under this administration, and it was about time, somebody fought back. All of us fought back," he said.

"And we won," Trump said of the Iran war. "It's just a question of when we want to end it. We want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93% victory."

Trump also pointed out Hegseth during the ceremony, saying he's done a "fantastic job" as defence secretary.

Trump has repeatedly defended Hegseth amid Democratic lawmakers' push to impeach him. On Tuesday, an effort to impeach the defence secretary under accusations that he waged war on Iran without congressional authorisation failed on Capitol Hill.

Hegseth has called the impeachment efforts a "farce" and a "stunt".

item.title: Democrat Scott Colom seals historic win in Mississippi Senate race
item.description: Colom is the first black person from the southern state elected to the US Senate in over 140 years.
item.content:encoded:
Democrat Scott Colom has won the US Senate race in Mississippi, delivering a shock victory for the party in a deeply conservative state that has elected Republicans for decades.

Colom's victory makes him the first black person from Mississippi to be elected to the US Senate in more than 140 years.

Only a few thousand votes separated him from his Republican opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.

The result means the Democrats will hold 55 seats in the 100-member Senate, with a knife-edge race in Alaska still to be called.

Colom won with 49.2% of the vote, while Hyde-Smith received 48.7% and an independent candidate got 2.1%, according to figures from CBS.

Hyde-Smith congratulated Colom in a video posted on X on Wednesday evening and wished him well.

"While this was not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said.

Dozens of people were gathered at the Mississippi HQ of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) in Jackson on Wednesday when Colom's victory was announced.

The room burst into deafening applause and cheers.

"This is an amazing result," said Leon Russell, chairman of the NAACP board.

"This is purely the work of particularly the black community," he continued. "There was not a whole lot of money, but there was a whole lot of organising.

"This is a historic election."

Across the room, filled with people embracing, Amber Thomas sat, revelling in the victory.

"When you fight, you win," Thomas said. "Right now, I am overwhelmed with joy."

The result wipes away a Republican winning streak in the Magnolia State that dates back to 1982.

The contest was never expected to be this close, with Hyde-Smith running for re-election in a state that President Donald Trump won in the 2024 election by more than 22 points.

But Democrats have scored a series of major wins in these midterm elections, taking control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate.

The party flipped Senate seats in Republican strongholds, including Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Iowa.

Polls suggest this was due in large part to voter frustrations with the economy and the Iran war under President Trump.

Colom appeared to a ride a national wave of resentment against Republicans.

Voter backlash against Trump's Republican party has been driven in large part by economic woes, blamed on his administration's tariffs and war with Iran, according to exit polls.

Colom, a local prosecutor, used the national mood to his advantage, highlighting his opponent's support for Trump's tariffs and giving her the nickname "Cindy High Prices".

The Democrat campaigned aggressively, visiting all of Mississippi's 82 counties.

Hyde-Smith's campaign assailed Colom as a puppet of billionaire liberal donor George Soros, whose family has helped fund the Democrat's political campaigns.

The Republican was criticised for a lack of public appearances.

item.title: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
item.description: Talks in Abu Dhabi centred around Europe's security framework, with US envoys due to meet Putin and Zelensky on Thursday.
item.content:encoded:
Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day.

Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion.

However, both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon.

Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team said that this round of talks - the first since February - "was one of the hardest."

"I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion," he said. But he added that he felt "good momentum" and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible.

Comments by Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky were less conciliatory. "Right now... a lot depends on Ukraine, on the position of the US, and on whether Europe comes to its senses," he said.

After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - President Donald Trump's son-in-law - would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky.

The meetings in Abu Dhabi had been framed as centred around the "security architecture" of Europe.

For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member.

For Moscow, a reworked "security framework" is likely to include a limit to the influence of Nato in eastern Europe - a central concern for the Kremlin since the alliance's eastward expansion.

Earlier this week Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while the Kremlin's Medinsky said the world needed a "new" and "fair" security system.

That framework would serve as "a new Yalta and Potsdam", Medinsky said, referring to the 1940s summits in which the victorious Allied powers carved up post-war Europe into spheres of influence.

Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.

Representatives of Britain, Nato and various EU countries were also in Abu Dhabi and met with US and Ukrainian negotiators, but the Kremlin - with whom the EU does not officially communicate - said its delegation had not had any contact with them.

Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.

Many - particularly in eastern Europe - feel their security is linked to that of Ukraine. Agreements cannot be implemented "if no consensus can be reached among Nato members," a German government spokesperson said on Wednesday.

Kushner said the US was keen to bring the Europeans on board and said that getting them "added to the format" would be on the agenda for his talks with Putin.

There is also disagreement on whether discussions on a future security framework should be preceded by a ceasefire, as the Europeans and Kyiv would want, or whether the fighting only stops after an agreement has been reached, as the Kremlin has insisted.

Any agreement on a peacetime security framework, however, is contingent on the war ending, Kushner noted. But that cannot occur "until there's an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues," he added.

Since talks began last year, a core obstacle to any settlement has been Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia. Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are essential to its security.

Moscow, meanwhile, has never backed down from its demand that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds. "Every inch" of land would be "returned to Russia one way or another", Medinsky said.

Kushner acknowledged that the territorial question remained the hardest, while Zelensky's chief of staff and negotiator Kyrylo Budanov refused to be drawn on whether Russia was still demanding a Ukrainian withdrawal from the region.

Later, Budanov admitted the talks had been "tough" and that Ukraine's priority was to ensure Russia could not attack it again.

"These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex," Kushner said. "The reality is there is no trust right now between the sides and that is to be expected after a conflict like this."

item.title: Police helped remove Russell Brand after 'violent incident' at Jemima Goldsmith's home
item.description: Police confirm they asked Brand to leave his ex-girlfriend's house after she reported an alleged assault.
item.content:encoded:
Police have confirmed they helped Jemima Goldsmith to remove ex-boyfriend Russell Brand from her property in 2014 after she claimed a violent incident took place.

Thames Valley Police said officers were contacted by an alleged victim and went to an address in Oxfordshire on 25 July 2014 but no arrests were made.

They listened to her concerns and gave support, and "also ensured the victim's partner left the address, as per the victim's wishes", the police added in a statement on Wednesday.

Goldsmith, who dated Brand for about a year, wrote on X on Monday that she "had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident" but chose not to press charges.

Brand was jailed for 10-and-a-half years for rape and sexual assault on Monday.

In her post, 52-year-old Goldsmith, who wasn't part of the trial, said she was "in awe of the courageous women who came forward at Brand's trial" and was "glad and relieved" he had "finally faced justice".

She wrote: "I have had my own personal experience of his violence, coercive control and abuse.

"I had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident."

The Press Association reported that Goldsmith had asked for Brand to leave the property, her wish was then communicated to him by police, and he agreed to leave the house.

Goldsmith added: "I chose not to press charges at the time and not to go public with this, as I was worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children.

"I have neither seen nor spoken to Brand since that period in 2014. Whilst my pain in relation to this, pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact."

She also said she had "assisted the journalists who finally exposed him", and had been willing to testify to his "abusiveness" if they were sued.

TV producer Goldsmith is also the former wife of ex-Pakistani prime minister and cricketer Imran Khan, the daughter of late billionaire entrepreneur Sir James Goldsmith and sister of ex-Conservative government minister Zac Goldsmith.

item.title: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent relocated after alleged Iranian threats
item.description: Bessent is now one of several Trump administration officials to live on military bases due to safety concerns.
item.content:encoded:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his Washington DC home to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life, according to US media reports.

CBS, the BBC's US partner, said the relocation came after a photo of Bessent's home was published in the Wall Street Journal.

Bessent has been at the forefront of efforts to isolate Iran economically through sanctions and a wider economic blockade.

While the exact nature of the threats against Bessent remain unclear, US intelligence has warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans, including US officials.

"After the Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase," a source told CBS.

Georgetown is an affluent part of Washington that is home to a number of government officials and prominent residents.

Those security concerns, the source added, prompted authorities to move Bessent to a military base in the area.

In a statement, a Treasury Department spokesperson said only that Bessent "will not be deterred" by threats and "remains committed" to the US effort to pressure Iran's economy.

The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

In September, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans.

The New York Times has reported that the Iranian effort includes the targeting of current and former US officials. One source told the newspaper this has "reached a more advanced stage".

Other US officials reportedly on Iran's list of potential targets include former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, former National Security Advisor John Bolton and Mark Milley, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

Milley and Bolton's security teams were taken away by the Trump administration shortly after he returned to office last year.

Bessent is one of a number of administration officials that live on military bases. The White House's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, was moved to a base in late 2025 - before the conflict with Iran began.

Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio both live on military bases, as did former Attorney General Pam Bondi and former intelligence chief Tulsi Gabbard.

The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.

In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a blockade targeting Iranian ports.

item.title: Four grizzly bears killed in Canada after fatal attack on mother and daughter
item.description: The sow and her three cubs were responsible for killing Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, earlier this month.
item.content:encoded:
Four grizzly bears have been killed in connection with a fatal attack on a mother and daughter in the Canadian province of British Columbia.

Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, died earlier this month after going on an afternoon walk in a trail area in Bella Coola.

The British Columbia Conservation Office Service (BCCOS) launched an investigation into their deaths and forensic testing has since confirmed a sow and her three cubs were responsible for the attack.

All four were destroyed "in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines" to protect the public, BCCOS Inspector Jeff Tyre said in an update on Tuesday.

"Evidence from the investigation as well as animal DNA was analysed and conclusively linked to a sow and its three offspring," he added.

The attack "likely involved predatory behaviour", which Tyre said was "very rare".

He added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the investigation over the past week, amid "difficult terrain and weather".

Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh, told CBC.

"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.

Tyre said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a school group also in the Bella Coola area.

The incident in November of last year saw 11 people injured, two of them critically, while the bear responsible was never found.

"Today, we have learned from the BC Conservation Officer Service members that they have captured and euthanized the bears involved in the recent fatal attack," said Samuel Schooner, Elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, in a statement.

"We would like to thank the BC Conservation Officer Service for their dedication and hard work to resolve this incident. This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack. Our thoughts remain with the victims' families."

item.title: Spain sees widespread disruption in first general strike for 14 years
item.description: Protests are also expected in the biggest cities less than three weeks before Spaniards vote in parliamentary elections.
item.content:encoded:
Transport and other public services across Spain have faced serious disruption in the first general strike for 14 years called by the main unions over housing and the high cost of living.

Demonstrations have taken place across the country, including in Madrid and Barcelona, where tens of thousands marched in the evening.

Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November.

The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Álvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant."

However, the Spanish Confederation of Business Organisations said participation was "low and uneven", depending on the areas and sectors involved.

Some of the biggest disruption on Wednesday was seen in the main industrial hubs of Madrid and the north-eastern region of Catalonia where traffic was halted on several main roads.

The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested for a variety of incidents and Spanish reports said estate agencies had seen attacks on their offices.

The strike was triggered by widespread protests over affordable housing and rising living costs, after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a flat in Madrid where she had lived for seven decades. She died in hospital weeks later.

Rental prices in the capital have soared in recent years. The monthly cost of a 50m sq apartment in Madrid was an average of €1,170 in October, according to property portal Idealista, while Spain's average gross monthly salary is about €2,460 (£2,056).

That amounts to nearly half the average gross salary, well above the 30% level of affordability often recommended by housing experts and public institutions.

Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called snap elections last month after parliament failed to approve his plan for housing reform.

Not since 2012, under the conservative government of Mariano Rajoy, has Spain held general strikes.

And while previous strikes have been problematic for the government in power, this one is different. Sánchez and his ministers have even encouraged workers to down tools and demand affordable housing.

"Your eight-hour day. Your pension. Your public healthcare… These were collective conquests," he wrote on social media, praising those who took part in previous strikes.

The conservative People's Party (PP), by contrast, has accused the government of attempting to weaponise the strike for electoral gain.

PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo called the general strike "nonsense", calling the unions "mafia" and "trash". Feijoo's party is leading in the polls and party spokesman Miguel Tellado accused the government of exploiting the strike to warn voters against allowing a right-wing government to be formed, which looks the most likely outcome of the 29 November election.

Sánchez told Spanish TV this week: "What is nonsense is to question the rights of workers to strike."

Among those taking part in the general strike was Gonzalo Álvarez, 27, who was visiting different picket lines in central Madrid.

Although he works in sales, he has been volunteering for a housing union that tries to protect tenants and makes them aware of their rights.

The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal at the end of September "was the little fire" that sparked this protest, he told the BBC.

Álvarez knew the 87-year-old, who had faced a tripling of her rent under new landlords, and says he was deeply upset by her treatment.

He rents a small, one-bedroom flat with his girlfriend, a dental hygienist, in the city's southern Arganzuela disrict. The couple pay €1,000 between them, which means each spends about half of their salary on housing, even before other bills.

"It's absolutely crazy… with the food, with the electricity, with the water, with gas."

He sees no way of getting on the property ladder: "You have to collect an insane amount of money to be able to buy a house. So with these salaries, it's impossible."

With current rent and purchase prices, he believes buying somewhere is "completely impossible".

However, the vice-president of the CEOE, Spanish biggest business association, Miguel Garrido, criticised the strike, complaining that businesses had little to do with the price of housing.

"This is not a strike for labour-related reasons, but rather for political ones, and it is closely linked to the early calling of elections," he said.

Demonstrations were planned for some of Spain's biggest cities later in the day and the scale of support will be widely viewed as an indicator of public discontent ahead of the election.

Another reliable indicator of support for strikes is the level of demand for electricity with Spain's industrial sector.

Power usage in Spain fell by 7.5% during the early hours of Wednesday, according to data from operator Red Eléctrica. During the last general strike 14 years ago, equivalent consumption was down by more than 15%.

item.title: In Mississippi, voters await cliffhanger Senate result with hope and frustration
item.description: Democratic voters tell the BBC their candidate is on the brink of history, while Republicans vent disappointment.
item.content:encoded:
Mississippi's nailbiting wait to find out who won the southern state's Senate race is nearly over a week after the US midterm elections, in a contest that could deliver their first Democratic senator in nearly four decades.

Scott Colom, the Democrat, holds a lead of about 2,500 ballots - less than 1% - over his Republican opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, according to the latest tally.

If he wins, Colom would become the Magnolia State's first black senator in over 140 years.

He would also pad the Democratic Senate majority-elect to 55 seats, with a knife-edge race in Alaska still to be called.

The Democrat's razor-thin advantage has defied political gravity in a conservative fortress that President Donald Trump won in 2024 by over 22 points.

State law holds that the deadline to certify results is this Friday, but thousands of postal and affidavit ballots remain uncounted.

Affidavit ballots are ones that were not immediately accepted because of a discrepancy such as lacking proper ID on election day.

In such cases, voters are asked to fill out a provisional ballot and return to resolve the issue. The deadline for both affidavit and mail-in ballots is on Tuesday.

State officials estimate between 12,000 and 20,000 affidavit ballots were cast. As of Tuesday morning, roughly 15,500 had been processed – a difference that could be enough to swing the race.

A Colom victory would wipe away a Republican winning streak in Mississippi that dates back to 1982.

It would add to a string of Democratic successes nationally this election, including a landslide majority in the House of Representatives.

Each party has sent teams of lawyers into Mississippi, setting up the possibility for legal challenges over the result.

As the sun began to set on campus at Jackson State University, a historically black college in Mississippi, students walking through the tree-shaded lawns spoke to the BBC about the race.

Many of them voted this year for the very first time. All of them said they had cast their ballot for Colom.

"I really feel like a change is what we need," 18-year-old Jamyria Dunn told the BBC.

"I've had some amazing days in my life," she continued, "but seeing Mississippi, this state in particular, turn blue, would really bring a light to my heart that people just would not understand."

Dunn's friend, Journey Moore, told the BBC how excited she would feel if Colom won, leaving his mark on African-American history.

"On a scale of one to 10, it's definitely 1,000," she said.

"I'm witnessing it, and I'm a part of it. It's pretty great."

The BBC also visited Brookhaven, in Lincoln County, where Hyde-Smith was born and where Trump won a whopping 72% of votes two years ago.

Party loyalty here was on stark display, with everyone saying either they didn't vote or they voted for Hyde-Smith.

No-one denied the cost of living had gone up, but few here blamed Trump or Hyde-Smith.

"It always seems, no matter who's in office, there's a spike in gas prices. There's always a war. Things are always going up and down," said Travis Powe, a 29-year-old logger who voted for Hyde-Smith.

Keith Scott, a Trump supporter, said both parties had been "attacking Trump at all angles, which was why we voted for him".

Still, Scott said the race in Mississippi was unexpectedly close because the president had not delivered during his second term.

"Trump and his administration did not hold up what they ran on. Bottom line," Scott said.

"And the people like me that voted for him the first two times, that saw the benefits in his first term, we've seen none of it in his second."

Down the street from the railroad tracks cutting through the centre of town was Lee Barry, also a lifelong Republican.

"The price on gas is really high, so that cuts into your pocket," Barry said. "And then you go into the grocery store, prices are high.

"You get your shopping cart, and you got five things in it, and it's 100 bucks before you get out of there.

"So, I think that hurt her a good bit," he said about Hyde-Smith, adding that he also thinks she "should have been out a little bit more" on the campaign trail.

The race was never supposed to be this close.

Colom appeared to be riding a national wave of resentment against Republicans, with the party suffering several defeats this election in typically conservative strongholds like Texas, Kansas and Iowa.

Voter backlash against Trump's Republican party has been driven in large part by economic woes, blamed on his administration's tariffs and war with Iran, according to exit polls.

Colom, a local prosecutor, used the national mood to his advantage, highlighting his opponent's support for Trump's tariffs and giving her the nickname "Cindy High Prices".

The Democrat campaigned aggressively, visiting all of Mississippi's 82 counties.

Hyde-Smith's campaign assailed Colom as a puppet of billionaire liberal donor George Soros, whose family has helped fund the Democrat's political campaigns.

The Republican was criticised by her opponents for a lack of public appearances.

Democrats accused her of insensitivity when she told voters worried about the price of beef that "you have so many proteins to choose from". The Colom team spun the remark into a viral attack ad.

The race also became competitive because of Mississippi's large black population, who are expected to have turned out in record numbers this election.

Early exit polls show the state's black voters, who historically vote Democrat, drifted even further to the left this year, giving Democrats 91% of their votes.

item.title: Acquitted 'China spy' tells BBC: I was fall guy for security services but also naive
item.description: Thousands of messages seen by BBC show how a Chinese official sought details of sensitive political matters.
item.content:encoded:
A British man who was charged with spying for China has told the BBC he was a "convenient fall guy" for UK police and security services who wanted to put espionage threats by foreign states "on the map".

Chris Cash, a former parliamentary researcher, has shared more than 6,000 messages with us revealing how a Chinese official sought information about sensitive political matters in the UK - including the 2022 Tory leadership battle to decide the next prime minister.

The messages show how Cash's friend in China, Chris Berry - with whom he had been sharing information - dramatically described a "secret" meeting between Berry and a high-ranking Chinese official.

Berry said he had been told that China was concerned about how a British MP it had sanctioned might be promoted to a cabinet role.

The messages also reveal how Cash used his friend as a reference during vetting for a parliamentary pass - which was approved.

Like Cash, Berry was also charged with espionage. The two men consistently maintained their innocence.

In Cash's first interview since his acquittal, which sparked a political row over the government's failure to designate China as a "threat", he says he would "never do anything" to harm UK national security.

But he admits he was "unprofessional and naive" to send "gossiping" texts to his friend, whom he met in 2018 when they both taught English in a school in China.

Although the trove of messages shows him discussing sensitive topics, there is no evidence in them that Cash was paid by, or sympathetic to, the Chinese Communist Party.

With the government having previously said that Chinese spies were targeting UK officials across the political, defence and business sectors with increasingly sophisticated espionage operations, Cash believes his case was pursued as a warning to others.

Berry declined to comment on this story, but at the time of his acquittal said he denied any wrongdoing and that he had been "unfairly subjected to a trial by media".

He said he had provided reports to a Chinese company, which he believed had clients seeking to develop trading links with the UK, and those reports contained no classified information and relied on public sources.

Cash returned to the UK in 2019, saying in his resignation message for his job in China that he felt "guilty sitting back and participating in a system that I am uncomfortable with".

He later became the director of a small policy group run by China-sceptic Conservative MPs in Westminster.

Meanwhile, Berry stayed in China writing reports for a large consultancy which, like many Chinese companies, has links to the government.

UK security services alleged that information from the men's messages, sent on the encrypted messaging app Signal between January 2022 and March 2023, had been passed to people linked to the Chinese state.

England and Wales' top prosecutor said the case had collapsed last autumn because government officials could not say China had been classed as an "enemy" at the time.

This prompted accusations of UK political interference to placate the Chinese government.

China has previously called the allegations of spying "pure fabrication and malicious slander".

'A psychological game of chess'

The most striking section of the messages handed to the BBC concerns Berry's account of his meeting in summer 2022 with a senior Chinese official who wanted to have "a more detailed co-operation".

In voice notes Berry describes how, beforehand, work colleagues had told him the official's interest had been piqued by reports Berry had written, which included details of the UK's foreign policy approach to China.

In the voice notes, Berry says he was initially aghast, but then decided: "I thought it would be interesting to go anyway… not really intending to do anything."

Berry tells Cash he was driven to a government-owned villa in a grand compound.

The experience "felt like a psychological game of chess" and "like a test", Berry says.

He kept his hands under the table as tea was served: "I didn't want it to be obvious if I was nervous. I tested to see if my hands were shaking first, then drank the tea."

Berry describes the senior Chinese official asking via an interpreter "about the situation in the UK at the moment, about the Tory leadership thing".

At that time, Boris Johnson had just resigned as the UK's prime minister, and a Conservative leadership battle was taking place, which Liz Truss would go on to win.

Berry says he jokingly tried to ask his host which candidate China wanted, but the interpreter did not translate his question.

"And then the main guy just shakes my hand like it's time to go," Berry tells Cash.

After receiving the voice notes, Cash replies via text the next day: "You, my friend, have just been elite captured" before adding: "You're in spy territory now".

In many media reports these particular messages, previously released in a government witness statement, have been presented as a smoking gun - evidence that Cash knew his friend was passing on information to the Chinese state.

But Cash insists it was a "tongue-in-cheek joke" because he knew his friend to be "a staunch critic of the Chinese Communist Party".

The next morning, he made a joke about Berry spying for the UK and getting in trouble with the Chinese authorities, he says. Cash texted: "Keep him sweet… We may have a use for you yet".

"I didn't believe he was knowingly spying on the UK through me," says Cash. "I trusted my friend… I wish I had seen the danger earlier, spotted it and cut off all contact."

'Bigger deal than I thought'

So who was the mystery official Berry had met?

"I found out who this guy is," Berry text-messaged Cash a few hours later. "Bigger deal than I thought."

Berry posted a link to the Wikipedia page of Cai Qi, who at the time was one of China's most influential politicians and is now, in effect, President Xi Jinping's chief of staff.

Whether Berry correctly identified his host remains unclear. He has since disputed the suggestion that he met someone as senior as Cai Qi.

What is beyond dispute is that he believed he may have met someone highly placed within the Chinese political system.

For Chris Cash, this unusual encounter did not prompt alarm bells. Asked why not, Cash tells the BBC: "Because I didn't think anything of the meeting, really."

We ask Cash why his friend might have been asked to such a meeting. "Strange things happen in China... you know we would often brush shoulders with sort of quite senior members of the Chinese communist party," he tells us.

Challenged about whether he had read the Wikipedia link at the time, Cash says he had "skimmed it", adding that it described him as a judge and a provincial-level official. "I just thought it was a weird meeting with a guy who'd taken an interest," he says.

Six months later, Berry said in text messages that "off the record" he had it "on pretty good authority" that China was considering dropping sanctions against Tom Tugendhat, one of the Conservative MPs in the China Research Group, where Cash worked.

Berry wrote that this would happen as long as the West "continued to show signals that they are willing to work together".

The Chinese believed it would be "extremely embarrassing" if Tugendhat became prime minister or foreign secretary while under Chinese sanctions, Berry said.

At the time of the meeting in summer 2022, China-sceptic Tugendhat was seen as a possible contender to succeed Boris Johnson, or become UK foreign secretary.

He was actually appointed as security minister by Liz Truss, and Beijing lifted sanctions on him in January 2026.

Was Cash concerned that Berry appeared to be passing information to him about Chinese foreign policy?

Cash says he assumed Berry had heard this "through the grapevine at his company" which was doing business with the UK.

He says he never doubted his friend's trustworthiness, to the extent he even named Berry as a reference on his application for a security pass for the Palace of Westminster.

The pass was granted and, a fortnight before their arrests in early 2023, Cash invited Berry to Parliament for lunch.

It was to be their final face-to-face conversation.

'Complete shock'

Cash was in bed at quarter to six on a March morning when he was woken by car doors being shut, he says. Within seconds, four UK counter-terrorism officers had barged into his bedroom at his parents' home in Edinburgh.

"They told me to sit up and not touch anything and then said I was under arrest for breaching the Official Secrets Act," Cash says.

"I was in complete shock… quivering... My mum was hysterical."

Cash says the officers dressed him in dirty clothes he had worn that weekend, handcuffed him and marched him down to an unmarked police car. He was later driven to London.

Chris Berry was also arrested the same day.

It remains unclear how, when and why British security services became interested in the exchanges between the two friends.

But they are likely to have found out far more about their relationship when Berry was stopped and questioned by counter-terror officers at Heathrow Airport.

His laptop and phone were taken - this may have enabled his Signal chats to be downloaded.

Berry later messaged Cash about it.

Cash says he had not been alarmed by this: "I thought it was just standard... for a guy who'd been in China."

As the investigation progressed, it became clear the authorities believed Cash and Berry had been involved in an informal, but dangerous, exchange of information that was "prejudicial to the safety and interests of the UK".

The allegations were based on 6,273 messages between the pair - the same ones Cash has now shared with the BBC. Cash's solicitor has told the BBC they are genuine.

They cover a period when Cash had joined the China Research Group (CRG), founded by Tugendhat and fellow Tory MP Alicia Kearns, and when Berry was working for a Chinese company called Strong, where part of his work involved writing political and economic reports for clients.

According to court documents, Berry was said to have compiled 34 reports for a man linked to the Chinese state spy agency, relaying information passed on to him by Cash. Strong did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

The CRG's office was across the Thames from Westminster, but Cash regularly had meetings in Parliament. Cash did not have government security clearance and there is no evidence he had access to classified documents.

Despite being thousands of miles apart, the two friends remained in close contact, often messaging daily.

The messages reviewed by the BBC show them discussing topics including sanctions on China, the tech company Huawei, human rights, Hong Kong, Taiwan and British foreign policy.

Cash says he used the Signal app for almost all his contacts with people in China - "more for their protection" - as he says discussing the government "could land someone… in trouble". He and Berry did not use the app's "disappearing messages" function.

Much of the information they discussed was publicly available, says Cash - who has given the BBC a detailed spreadsheet with links and references in an attempt to prove it.

But sometimes he did share with Berry his impressions from meetings and private discussions in Westminster. On 12 occasions in the messages, he labelled information "off the record" or "very off the record" before passing it on.

Cash says this was "just me excitedly sharing things that I was doing with him at work".

One message recounted views allegedly expressed in private by Britain's then-ambassador to China, Dame Caroline Wilson, during a discussion with the CRG about its work on China's influence on UK universities.

Cash also messaged Berry sharing unverified rumours about the sex lives of two UK cabinet ministers. There is no evidence Berry passed this to his Chinese colleagues.

Cash says he regarded such exchanges as routine political discussion. "We weren't working with classified information," he says.

Acquitted and 'traduced'

Cash was told by his solicitor the police investigation would blow over after six months and he would soon be able to return to normal life.

But in September 2023 - six months after the arrests - the case became public when the Sunday Times broke the story of an unnamed "spy" who had been arrested in Parliament.

Cash recalls travelling on a train while, around him, fellow passengers read the newspaper's front page story: "Commons 'Chinese spy' arrested". He says: "I wanted the world to eat me up."

Within 24 hours he was named and pictured in the press, and both men were later charged with espionage.

In September the following year, just weeks before their trial was due to begin, Cash received an unexpected call from his solicitor.

"Are you sitting down?" he asked Cash. "They've dropped all the charges."

His lawyers requested a court hearing for the prosecution to formally acknowledge that they would offer no evidence, but at the Old Bailey the newly-innocent Cash struggled to find anyone interested in his story.

At every previous court appearance he had been mobbed, but the press had not been informed about this hearing.

Eventually his team found a lone BBC journalist. "I said my piece outside the Old Bailey. And that was a real high point. I felt that I could start to move on with my life."

It wouldn't be that simple.

Across the city, House of Commons Speaker Lindsay Hoyle was seething. "It is this Parliament that has been spied on," he declared. "It is MPs' offices that have been infiltrated."

There would be days of political debate and a raucous prime minister's questions where Tory leader Kemi Badenoch would claim: "This all stinks of a cover-up."

"I'd been acquitted by law, but then I was traduced in Parliament," Cash says. "It was almost like I was convicted in the court of public opinion again, by people who I had worked with and trusted and that felt horrible."

Today Cash's life is almost unrecognisable. He has lost his dream job, his relationship, and his closest friend from university.

"We talked about being each other's best men," Cash says. Instead, when the friend got married last year, Cash was not even invited.

He is also no longer in contact with Berry.

"I've been applying for basic admin jobs and having trouble recently," Cash says.

"I'm angry and upset with how everything played out, and I do feel let down."

But when asked, Cash stops short of saying he feels Berry betrayed him. Does he think his friend was spying for the Chinese government?

"He would have to have his time in court to defend himself," Cash answers. "I think it'd be wrong of me to speculate and hypocritical given the speculation that I've been subject to. But we're no longer friends."

Berry declined to comment on this story, but at the time of his acquittal said his reports "concerned economic and commercial issues widely discussed in the UK at the time and drew on information freely in the public domain".

Like his former friend, Chris Cash is innocent in the eyes of the law, but his reputation has undoubtedly been trashed.

Many in Parliament still think they were spies. And with more of the messages between these former friends now revealed, the debate over their actions could be reignited.

"It was a gruelling ordeal," Cash says. "But I'm a fundamentally positive person… I'm positive about what the future holds."

item.title: Jonathan Ross 'horrified' by Walliams allegations and Brand conviction
item.description: The TV presenter says he was once "friendly" with David Walliams and Russell Brand, but was "genuinely unaware" of their conduct.
item.content:encoded:
TV presenter Jonathan Ross has said he is "horrified" by allegations of sexual misconduct against David Walliams and the rape conviction of Russell Brand.

In a statement, Ross said he was once "on friendly terms with both men", but that at the time he was "genuinely unaware of their conduct".

ITV News and the Guardian on Tuesday published reports alleging that Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women. Walliams denies all the allegations against him. Brand was sentenced to 10 years in jail for rape on Monday.

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said that the allegations against Walliams were the "latest in a long line of reported abuses of power" in the media.

Some of the women accuse Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers, or allege other inappropriate behaviour.

In a letter to journalists published by the Guardian, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

Ross is one of the country's best-known TV presenters, having regularly hosted celebrities on his Jonathan Ross Show, including David Walliams and Russell Brand.

He said he was "as horrified by the revelations about David Walliams and the crimes of Russell Brand as the rest of the nation".

He added: "My thoughts are with the many, many women who have bravely come forward."

The allegations include:

  • One woman alleges she met Walliams at a fan event when she was 15. She says he groomed her and they had sex when she was 17
  • Another woman alleges she met Walliams for a coffee when she was 15, before going back to his house where he allegedly tried to lift up her shirt and commit an act that she now describes as a sexual assault
  • A woman who worked as a model in her teens accused Walliams of grooming her. A different woman who also worked as a model said Walliams tried to kiss her while showing her around his home
  • The investigation claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another
  • Other women allege inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said on Tuesday: "These allegations are the latest in a long line of reported abuses of power in an industry where we have known for so long that the power imbalances are huge.

"Russell Brand's eventual conviction was a stark reminder that we are still far too reliant on the courage of brave women who choose to come forward despite knowing they will pay a heavy price and may not be believed - and a handful of persistent journalists who risk everything to tell their stories.

"Women must feel safe in their jobs, whistleblowers must be protected, and those who abuse their position must no longer be able to hide behind it."

Downing Street earlier called the allegations "deeply troubling".

  • If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

In the ITV documentary revealing the allegations, Jonathan Ross is pictured at an event also attended by a woman who later made accusations about the conduct of Walliams.

In his statement, Ross also addressed a joke he made at a comedy awards show in 2004, in which the punchline suggested Walliams would be "going home" with a 15-year-old.

Ross acknowledged the controversial quip and described it as "tasteless".

He added: "This joke was submitted to me by the Comedy Awards script writing team and I believed that the punchline was a reference to the fact he had publicly dated younger women, exaggerated for comic effect.

"Had I had any reason to suspect that it might be referring to actual events, I would not only have refused to use it, but I would not have felt comfortable continuing a personal or professional relationship with him."

Ross and Brand were also widely criticised for leaving lewd voicemails for Fawlty Towers actor Andrew Sachs, the grandfather of Georgina Baillie with whom Brand was in a consensual relationship in the mid-2000s, during a BBC Radio 2 broadcast.

Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years' imprisonment for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and the Metropolitan Police has confirmed several people have approached them about the disgraced star since his conviction.

Walliams rose to fame alongside Matt Lucas in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent, and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

A BBC spokesperson described the allegations as "serious" and said the corporation has removed Little Britain from BBC iPlayer.

Several women have spoken to the Guardian and ITV News as part of a joint three-year investigation by the media companies, accusing Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers. The investigation was published after Walliams lost a legal bid to stop the claims against him being made public.

One of the women now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault".

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Lilly Creightmore, who has alleged Walliams "groomed" her as a teenager, said she was "angry" at his behaviour.

She said that Walliams invited her to move in with him while she was "in between living situations". She was 18 at the time. She "felt instantly pressured to share a bed with him" but told him she was not interested in him in a romantic way.

After about a week of refusing Walliams's advances, Creightmore said "he started to become very moody and rude and cold".

According to ITV, Walliams says he did not act inappropriately and did not "target" her because she was "vulnerable" or "young".

TV agent Dermot McNamara, who has represented someone allegedly groomed by Walliams, told BBC Newsnight he had informed "authorities and broadcasters" about Walliams's alleged "inappropriate behaviour" but no action was taken.

Walliams denies all allegations, and in a statement to journalists shared by the Guardian said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".
